**`audit.passes` does not measure this.** It counts *amendments*, so a document can read `passes: 8`
and have never been attacked once - three of the rows above do. **The two are different things and the
frontmatter conflates them.**

Pass 1 (2026-09-02) took `third-party-middleware-inventory.md`: headline survived and improved,
attribution table overturned. Pass 2 took `authored-data-table-registry.md`: unreferenced-slot claim
overturned, span shown to be non-uniform. Pass 3 took `loot-drops-and-enemy-chain.md`: the
`% 100` universal survived exhaustive verification, AD-6 answered. Pass 4 took
`gambit-evaluation-and-enmity.md`: eight relation modes turned out to be eleven. Pass 5 took
the save-image doc: four-buffer count survived, the inter-image gap turned out to be occupied.
Pass 15 (2026-09-02) took `third-party-middleware-inventory.md` a second time, attacking the one claim
pass 2 had explicitly declined to test — *"at least eleven libraries"*. **BROKEN.** Both earlier
censuses enumerated the `CodeDomain.ThirdParty.*` family and reported it as the inventory of
third-party code; **111 functions carry bare-name tags with no `ThirdParty` token** (`EASTL` 72,
`Lua` +21, `Bullet` +18), so the query could not see them. Eleven libraries → **twelve**, 690 →
**801**, and **EASTL was absent from the document entirely**. The `ThirdParty.*` figures all
reproduced exactly — the arithmetic was never wrong, the boundary was. Pass 2 had re-run the *same*
scoped query and read the agreement as confirmation. **Standing lesson recorded: a selector copied
from the document under test cannot falsify that document; re-derive the selector, not just the
count.** The contradiction was already on disk — this category's `README.md` names the bare-name
families as its classification source, and `COVERAGE.md` estimated ~1,000. Three artefacts disagreed
and nobody had compared them.

**2026-09-02 — three sessions, one shared failure family.** Passes 15 (`repos-55`), and the blocks
delivered by `repos-f1` and `repos-94`, independently hit the same defect in three different
categories: **a population counted by its tag rather than derived from the image.** ThirdParty said
690 because it counted `ThirdParty.*` (true: 801). Static-init said 117 lazy magic statics because it
counted `CompilerGeneratedCpp.ThreadSafeStaticRecordAccessor` (true: **1,732 across 707 functions**,
counted at the `_Init_thread_header`/`footer` call sites). AO-5 said "differ by six" because it
compared two totals instead of two sets (true: **19 unnamed slots, 13 unslotted names**). In every
case the tag-derived number was self-consistent, plausible, and reproduced perfectly on re-running
the same query.

**The standing rule this produces:** *a count is only as wide as its selector, and a selector taken
from the artefact under test cannot falsify that artefact.* Re-derive the population from the binary
— structurally where possible — and state the selector next to the number. `repos-94`'s block is the
model: it re-derived the funclet population from `.pdata`→`FuncInfo` (magic check passing on all
4,518 records) rather than re-selecting the tag, **and that is the only reason it found six genuine
funclets the tag does not cover.** A prefix query would have returned 3,895 and been read as
confirmation.

**Two instrument defects recorded the same day, both found by their own authors.** `repos-f1`'s
first arity measure counted pops only, scored 60 % on `begin` callbacks, and would have supported a
false conclusion; counting **net** stack effect (pops minus pushes) scored 75/76, because
`camerasync` pushes 0 and immediately pops it and `setforcefight` does three push/pop round trips.
`repos-94`'s first address-taken sweep disassembled `.text` linearly from one start address, returned
0 hits for everything **including two known-positive controls**, and was numerically identical to the
correct answer for entirely the wrong reason — it had desynchronised in the first few bytes. Re-run
per function from each entry point, the controls fire. **A measurement that returns the right number
for the wrong reason is the hardest kind to catch; both were caught only because a positive control
was included.** Include one.

**Passes 130 and 131 (`repos-46`, 2026-09-02) — both targets overturned, nine corrections.** Details
in the two documents' §10 and in `_inbox/repos-46.md`. The headline results are recorded at the top
of the **K** and **L** sections of `OPEN-QUESTIONS.md`; the two that generalise beyond their subjects:

*Movement.* The walk formula was a **spherical** decomposition, not a planar one — `cos(pitch)`
foreshortens both horizontal components, so an actor on a slope covers less ground per frame at the
same requested speed. A planar branch recovers the old formula, which is why the wrong reading held.
**The GFZ annotation makes the identical omission**, and the pass named why that is not corroboration:
*two sources agreeing is not two pieces of evidence when one came from the other's neighbourhood.*
Separately, **K-5 was a dropped line, not a missing code path** — the `X` term is written
`*candidate_or_delta` while its siblings use `[1]`/`[2]`, so an excerpt matching the indexed form
lost it, and "the X term is missing" was promoted to an open question instead of being re-read.
**An open question can be an artefact of how a body was excerpted.**

*Instruments disagreed, and it changed a conclusion.* Ghidra's call graph reports `FUN_0023A520` —
the only writer of the spawn `39/42/43/180/1` defaults — with **zero callers**. An independent
capstone census over exact body extents found one: a ScriptVM **thunk**. Ghidra models thunk
forwarding; capstone counts the `jmp`. The same difference explains `003A1960` at 7 callers versus 8
sites. **Had only the graph been trusted, the document would say the default installer is
unreachable.** The correct reading is stronger and stranger: those radii are *script-installed, not
engine constants*, the globals are BSS, and a zone that never calls the installer runs with all-zero
radii (**L-10**). Where two instruments model the binary differently, a disagreement is a finding —
not noise to average away.

**Structural regression, found and fixed the same day.** `GHOST ADDRESS` had been zero in every prior
pass. `repos-46`'s re-run returned **10 ghosts and 1 body drift across three documents it had not
touched** — all newly written that day, all by other sessions, and every ghost the same defect: a
`.data`/`.rdata` address placed in a `§3 Key addresses` table, which asserts "this address is a
function" and carries a body-size column. Seven were in `Animation-Channel-Binding`, two in
`Bullet-Physics-Integration` (both `repos-55`), one plus the drift in `Exception-Handling-And-Unwind`
(`repos-94`). `repos-55`'s three were corrected immediately by splitting each document's §3 into a
function table and a separate **Data addresses** block with no size column, and re-running the audit:
**3 ghosts → 1**, the remainder being `repos-94`'s. The rule is now in `_templates/SYSTEM.md` §3 with
the reason attached, because the failure is invisible to the author — a data address in that table
looks like diligence. Note the parser detail that makes it easy to reintroduce: the check matches a
`<digits> B` token in the second cell after the address, so writing `336 bytes` is safe where
`336 B` is not.

**Mutation gate, 2026-09-02 — the first batch that was refused in part.** `repos-94` proposed six
rows of `CompilerGeneratedEH.ExceptionFilter`, evidenced as *"declared SEH filters in
`__C_specific_handler` scope tables"*. **A scope table is `.xdata` — an EH map — and the mission bans
that class of evidence absolutely; it is what cost a prior branch 182 classifications.** Every row
was therefore re-judged on its complete body with the scope table disregarded, and the batch did not
survive intact:

- **Accepted, tier 1–3, body-only:** `008A5B7C` (`return *(int*)*p == 0xC0000005` — the canonical
  `EXCEPTION_POINTERS->ExceptionRecord->ExceptionCode` filter shape) and `008A5B94` (calls the
  qualified CRT symbol `_seh_filter_exe`).
- **Accepted but relabelled:** `008A5BB2` and `008A5BDE` call `__ArrayUnwind`. They are **unwind
  scaffolding, not filters** — the proposed `ExceptionFilter` label would have been wrong on both.
- **Refused:** `0089BEF0` is `return 0xFFFFFFFF` and `008A5AD0` is a bare forwarder. `-1` is
  *consistent* with `EXCEPTION_CONTINUE_EXECUTION` and proves nothing; a forwarder proves nothing.
  Both would have rested entirely on the banned table. **Their existing shape tags are honest, and an
  honest shape label beats a wrong semantic one.**

Two further corrections fell out. The proposal described the six as carrying *"no
`CompilerGeneratedEH` tag"*, and the first merge into `OPEN-QUESTIONS.md` rendered that as
**untagged**. **All six already carry a CodeDomain tag** — these are re-classifications that move the
ledger by **zero**. "Carries a different tag" and "carries no tag" differ by exactly the thing that
decides whether coverage changes. And the four accepted rows were **not applied**: a four-row
re-classification does not carry enough understanding forward to justify a mutate → pack →
fresh-import → re-certify cycle, so they are staged in `Tools/work/pending_batch/` for the next
substantial B-1 batch.

**A related tooling fact, established the same day.** `repos-f1` asked for `00267DB0` to be renamed
`VMValueStack_PopFloat32Coerce`, the GFZ name `VMValueStack_PopNumericDiscard` being simply wrong —
the function returns a float in xmm0 on all four exits and callers consume it. **The sanctioned
pipeline has no rename script**: its only writers are the two `ApplyCurrentBodyCodeDomainBatch`
variants, which write CodeDomain tags. Renaming through the GUI would mutate outside the gate and
invalidate the snapshot hash every verification depends on. Recorded in `NAME-EQUIVALENCES.tsv`
instead, following pass 131's *"recorded, not renamed"* precedent. **Working names are a
documentation concern; the GZF is not the place to fix them.**

**The counting family, third instance — and the sharpest statement of it.** `repos-94` closed BK-1
by correcting `117` → the real census, then immediately found that its own replacement figure was
also a count of the wrong noun. **1,732 is a count of `_Init_thread_header` *call sites*; the number
of *objects* is 1,681.** Nineteen guards appear at more than one site, where the compiler inlined one
accessor into several callers, which accounts for the 51 difference exactly. So the day produced the
same defect at three levels: a tag population read as a mechanism census (117), a site count read as
an object count (1,732), and two totals compared instead of two sets (AO-5). Every one was internally
consistent and reproduced on re-running.

**The important part is what this says about the limits of Phase D.** The static-init document had
already survived **four** falsification passes. None of them was negligent and none *could* have
caught the defect: each re-checked the claims the document made, and the document was consistent with
itself throughout. **A population error is not broken by a better audit of the document — only by
counting the mechanism independently.** That is a real gap in the audit protocol as practised, and
the remedy is procedural rather than diligence: *any claim of the form "there are N X" must state
what was counted and how the population was derived, and a pass must re-derive the population, not
re-check the claim.*

Also kept, because it is fairer to the original author: **117 was a true subset, not a wrong label.**
Every function tagged `ThreadSafeStaticRecordAccessor` really does hold a lazy static — the tag fires
precisely when the accessor *is* the whole function. The other 590 holders have one buried inside a
larger routine and were labelled by what that larger routine looks like. The original number was not
careless; it was the honest answer to a narrower question than the one the document appeared to ask.

**An ID collision of the coordinator's own making, caught by the same reading.** `repos-94` reported a
correction against "BI-3", which in this ledger is a PostEffects question — because `repos-55` had
opened a new `BI.` section while `BI-1`..`BI-16` were already in use in the `AQ.` section and cited
throughout this log. The new section was renamed to `BK.` and its inbound references fixed. **The
peer's report was wrong about the ID and right about the substance; checking the file rather than
acting on the report is what separated the two.**

### A ledger body extent can over-run the function — database-wide caveat

Found by `repos-f1` on 2026-09-02 while measuring verb arity. `00350320` is given **56 bytes** in the
ledger. The real function is **11 bytes**, ending in a tail jump; then `int3` padding; then a
**different function** at `00350330`. An instrument walking a function as `entry + body_bytes` reads
the second function's code as part of the first — **and the result looks like ordinary code, because
it is ordinary code, just not that function's.**

This generalises past arity measurement to **anything** that walks bodies by extent: the capstone
censuses, the structural funclet enumeration, clone detection, and `audit_crossrefs.py`'s own
`BODY DRIFT` check, which compares a stated size against the same extent it would need to distrust.
The mitigation `repos-f1` used is cheap and should be standard: **stop at the first `int3` following
a terminator.**

Spot-checked against `repos-55`'s three published documents the same day — `005C72A0` (ret at
`005C7929`, padding after) and `005C0820` (ret at `005C0B5A`, padding after) both terminate exactly
at their stated extent. **So the defect is real but not universal; extents must be checked, not
assumed sound and not assumed broken.**

### Four more instrument defects, all from the same author, all producing plausible numbers

`repos-f1` reported four defects in its own measurements across two blocks, every one of which
returned a believable figure rather than an obvious failure:

1. **Counting pops instead of net stack effect** — 60 % where the truth was 75/76.
2. **Over-eager ambiguity filters** — a loop elsewhere in a body does not make argument reads
   ambiguous, and a call to a function that cannot reach a value-stack primitive cannot change the
   net (only 1,245 of 38,161 functions can reach one). Removing both took the sample from 646
   unmeasured to 1,128 rows at 99.3 %.
3. **Path-insensitive counting** — `maskopen` is an if/else where *both* arms pop once; summing
   sites gives 2 against an arity of 1, and `sethpmenu_436` came out exactly doubled. Fixed with
   per-block net plus an all-paths-agree requirement; 41 rows genuinely differ between paths and are
   now marked **unmeasurable** rather than carrying whatever the sum produced.
4. **The over-running body extent above.**

**Every one was caught the same way — by reading the individual rows that disagreed with an
independent source, rather than by inspecting the aggregate.** An aggregate cannot report its own
bias. That is now the third distinct mechanism by which today's work produced a wrong-but-plausible
number, alongside the tag-population family and the truncating regex.

### Why the opcode rotation could survive a falsification pass

`repos-f1`'s account of BF-7 is worth keeping as method rather than as a result. The mnemonic blob is
laid out **in table order**, so walking the `+8` pointers yields a clean contiguous sequence, and
**every check one would naturally run on a name column passes**: contiguity, distinctness, all in
`.rdata`, one per record. **Nothing inside the name column can reveal a rotation of the column.** It
is visible only by leaving it — comparing names against the lengths in the same records, against a
handler body, or against `ff12-script`. The earlier pass compared the name column against itself,
and it was self-consistent, because it was.

Two symptoms were **already written down** — the unreferenced `'NOP'` and record `0x63`'s non-pointer
`+8` — and they are the exact predictions of a one-record rotation: one dangling string at each end.
**They sat in the ledger as curiosities for a whole pass instead of being read as the test.** The
engine reads the length column at 22 sites and never reads the mnemonic column at all, which is why
a rotated name table could ship without anything breaking.

### A decompiler's argument list is a claim about a signature, not a signature

`repos-94`, 2026-09-02, on answering its own **BJ-4** and finding the question's premise wrong. The
question asked what the `typeId` constants passed to `00632960` mean. **There is no type id.** Ghidra
printed `(undefined8, longlong*, undefined8, undefined8, undefined4, undefined4, int, undefined8)`
and the author supplied the nouns without reading the callee: **two of three were wrong, and wrong in
a way that looked right** — `0x20` is a plausible size, `0x12` a plausible enum. The fifth argument is
a **byte offset**, the sixth an **attribute bitfield**, and the type is the *third* argument, a
pointer.

**What caught it was cheap and structural, and is reusable:** sort the recovered values per class and
see whether they form a *layout*. Floats 4 apart, pointers 8 apart, two single-byte fields in adjacent
bytes. **A size column cannot produce that.** This belongs beside the 127-byte-function test from pass
132 — both are free, structural checks that a printed reading is physically possible.

It also produced the day's cleanest independent corroboration: attribute **bit 0** means *the name
string is heap-copied and must be freed*, derived here from the **construction** side, while the
existing class-descriptor document had reached the same bit from the **teardown** side (its helper
tests byte `+0x28` bit 0 before freeing the string, and `+0x28` is where `00632FB0` stores the
attribute word). **Two sessions, opposite ends, same bit** — that is corroboration in the sense the
evidence standard means, unlike two sources one of which came from the other's neighbourhood.

And the refusal is as valuable as the finding: bits 3–4 are constant per class in all 146 measured,
which makes "descriptor template kind" the obvious reading. It was **tested and refuted**
(`PClassDescriptorConcrete` takes all three values, 229/118/21) and filed unresolved as **BL-1**
rather than written up as a plausible sentence. An extraction artefact was ruled out too — 339 of 484
resolved values come from non-first registrations, which constant hoisting could not produce.

### Pass 133 — a census is right for the set it measured and wrong for the sentence it is written into

`repos-46`, 2026-09-02, on `character-render-object.md`. **All three overturns share one shape**, and
it is worth more than any of them individually:

- *"11,874 bytes of method code"* — **the document's own §3 table sums to 11,879.** The headline was
  short by exactly 5, the size of slot 29, the one method living outside the class's `001Fxxxx`
  cluster. The total was taken over the clustered slots with the outlier dropped **and the exclusion
  never stated.**
- *"the ready flag has one writer"* — it has **two**. The census ran across the **vtable**, and the
  constructor is not in the vtable. The conclusion is unharmed and the evidence is now *better*: an
  explicit `+0x4B4 = 0` at construction supports "ready flag" more strongly than relying on the
  allocator's zero-fill.
- *"reads within the first 12 instructions: 12 of 12"* — thirteen readers, and one is not a gate
  (slot 16 reads it at instruction 118 inside a submission loop). **That sentence contradicted the
  "reads: 13" two lines above it in the same block** — a block that disagreed with itself and had
  stood unchecked.

**Each number was correct for the set it measured — the clustered slots, the vtable, the gate-shaped
readers — and wrong for the sentence it was written into, which spoke about the class.** This is the
same shape as the ScriptVM superlative in pass 128 and it is now three sightings. *State the
population beside the number, or the sentence will silently widen it.*

**And an instrument caught before it produced a fourth overturn.** A scan for the highest displacement
on any non-RIP base returned `+0x10D9`, which would have overturned the documented `+0x664`. It was on
`rax`, holding a *different object* inside slot 16. Re-run with a bounded `this`-tracker the answer is
`+0x664` exactly, with `+0x654/+0x634/+0x624/+0x614` beneath it — a coherent tail. Pair this with the
noise-floor rule from the funclet block: **that one covers scans too broad in DECODING, this one
scans too broad in ATTRIBUTION. A scan that is too broad invents a finding exactly as readily as one
that is too narrow misses one.** Both are cured by characterising the instrument before believing it.

`BB-5` closed: `FUN_001F51E0` is the class's **destructor body**, not a second construction site.
`BB-1` upgraded from *"no draw call has ever been traced"* to a bounded negative — the 31 methods
call 46 real functions at one hop and **the complete named set is CRT and nothing else**; no graphics
API entry point anywhere. That does not prove the class never causes a draw, it says whatever draws
is not reached in one call, and it points the next search at the record array's dispatcher (**K-10**).

### A claim measured over the resolvable subset is a claim about the instrument as much as the binary

`repos-94`, 2026-09-02, breaking its own claim on closing **BL-4**. It had recorded that Phyre
attribute bits 3–4 are *"constant across every field of a class in all 146 classes measured."* With a
forward abstract interpreter resolving **680 of 682** sites instead of 467, it is **243 of 246**, with
three genuine counterexamples.

**The sample was not biased in any way anyone could have spotted — it was simply the subset the
instrument could resolve.** The tell, visible only afterwards: the attribute value `0x00` occurs 196
times in the full data and had **never been seen at all**, because those were exactly the sites that
failed to resolve. A silent resolution failure does not look like missing data; it looks like a
cleaner population.

This is the counterpart to the tag-population family. Those were *"I counted the wrong noun"*; this is
*"I counted the noun I could reach."* Both produce a self-consistent number that survives re-running
the same query. The remedy is the same: say what the population was, and what fraction of the intended
population it covers.

**And the instrument was checked against its predecessor rather than believed.** Field by field:
**0 disagreements, 0 losses** — all 484 attribute, 523 offset, 593 class and 629 type values
reproduced identically, plus 491 new. *"A rewritten extractor that just resolves more is the exact
shape of a tool that has started guessing."* Two bugs surfaced during that check and **both produced
quiet wrong answers rather than errors**: an assignment that stored `None` when the source was
unknown, and a `ret` handler placed below an `if not ops: continue` guard so it never ran — whose
visible symptom was *"accessors returning a fixed object: 0"*, which is the kind of zero that reads as
a finding. Sixth instrument defect in the run; sixth to produce a plausible number rather than a
failure.

### Decompiler array indices transcribed as byte offsets — a new defect class, and it is checkable

Found by `repos-94` in `class-descriptor-and-metadata-system.md`. Its §2 and §4 give the
`PClassDescriptor` layout with four intrusive lists at `+0x10`/`+0x12`/`+0x14`/`+0x16`, class name at
`+0x0C`, counter at `+0x1D`. **Those are qword indices, not byte offsets** — the decompiler prints
`param_1[0x10]` on an `undefined8 *`, and the index was transcribed straight into a layout table. In
bytes the lists are `+0x80`/`+0x90`/`+0xA0`/`+0xB0`, class name `+0x60`, sub-object `+0x70`, counter
`+0xE8`, confirmed independently by the attach path and by the reset helper `0063D550` — which
re-initialises **six** lists, so there are two more at `+0x50` and `+0x60` the destructor never walks.

**A modder using `+0x0C` as a byte offset reads the wrong memory**, which is why this is worth a class
of its own rather than a footnote. It is the same species as `GHOST ADDRESS`: *a printed reading that
is not physically what it claims to be.* The structure described is correct; only the unit is wrong,
so it was corrected in place with a marked block rather than by rewriting the table.

**It is mechanically checkable and should be**: a layout block whose consecutive "offsets" differ by 1
or 2 while its fields are described as pointers or lists is almost certainly indices. Any document
transcribing decompiler array subscripts can carry this. *(Built the same day as
`check_layout_units.py`.)*

### Pass 134 — the interpreter survived, re-derived without the source that corrected it

`repos-46`, 2026-09-02. The brief was to attack `worldactor-scriptvm-interpreter.md` using a test its
rewriter had **not** used, since §11's correction rested on `ff12-script`. It excluded that source
entirely and re-derived the opcode rotation from the PE image and the interpreter's own body. **Zero
claims overturned.**

**The rotation closes arithmetically, and only under the rotation.** Records `0x00`–`0x62` carry
mnemonic-shaped strings and record `0x63` holds `0x0A`, not a pointer. Rotated, those 99 strings name
opcodes `0x01`–`0x63` and `'NOP'` at `00D11A10` — immediately before record 0's `LABEL` at `00D11A14`
— names opcode `0x00`: **exactly 100 names for exactly 100 opcodes, no remainder.** Unrotated you get
99 names for 100 opcodes *plus* an orphaned string: one opcode unnamed, one string unexplained. Only
one alignment balances.

**And the mechanism by which it shipped is now measured rather than asserted.** A displacement scan
across all 38,161 bodies finds the descriptor table touched by **exactly one function in the binary**
— the interpreter — at 22 sites, **every one of them `+0x00`**. Not one instruction anywhere reads
`+0x08`. *A column no code reads is a column nothing can keep honest.*

**Three mechanisms the document did not have**, all with consequences beyond it:

- **Suspension is a program-counter rewind.** The interpreter modifies `r14` by an instruction length
  at 25 sites: 4 advance, **21 rewind**. A handler that must wait subtracts the length of the
  instruction it just executed, so on re-entry the VM re-fetches and **re-executes the same
  instruction**. There is no continuation and no resume state. **Any side effect performed before the
  decision to wait repeats on every retry** — a live hazard for anyone hooking a script command, and
  for XIIOnline it means a replicated script step can fire its effects repeatedly on one client.
- **The operand pre-decode is off by one from the length bands.** Operands are decoded for opcodes
  `>= 0x47`; the length-3 band begins at `0x48`. Exactly one opcode falls in the gap — `0x47`,
  length 1 — and the VM reads two bytes past its end. It never manifests because `0x47`
  `LONGCODESTART` is inert and the operand is discarded. **That is a fourth independent argument that
  `0x47` really is inert: were it live, this would be a shipped bug.**
- **The third shared-handler group settles the names.** There are 92 distinct jump-table targets for
  100 opcodes, so exactly three are shared. §11 cited two. The third is the six inert opcodes — and
  *rotated*, that group contained `PUSHA` and `PUSHV`, which would make this a stack machine whose
  PUSH instructions do nothing. Corrected, it is six markers and pseudo-ops. **All three groups: 0/3
  coherent rotated, 3/3 corrected**, from engine data only.

**The one defect: a document disagreeing with itself.** §7 ticks `BF-2` answered and §10 answers it,
while §4 still read *"What `FUN_0025D740` does is not established. BF-2."* — a stale sentence left
behind when the answer landed in a later section. Identical in shape to `character-render-object.md`'s
*"12 of 12"* against *"reads: 13"* found the same morning. **Append-only correction sections make this
the characteristic defect of a heavily-revised document**: the correction is written where it was
discovered and the original statement stays where it was. Proposed and now built as
`check_answered_not_established.py`.

### Attribution failures, third of the session — and the rule they produce

`repos-46` again, and this one is a **near-miss it caught itself**. Reading from a mid-function
address it found `sub r14, rax` where §10 quotes `add r14, rax`, and nearly reported the document as
having inverted the program counter — which would in turn have made §6's advice wrong. **The document
was right; it was reading a different site.** There are 22 descriptor lookups in a 14,646-byte
function, and §10 quotes the one at `0x25E631`, followed by `add r14, rax` at `0x25E641` exactly as
written.

With `+0x10D9` from an untracked register and 37 phantom callees from counting `JMP imm`, that is
**three instrument attribution failures in one session, none of them a decoding failure**, and each
would have produced a confident wrong correction to a correct document.

> **When a document quotes assembly, identify which site it quotes before concluding it is wrong.**
> In a function containing 22 copies of one idiom, *"the binary says otherwise"* is a claim about
> which copy you happened to read.

### A correction derived from the artefact being corrected is not a correction

`repos-94`, 2026-09-02, retracting its own correction from the previous block — and it failed in
exactly the way it was written to warn about.

Having correctly established that `class-descriptor-and-metadata-system.md` transcribed **qword
indices as byte offsets**, the same note asserted that *"the class name is at byte `+0x60`, the
sub-object at `+0x70`, the counter at `+0xE8`"*. Those figures were obtained by **multiplying that
table's own mislabelled indices by 8** — arithmetic performed on the very table under correction —
and stated as fact. `+0x70` and `+0xE8` survive, because they appear directly in the destructor's
operands. **`+0x60` does not.** It is a sixth intrusive *list*, cleared by a list-unlink helper, not
the "embedded-string destructor" the original table called it. The type name is a `char *` at
**`+0x30`**, loaded by `006388C0` as `mov rsi,[rcx+0x30]` with an early return when null.

**So the original table was wrong about the *kind* as well as the unit, and the correction inherited
the error by trusting its labels while fixing its arithmetic.** Fixing one axis of a wrong statement
leaves a statement that is still wrong and now looks verified.

### Two scans discarded for failing their own controls

Same block, and both worth recording because the discipline is what makes the rest believable.

To settle whether anything inserts into a particular list, a scan for the circular-insert idiom
returned **nine candidates** — and was thrown away, because the identical test against the pair the
attach function *demonstrably* uses did not return the function that uses it. **An instrument that
cannot find the case you already know about cannot be trusted on the case you do not.** A broader
variant returning 159–425 functions per list was dropped earlier still: that displacement is shared
by thousands of unrelated structs and has no discriminating power.

The block also produced the strongest confidence a static reading can get. Descriptor virtual slot
`+0x50` is a **default-value constructor**, and for `VPLight` every value it writes lands on an offset
the schema recovered independently *from the registration side*, with values that are semantically
right for the field named there: `m_outerConeAngle` = `0x3EC90FDB` = 0.3927 rad = **22.5°**,
`m_intensity` = **1.0f**, `m_outerRange` = **FLT_MAX**, both object pointers null. **A wrong offset
table would not produce sensible defaults at every slot.** It is a second derivation from an
unrelated function rather than a re-reading of the same one — and it is still static, so **BL-7 (one
live read) remains the outstanding verification.**

### Address adjacency, wrong in both directions, inside two blocks

`repos-f1`, 2026-09-02, correcting its own block-4 clustering while answering **BQ-13/BQ-14**. Both
errors were the same banned inference:

- **Merging.** The shared page was reported as *"one 660-byte buffer with 215 writers"*. It is three
  separate 64-byte row blocks, a 20-byte hot spot, a 148-byte area with **one** writer, and isolated
  slots.
- **Splitting.** The page was reported as **13 objects**. Re-derived from **writer-set overlap** it is
  **62**. The earlier count coalesced write targets whose addresses lie within 8 bytes.

**Adjacency splits one object into many when access is byte-wise, and merges many into one when they
are packed** — and neither failure announced itself in the number. The corrected method uses *who
writes it*, not *where it sits*.

What replaced the clustering is the right kind of evidence: `003970A0` (44 bytes, and it does nothing
else) performs four `movups` loads at `022D91B0/91C0/91D0/91E0` and stores them to `dst+0x00/0x10/
0x20/0x30` — **four consecutive rows copied out as one 64-byte block, which fixes a 4×4 matrix from
the engine's own code** rather than from anyone's grouping. And the boundaries that *could not* be
proven were filed as **BQ-16** rather than published: rows are accessed in runs of 4, 6 and 8, so a
sliding window makes every 16-byte offset look like a base.

**The ownership finding is a genuine addition to the database's vocabulary.** 144 of the 152 owned
writers are Presentation, which invites *"Presentation owns it and the rest borrow"*. Three tests say
no: no other owner keeps a private sub-area (ActorEntity, UI and Movement write **zero** slots
Presentation does not also write); the only whole-area initialiser is **unowned**; and **exactly one
function in the image reads a row it did not write**. It is an **argument-passing area** — write your
operands into the shared rows, call the shared routine, read the result back. A *memory* calling
convention, which is what an engine descended from fixed vector-unit register banks would look like,
and structurally the same idea as the verb-to-verb hand-off one layer up.

Note also what the author refused to argue: **the head count is deliberately not the evidence.**
Inferring ownership from a population of users is the same inheritance error this database bans for
callers. *A parameter area cannot be owned, because nothing is held in it.*

**And for the third time in a day, cross-checking against an existing document is what stopped an
over-claim.** `rng-streams.md` already documented `022D9138`; its writer set is two and no float
instruction ever touches it, so it is not workbench data — and noticing that is what forced the look
that broke "one 660-byte buffer".

### Pass 135 — a document that cites slot numbers without citing its vtable cannot be checked

`repos-46` on `game-application.md`, 2026-09-02. **Six claims overturned**, and four of the six trace
to one root cause: **the document never stated which vtable its slot numbers referred to.**

Three cited slot addresses were read from a **different vtable** — `01CB2508`, which turns out to be
GameApplication's **base class**, proven from the destructor chain (`00793250`, called from slot 0
immediately after this class's vtable is installed, writes `01CB2508` into `[this+0]`). One more, slot
5's `0017CE40`, is **not a function at all** — it is a mid-body address inside slot 24.

That mix-up also **overturns the folding claim in mechanism**. The document said 13 slots were "folded
with other classes and absent from this analysis entirely". In fact **10 of them are inherited and
fully visible in the base vtable at identical indices** (1, 12, 13, 17, 18, 19, 20, 28, 29, 30); only
3 are genuine stubs. *Identical indices across two vtables is inheritance; ICF folding would place a
shared body at arbitrary unrelated indices.* The observation was right and the mechanism behind it
was not.

**The method that exposed it is the rule:** the auditor located the vtable *independently* — searched
the image for slot 2's address as a qword, found one occurrence, then confirmed the base by checking
that four separately documented slots landed on their stated indices. Four landed, three did not.

> **A document that cites slot numbers without citing the vtable address cannot be checked.**
> `game-application.md` now states `0x008C5760`.

**BE-4 answered, and the retracted reasoning is instructive.** §4 argued the root is never deleted, so
no sized `operator delete` exists to state its size, leaving `>= 0x1140` as a lower bound from field
access. Slot 0 is a textbook MSVC scalar deleting destructor and its sized path carries
`mov edx, 0x1140`: the object is **exactly 4,416 bytes**. **The reasoning was sound and its premise
was simply unchecked** — *a C++ compiler emits the deleting destructor for any polymorphic class
whether or not the program ever calls it.* "This never happens at runtime" does not predict "the code
is not there." The auditor also kept `0016D6A0` **out** of the claim: a 3-byte `ret 0` with ~2,479
callers is an ICF fold and worthless as evidence about deletion, while the size immediate is emitted
at the call site and does not depend on what its target was folded with.

**Fifth self-contradiction found today, and the first that was load-bearing.** §3 said `+0x1138` is
the highest field while §2 of the same document documents `+0x113C` and `+0x113D` at length — and the
`>= 0x1140` bound was *derived* from `+0x1138`, reaching the right answer only by alignment
coincidence.

**BE-1 answered: slot 4 is the frame tick.** It gates on the latch, converts a double at `this+0x48`,
and calls `0017D6E0` on all three exit paths. That callee is the **per-frame subsystem pump** — 404
bytes, 37 callees, of which 16 are 8–10 byte singleton getters each paired with a substantial update
body. The one recovered pair fixes the pattern: `SaveloadManager_GetSingleton` (8 B) then
`SaveloadManager_ProcessPendingCaptureCopy` (43 B). **BE-6** records that the other fifteen name the
engine's per-frame subsystem set.

**A bounded negative worth having:** GameApplication does **not** reach the shared transform workbench
at `022D91B0`, at one hop or two — not slot 4, not `0017D6E0`, none of the 22 vtable bodies, none of
the tick's 37 hop-1 or 109 hop-2 callees. The two documents were **not** made to cite each other on a
guess.

### `check_consistency.py`'s first true positive — and it was the coordinator's own document

2026-09-02, one merge after the checker's false-positive rule was fixed. The freshly written
`how-the-engine-chooses-3d-or-flat-movement.md` (by `repos-55`) carried:

> `| 002E5380 | Movement_IntegratePositionAndMeasureDisplacement | 273 B | consumer; calls the 3-D selector |`

The binary:

```
002E5380  Movement_PrepareCandidatePosition                 273 B   calls 00264460 : NO
002E5610  Movement_IntegratePositionAndMeasureDisplacement  314 B   calls 00264460 : YES  (site 002E56B7)
```

**The name and the behavioural claim were right and both point at `002E5610`; the address and the body
size were both `002E5380`'s.** `002E5380` came from the K-4 open question, which names it; the caller
list came from an xref census returning call *sites*, and `002E56B7` falls inside `002E5610`. **Two
rows of source data were combined** — a transposition, not a mistyped label, so the fix was the
address and the size and **not** the name.

**Why no other instrument would have caught it:** the size travelled *with* the wrong address, so the
row was internally consistent and a body-size check passes. Only the **name/address pairing** was
wrong, which is exactly and only what `check_consistency.py` compares.

Two things worth drawing from this. First, **a checker earns its keep the merge after it stops crying
wolf** — the same tool had been producing a false disagreement that morning, and suppressing that is
what made this signal visible. Second, **it was found by a different session than the one that wrote
the defect**, and flagged rather than silently fixed even though the finder had the category loaded.

### Defects 6 and 7 — a rate is an instrument report until the instrument is characterised

`repos-f1`, 2026-09-02, closing **B-4**'s successor question on category 24's C++ runtime families.
Both defects were in the test, not the code, and both produced a *number* rather than an error.

**Defect 6 — a detector built from one instance of the idiom.** The first census looked for
`test dl,1` and scored `CxxObjectLifecycle.ScalarDeletingDestructor` at **0 of 135** — which reads as
"this label is wrong for every member it has". It is wrong for none. Those destructors call an inner
destructor first, that call clobbers `rdx`, so the compiler moves the flag to a callee-saved register
and tests it there (`mov ebx,edx … test bl,1`). **The detector could not see the more common spelling
of the thing it was detecting.** Following the flag through the register copy turned 0/135 into
135/135.

> **A 0 % score on a 135-member label is not a finding, it is an instrument report** — and it was
> caught only by reading four bodies instead of trusting the rate.

**Defect 7 — one instrument applied to two mechanisms.** The same census lumped eager initializers
with lazy accessors and tested both against `_Init_thread_header`, scoring **58.1 %**. That number
measures nothing: eager initializers are registered in a table and are *supposed* to score zero on
the guard test; lazy ones are guarded and *supposed* to score zero on the table test. **A blended rate
over two mechanisms is not weak evidence, it is not evidence.** Split apart, every group is perfect,
with **separation in both directions** — eager 100 % registered / 0 % guarded, lazy 100 % guarded /
0 % registered.

**And the layer separation held up twice more.** 178 functions perform the deleting-destructor idiom
without one of these labels, which looked like under-inclusion until they were classified: 99
`PrimaryOwner:Audio`, 42 Phyre, 17 `NativeRoutine`, 8 Input. **They are owner-tagged, and the two
ledger layers are disjoint by design** — a destructor for an Audio object is Audio's, and its
compiler-generated *shape* does not transfer it to a CodeDomain family. Same for the 1,071 registered
initializers and 566 guard callers outside the families. That is the second block running in which an
apparent gap turned out to be the layer separation doing its job.

**Two practical facts from that block, worth more than the audit result to a modder:** a deleting
destructor's `mov edx, imm` immediately before the free call is **its class's exact size**, so those
226 functions each hand out a `sizeof` for free — probably the fastest way to size a structure in this
binary. And all 63 `AlignedOrGuardedFree` destructors route through `0016D6A0`, the disabled CFG stub,
**inert in the shipped game and therefore free to hook**.

**Seven instrument defects across the run, none in the binary:** pops without pushes; branch-insensitive
summing; an over-running body extent; a sweep past a table's end; a census counting addresses as
objects; a detector blind to the commoner spelling; one instrument for two mechanisms.

### A control proves the instrument fires. It does not prove it measures the right thing.

`repos-94`, 2026-09-02, on closing four of six lists in **BL-8** — and this is the sharpest refinement
of the control rule the run has produced.

The rebuilt list-writer scan **passed its positive control** and then returned **the same ten
`ThreadSafeStaticObjectInitializer` functions as writers of every single head**. No error, and a
plausible count per list. It was caught for one reason only: **that is not a shape a list-specific
writer set can have.** The cause was that `mov [R+8], R` is the empty-list **self-link** a constructor
emits, and the test counted it as an insert. Excluding stores whose value register *is* the head
register dropped those ten everywhere and left writer sets that genuinely differ per list.

> **Beside the control rule: check that the answer has the shape the question implies, not only that
> the tool ran.** A control catches an instrument that finds nothing. It does not catch an instrument
> that finds the same thing everywhere.

The same block records a second carried-over failure with a mundane cause worth naming: a scan keyed on
the base register could never fire, because `AttachMember` materialises the head once with
`lea rbx,[r14+0x80]` and everything afterwards goes through `rbx` — **the base register never appears
again.** Rebuilt around the real idiom, the control passes.

**And the author stopped re-deriving from its own corrected table.** Having been wrong twice on this
structure — first the unit, then the kind — the layout was taken from the constructor `00632D80`,
which writes every field in one body, with `005A7ED0` calling it as
`ctor(this, registry, "PAnimatableComponent", 0x108, 8, …)`. The name at `+0x30` now has **three
independent derivations**: a load, a store, and a caller passing the literal. That is the correct
response to *"a correction derived from the artefact being corrected is not a correction."*

### Control → shape → read the rows. The third is not optional because the first two passed.

`repos-94`, 2026-09-02, **retracting a table it had published one block earlier**. The writer census
giving `+0x50` 7 writers, `+0x60` 4 and `+0xB0` 2 was presented as *"a second, mechanical
derivation"*. It was not: the scan matches **any** structure with a self-linked pair at that
displacement and has no descriptor specificity at all. Opening all six candidates found **none is a
class descriptor** — an EASTL list constructor, two Steam callback registrars, a `PPFX::CTinyEffect`
constructor, a `Phyre::VTS::ScreenState*` constructor, and an unrelated parameter-block copy.

**And the shape check passed.** Writer sets *did* differ per head, unlike the
ten-functions-everywhere case that produced the shape rule in the first place — because *"different
per head"* is equally consistent with **per-head noise**. What worked was opening the rows, which for
a six-candidate set is one decompile batch.

> **Control → shape → read the rows.** A control catches an instrument that finds nothing. A shape
> check catches one that finds the same thing everywhere. **Neither catches one that finds a
> different wrong thing each time.**

The replacement instrument was rejected too, and for a reason worth keeping: anchoring on
rip-relative references into a known descriptor's interior is descriptor-specific *by construction*
and its control passed — but **descriptors are ~0x110 bytes packed in `.data`, so an interior address
can be another global's start**, and two magic-static accessors for unrelated `PType` singletons came
back as hits. Two instruments built for one question, both rejected, **one negative retained**: no
function in any class-descriptor vtable slot touches `+0x50`, `+0x60` or `+0xB0`, while the identical
query for `+0x80` returns `AttachMember` — so the instrument fires, and whatever fills those lists
does so through **non-virtual** code.

### A control cannot validate an instrument that is merely silent

`repos-46`, 2026-09-02, on **BE-6** — and this is a genuinely new qualification of the control rule.

Seven instruments were run against the five already-named singletons as controls before being pointed
at the eight unknowns. Six failed, and one row is worth keeping forever: **named callees at depth 2
would have named a *camera* singleton after `vpx_codec_destroy`, a VP8 video-codec teardown function,
reached by a real call edge.** Without controls that is a name anyone could publish with a straight
face.

The seventh worked — **the engine's own authored profiler-scope labels**, the same
`FUN_001EB150(...)` mechanism that pushes the `"display character : …"` strings. It named
`01F82CE0` **`ScreenImage`**, and the body confirms it: a level at `+0x1C` moved by `+0x20` per frame,
**up in mode 0 and down in mode 1, clamped at 255.0**, constructed disabled in mode 3. That is the
**screen fade** — the object behind the screen going to and from black on area transitions — and it
is one of the thirteen things the application root pumps every frame.

**But that instrument also returns nothing for the controls**, because those subsystems carry no
label:

> **A positive instrument with no false positives cannot be validated by a control that has nothing
> to find.** Controls disprove instruments that **invent** answers; they cannot disprove one that is
> merely **silent**. What validates a single hit is that it is an authored string, in the right
> place, corroborated by the body it wraps.

The instrument that worked nearly got discarded for failing the same control the six bad ones failed.
Note also that it **fires exactly once in thirteen** — the shape a sound scan should have. A label
scan returning a name for all thirteen would have been reporting its own noise.

### A name inherited from an external reference is as unproven as one inherited from a neighbour

`repos-f1`, 2026-09-02, refuting the framing of its own **BQ-26**. The question was filed three blocks
earlier as *"the vector deleting destructor form"* — because that is what MSVC's second flag bit is
called in some references, **not because it had been measured here**. Only **14 of 1,608** members
contain any backward branch; a vector deleting destructor must iterate over the array, so there is no
array. **The question's own name was the hypothesis, and it sat in the document unexamined.**

**Defect 8**, caught by the shape rule before the census was believed: a sweep that promoted any
register receiving `edx` to "the flag register" anywhere in the body returned 1,616 functions with a
**maximum body of 3,175 bytes**. Nothing in the tool complained — the *shape* did, because a
3,175-byte compiler-generated destructor does not exist. Tightened, it became 1,608, median 92,
max 317, and a cross-check against an instrument that has never seen a flag test — the recovered
vtable index — puts **1,607 of the 1,608** as recovered virtual methods.

What bit 2 actually selects: the set side calls `0016D6A0` in **1,606 of 1,606** cases; the clear side
calls `00584730` (1,494), `007AD450` (93) or `0085E710` (19). So it chooses the sized `operator
delete` over `_aligned_free`, which is exactly what the GFZ's `DeletingDestructor.AlignedOrGuardedFree`
says — a label correct and applied to 4 % of its population, the other 1,545 being Phyre- and
owner-tagged. **Third block running in which an apparent classification gap was the layer separation
working.**

**And the author narrowed its own earlier claim rather than waiting to be audited.** *"A deleting
destructor's `mov edx, imm` before the free gives the class's exact size"* holds **per call site**
(verified at 0x90, 0x98, 0xD8) but **not as a bulk census**: sweeping the first `mov edx, imm` in each
of the 1,608 returns `0x100` for 1,186 of them, which is not 1,186 classes of 256 bytes — it catches a
different instruction. Recorded in the document rather than left for a reader to trip over.

### Two sessions, one boundary, and a discrepancy that reconciled instead of contradicting

`repos-94`, 2026-09-02, taking the PhyreEngine boundary revision and **re-deriving `repos-46`'s
result rather than absorbing it.** Both reached `GameApplication : Phyre::PFramework::PApplication`;
the counts did not match.

- `repos-46`: **18 supplied, 10 inherited**
- `repos-94`: **18 overridden, 13 inherited**, and 18 + 13 = 31 exactly

**Both are true of different things.** Three of the 13 inherited slots are do-nothing stubs — slots
11 and 27 are a constant-return, slot 26 is `0016D6A0`, the folded 3-byte `ret`. So *"10 inherited
implementations"* and *"13 inherited slots"* are the same binary described with two different nouns.
Recorded as a **reconciliation rather than a correction**, because a reader comparing the two
documents would otherwise meet a bare discrepancy with no way to resolve it — and the resolution is
more informative than either figure.

**The proof worth keeping above all the RTTI:** slot 6 of `PApplication` is `0079BF70`; slot 6 of
`GameApplication` is `0017CDC0`, whose entire 27-byte body is `FUN_0017d670(); FUN_0079BF70(this);`
— **an override calling the exact function occupying the base's matching slot.** That is
`Derived::F() { extra(); Base::F(); }` compiled, it needs no RTTI, no destructor chain and no
adjacency, and **it settles the direction too**: a base cannot call its derived class's override by
direct address. Four more overrides fall through to the middleware's own stub in the same shape.

**It also explains a standing finding rather than contradicting it.** The Phyre subsystem map records,
as a result, that *no documented game subsystem calls Phyre*. The measurement was right and the
inference from it was the wrong way round: **the top level is Phyre → game, not game → Phyre.** A
search for game→Phyre calls at the top level finds nothing because the control flow runs the other
way. Equal slot counts (31 and 31) say the same thing from another angle — **the game adds no
virtuals of its own; it fills in the framework's.**

### A correction must be swept, not applied — and three more instrument lessons

2026-09-02, from `repos-78` and `repos-ec`, and the first one is against the coordinator.

**Applying a correction in the place it was discovered leaves the rest of the document wrong.** After
adopting a peer's corrected names and their §2 pan/volume finding into the audio boundary document,
**§4's pseudocode still carried the superseded nullary signature** — the fifth-self-contradiction
shape, landing in the very file the correction was written into. Worse for tooling: **no name-based
checker can catch that class**, because the disagreement lives in a pseudocode signature rather than
a name. *A correction is a sweep, not an edit.*

**An attribution error of the coordinator's, corrected by the session it misattributed.** The log had
recorded three independent routes converging on `0016D6A0`'s identity and described one of them
wrongly — `repos-78`'s evidence was the **call-site shape** (a 3-byte `C2 00 00` body, callers passing
a *comparison result* in `ECX`, and **no indirect call following** — an assert helper, not a CFG
check), not the deallocator signature, which was two other sessions'. As they put it: **three routes
converging is only impressive if they were actually three different routes.** Collapsing them
overstated the corroboration.

**A number quoted as settled that was not — now reconciled, and the resolution is instructive.**
`0016D6A0`'s caller count was propagated as **2,480** from one regeneration while another gave
**2,479**. Off by one, in the same direction, from two derivations that should agree. Chased down by
enumerating what could legitimately be counted:

```
distinct calling functions (call graph)          2,479
DumpDataXrefs kind=CALL, distinct func_entry     2,479   (set-identical to the above)
DumpDataXrefs kind=CALL, rows                    2,867   call SITES
DumpDataXrefs all kinds, distinct func_entry     2,511   references of ANY kind (1,515 data slots)
```

**2,480 is not reproducible under any definition.** The three defensible numbers are 2,479 / 2,867 /
2,511, and *which one a sentence wants depends on the sentence* — the same distinction the
caller-count checker already encodes as direct/total/distinct. **An off-by-one between two honest
instruments was not a rounding difference; it was one figure with no definition behind it**, and it
had been repeated in four documents before anyone asked which noun it counted.
**Nobody should quote either figure as exact until the extra one is found.**

### An instrument that reports the database instead of the binary — and it underpinned a premise

`repos-9e`, 2026-09-02, working **A-1**, the 158 unclassified functions. **The most consequential
instrument defect of the run**, because unlike the others it was not inside one block's tooling — it
was inside a *premise* that three documents and the mission prompt itself repeat.

A-1's evidence summary reads *"no strings, no exact-body clones, no qualified symbols"*.
`DumpUnresolvedStringReferences.java` returns zero, and a fresh dump reproduces it.

> **CORRECTION, same day, by the coordinator — against its own first version of this entry.** The
> explanation published here was that the zero is structural because `Invoke-GfzHeadless.ps1` passes
> `-noanalysis`, so the script *"reports Ghidra's database, not the executable"*. **That was accepted
> from the reporting session and not tested. Three separate tests refute it:**
>
> - **References are complete.** `getReferencesFrom(00249C64)` returns the `DAT_02091098` READ, and
>   `getReferencesTo(02091098)` returns all four of its references with their owning functions.
> - **Strings are defined `Data`.** `MWeather` is a typed string at `00D11150`; a filter for
>   "Rotation" returns 14. So `getDataContaining` → `instanceof String` resolves normally.
> - **The script iterates the body correctly** — `getInstructions(f.getBody())` then
>   `in.getReferencesFrom()` — so it is not the per-entry-address error either.
>
> **What actually stands:** the script scans **only the 158** (its `free()` filter) and measures
> **direct** string references. A byte-level rescan finds **2 of 158** direct — so the script misses
> two, and **the cause of those two is not established.** The **13 one call away were never in the
> script's scope at all**; that is an extension of the question, not a defect in the instrument.
>
> **The finding is unharmed and the explanation was wrong.** Eleven residual functions still gain a
> name. What is retracted is the sweeping claim that this class of script reports the database rather
> than the binary — and with it the implication that every `Dump*`/`Scan*` result is suspect.
>
> **This is the third time tonight a mechanism was adopted from a peer report without a test, and the
> first where the coordinator did it after writing the rule against it.**

A byte-level rescan — every RIP-relative LEA in `.text` against every NUL-terminated printable run,
with two positive controls that pass — gives **2 of 158 with a direct string reference and 13 with a
string one call away**, both lower bounds. **Eleven residual functions gain a name from it**, and one
of them is `002AAE40`, which the residual document had held up as *"the purest example of why a
call-context classifier cannot touch these"*. It is font drawing. **The evidence was one call below
where every scan was looking.**

**Scope, checked here rather than inherited from the report — the three scripts do not share a
cause:**

| script | primitive | affected? |
|---|---|---|
| `DumpUnresolvedStringReferences` | `getReferencesFrom` + `getDataContaining` + `instanceof String` | **yes, entirely** |
| `ScanUnresolvedQualifiedSymbols` | `getSymbolTable` / `getPrimarySymbol` **and** `getReferencesFrom` | **partly** — the symbol table is populated at import, so symbols *on* a function were tested; symbols reached *via references* were not |
| `ScanUnresolvedExactByteCloneDomains` | `getBytes` | **no** — it reads the raw image; its empty result stands and needs a different account |

That distinction matters: the reporting session observed all three returning empty and reasonably
suspected one cause. **Two have it and one does not**, and treating the clone result as also
discredited would have thrown away a true negative.

> **A negative from a tool is a claim about the tool until you know which layer it queried.** Every
> `Dump*`/`Scan*` script in this pipeline should be audited for the same dependency, and each should
> state in its header whether it reads the image or the database.

### The completion metric was counting the wrong noun, and it was written down all along

2026-09-02. `audit_coverage` counted documents with `audit.passes > 0`. **`COVERAGE.md` has recorded
since this morning that this counter counts *amendments*** — *"a document can read `passes: 8` and
have never been attacked once - three of the rows above do."* The scorer and the ledger disagreed
about what the field means, **in writing**, and nobody compared them.

Surfaced when a session found a document claiming `passes: 1` while the audit-debt table listed it as
never attacked. **One of the two was wrong and neither was checkable from the other**, because the
fields recording *what program state a pass ran against* were absent. A strengthened check then found
**six documents claiming a pass with no recorded state, five of which the debt table lists as owing a
first pass.**

`progress.py` now requires `passes > 0` **and** a non-null `last_pass_state`: an amendment bump does
not produce that field, and a real pass cannot omit it. The effect on the headline:

```
audit_coverage   86.81 % (79/91)  ->  80.22 % (73/91)
OVERALL          43.69 %          ->  42.70 %
```

**The figure was wrong, not the documents.** Six audit claims are now visibly unsupported rather than
invisibly counted, and the reported percentage has been an **upper bound** for as long as it has been
reported.

Two related defects fixed in the same pass. `frontmatter_audit_gaps` only fired when a state key was
present and explicitly `null` — it reported **nothing when the key was absent entirely**, which is
the worse case and the actual one. And `frontmatter_dupes` matched only top-level keys, so duplicates
nested one level down were invisible; it found two documents where YAML was silently keeping
superseded values, **one stamping a superseded checkpoint's snapshot hash as its verification
provenance.**

> **A metric is a claim about the database, and it needs the same evidence standard as a claim about
> the binary.** Three of this project's checkers were, this session, measuring something adjacent to
> what their name said.

### False corroboration: a derived figure agreeing with the figure it was derived from

`repos-78`, 2026-09-02, on `phyre-script-object-accessors.md` — **the first pass run under the
provenance-ordering rule, and it found the overturn first because it was the cheapest claim in the
document.** The method works.

§9 said *"588 of these 747 are among them, 159 are not"*. The real intersection is **591 / 156**.
`588` is `323 + 265` — the two accessor sub-tag counts from **§8's own table two sections earlier** —
carried into a sentence about a *different* population. Membership in the 1,219 means any
`Phyre.ScriptVM.*` CodeDomain, which includes `ReflectionBridge`, and §8 of the same document records
that **3 of the 747 carry exactly that tag**. Those three are inside the set and were counted outside
it.

**The part worth the entry is why it looked safe.** `747 − 588 = 159`, and §8's other figures give
`156 + 3 = 159`. So the wrong number appeared to be **confirmed by a second measurement** — when it
was the same measurement twice, re-derived. *An arithmetic identity between two figures from one
source is not corroboration; it is a tautology wearing corroboration's clothes.* This is the
inverse of the neighbourhood rule: there, two sources agreed because one came from the other's
neighbourhood; here, two figures agreed because one was computed from the other.

**AZ-4 answered by a clean feature test**, and the separation is total: **140 of the 156 mis-tagged
accessors bind a type that is itself a template instantiation** (`PArray<…>`, `PSharray<…>`) and
**zero of the 591 do** — 140/140. The remaining 16 are ten binding a non-Phyre `struct`, two binding
`Phyre::PTimer`, four cv-qualified. So the classifier awarded the accessor CodeDomain only for a
plain, non-template, `Phyre::`-namespaced class and fell back on a nested `<`, a foreign namespace or
a `struct`.

### A document's recorded instrument failure is a warning about the next instrument

Same pass. Hunting a `Set` counterpart, a message scan filtered on *"obtained from script"* and
silently missed *"Unable to **obtain** object pointer from script…"* — which would have reported one
diagnostic message where there are two. **The document's own §8 already records an instrument that
returned a clean zero on these very strings through a printable-byte filter.** The warning was in
writing, in the file being audited, and the same failure class was reproduced anyway.

> **A recorded instrument failure is not an epitaph for the last tool. It is a specification for the
> next one.** The re-run now asserts a known-present string before reporting any absence.

### Provenance ordering says which claims to hit. It does not say to read what the database knows.

Also `repos-78`, and reported against itself. The fix for the `AudioController` misidentification it
had retracted an hour earlier **was sitting in `audio-bank-and-controller-family.md`** — a document in
its own category, covering the same objects, with the five-controller layout already correct and
matching slot for slot.

> **Provenance-ordered attack tells you which of a document's claims to attack. It does not tell you
> to go and read what this database already knows about the same objects.** That is a separate check,
> and it is cheap: before attacking a document, list the other documents covering the same addresses
> and read them.

Three times tonight, cross-checking against an existing document is what stopped or would have
stopped an over-claim — the RNG global that broke "one 660-byte buffer", the `002E5610` transposition,
and this. It is now the most reliably productive check in the run and the least consistently applied.

### A falsification pass goes where the author's attention already is

`repos-78`, 2026-09-02, finding **the banned inference in its own `DOCUMENTED` document** — one that
had already survived a falsification pass.

The claim was that a singleton at `01FD36A0` is an `AudioController`, and it ran through five
sections and the data table. It is not: `002105E0` constructs **five** objects into slots
`+0x00`..`+0x20`, each deriving from `AudioController` and each named by real RTTI —
`MusicAudioController`, `SebAudioController`, `SepAudioController`, `StreamAudioController`,
`ShoutAudioController`. The original name came from `00212760`, an `AudioController` destructor,
**sitting in the neighbourhood and being the only class name nearby.** Address adjacency wearing a
class name.

**Why the earlier pass missed it, in the author's own words:**

> *"It survived my own falsification pass because I attacked the pan/volume claim, the 512 split and
> the census — the three things I had worked hardest on — and never attacked the one claim I had not
> derived from a body. The pass covered what I had invested in, not what I had assumed cheapest."*

**This is a structural gap in Phase D as practised, not a lapse.** A pass naturally targets the
claims its author found hard, because those are the ones they remember reasoning about. The claims
that were *cheap* — a name picked up from a neighbour, a figure carried over from a question's
wording, a size quoted from another document — leave no memory of effort and so attract no attack.
Every one of tonight's inherited-name defects is of that kind.

**Remedy, and it is procedural:** before a pass, list the document's claims by **where each came
from**, not by how important it is — body-derived, tool-derived, inherited, assumed. **Attack the
inherited and assumed ones first.** The contradiction here was sitting in bodies the author already
had: `00212710`, the real `AudioController` constructor, builds **one** EASTL list at `+0x08`/`+0x10`,
a layout that cannot produce the two-separate-objects accesses the code actually makes.

**Two instrument failures of the "plausible output from a broken tool" family:**

- A `.text` **linear-sweep** xref scan returned **0 hits for all 13 targets**, including one provably
  referenced — capstone desynchronised on inline data and never recovered, and **the zero looked
  exactly like a clean negative.** Third sighting of a linear sweep desynchronising; the fix each time
  is to disassemble per function from its entry point.
- A scratch helper named `dis.py` **shadowed the standard library's `dis`**, which capstone imports
  transitively. It raised — *and still printed a page of correct-looking disassembly.*
  **A scratch script's filename is part of the instrument.**

Two further results with practical value: the startup latch is **not a separate mechanism but a byte
at `this+0x113D`**, tested every frame inside the tick and set on the first, never cleared — so a mod
wanting *"the game has really started"* polls one byte instead of timing a sleep. And slot 0, the
deleting destructor, is the declared parent of a `__std_terminate` funclet from that session's *first*
block: **`~GameApplication` is a `noexcept` boundary** *(annotated 2026-09-15, pass 6: withdrawn as evidenced; it rested on the EH table's
funclet-parent relation, which is banned. See the-game-is-a-phyre-application.md)*, so a throwing destructor hook terminates the
process rather than unwinding. Two blocks eight steps apart meeting on one address.
Pass 6 took the render-parameters doc: parameter count survived, asset count was 15 of 18.
Pass 7 took the PhyreEngine reflection doc: the 4,557 total survived exactly, the family
breakdown misfiled 256 functions. Pass 8 took the Lua bindings doc as a deliberate control on pass 7's defect: every row
exact. Pass 9 took the accessor-hubs doc: 33 of 33 table rows exact, but its "most-consulted"
superlative was false. Pass 11 took the item-encoding doc: the asymmetry survived and its own open question was
answered, but an edge-count confusion forced a self-retraction in pass 9. Pass 12 took the Steam doc: 41 achievements exact, but three counts wrong and the
multiplayer caution strengthened with positive evidence. Pass 13 took the slot-pool doc and answered its own open question M-3: the pool holds
**32**. Pass 14 took the party doc: the four-slot roster survived and its open question O-2 was
answered - a shared mode predicate with seven test sites. **26 → 13.**
