## 2026-09-02 — the scorer had no provenance, and ten tools read the same undated dump

Two falsification passes landed within minutes of each other and both bottomed out in the same
place, which is why this is a section rather than a line.

**repos-9e, pass 1 on `the-largest-unclassified-functions.md`.** Its headline census was stale by
two functions — 10,154 / 2,667,070 B where the certified state gives **10,152 / 2,666,058 B**. The
cause was proven rather than guessed: re-running the census over `Tools/work/graph/functions.tsv`
reproduces all three of the document's figures *exactly*, and that dump is the 01:09 program state,
missing two closures landed since. I confirmed the dump's mtime independently — `2026-09-02
01:09:37` — and the corrected figure has an arithmetic route with nothing in common with the dump:
`owner(9,409) + finalNo(585) + unresolved(158) = 10,152`.

**The document's own folder contains the warning it walked into.** `the-unresolved-158.md` §13
documents this exact defect. Writing the warning down is not the same as being protected by it, and
nothing in the toolchain closed the gap between the two.

**So I turned the check on my own instrument, and found the same hole.** `progress.py` — the scorer
behind every percentage I report — reads that same undated dump, and printed no statement of what
state it measured. Ten tools read it.

What the check found, stated precisely rather than dramatically:

- **The scorer is NOT materially stale.** It reads only `entry`, `name` and `body_bytes`, which are
  properties of the binary, not of the ledger. The two closures changed *tags*. The document was
  affected because it reads the tags column; the scorer does not. `total_fn + excluded = 34,270 +
  3,891 = 38,161`, matching the certified `internal=38161` exactly.
- **But it was mixing two states with nothing checking they agreed.** `ledger_resolved` divides a
  numerator sourced from the 20:47 verifier output by a denominator sourced from the 01:09 dump. It
  happens to be sound. Nothing made it sound, and nothing would have said so if it stopped being.
- **The mixed-state ratio survived its own attack, and that is recorded because an unrecorded audit
  did not happen.** All 158 residual addresses appear in the dump and **none is an `Unwind@` or
  `Catch_All@` funclet**, so the 158 lie wholly inside the 34,270 denominator. A residual that *were*
  a funclet would have sat in the numerator and not the denominator — a ratio quietly wrong in the
  fourth digit forever.

`progress.py` now prints the mtime and identity of all three inputs, cross-checks `internal=` and
`unresolved=` against the certified header, checks for residuals absent from the denominator, and
**exits 2 with a PROVENANCE WARNING** if any of that fails. A figure with no state behind it is now
visibly a figure with no state behind it.

> **A metric must say what it measured, or it is only a number that agrees with itself.**
> This is the second correction to the same scorer in one night. The first found it counting the
> wrong noun (`audit.passes` counts amendments, not attacks — recorded above). The second found it
> unable to say which program state it counted that noun in. **Both defects were in the instrument
> that scores the work, not in the work** — and the instrument is the one artefact in the project
> that nobody had been assigned to attack.

### Corroboration from the second pass, and the sharper form of a known trap

**repos-78, pass 8 on `gi-render-command-family.md`** independently reported the frontmatter gap
from the other side, and its own instrument failure is the more instructive half. Its census regex
accepted vtable displacements only in `0x`-prefixed form; capstone prints small ones bare, so
`[rax + 8]` was invisible and the scan returned **19 of 20 slots** agreeing with the document and
one disagreeing.

> **A scan that agrees with its target in 19 places and disagrees in 1 is far more likely to be
> broken in that 1 place than to have found something.**

They chased the disagreement instead of publishing it. Note the ordering that saved it: **suspicion
of their own tool, not of the document.** Every prior instrument defect this session was found the
same way and none of them was found by suspecting the document first.

Two further entries from that pass:

- **False corroboration, second form.** The established form is an arithmetic identity between two
  figures drawn from one source — a tautology wearing corroboration's clothes. The new form is a
  figure from a *genuinely unrelated mechanism* that happens to match: a `3` offered as a vertex
  reservation count is the second argument to a **direct `call FUN_00600A60`**, not a call through
  `[dev+0x000]`, so it is not a reservation at all. Different origin, identical effect — a
  discriminator that looked like it had three legs had two. **And in both forms the refutation was
  already inside the document**: neither reset command contributes a single slot to its own census.
- **An absence whose positive control comes back short is not an absence at the strength stated.**
  "The reserve idiom occurs at exactly 4 sites image-wide" reproduces — and reproduces *because* the
  filter misses GiPrim at `00863DD1`, a site the same document describes three sections earlier.
  A demonstrated **1-in-5 false-negative rate on its own known-positive set**, under a negative
  (BG-1) that other work is leaning on. Not refuted; not established at the strength stated.

### The "no strings" claims are unsupported by default, database-wide

`DumpUnresolvedStringReferences.java` requires *typed string data* at the target, and this program
has none — every string target decompiles as `&DAT_…`, and the only `data_type` values in the whole
certified dump are three hand-defined EH structures. It therefore reports "no strings" for **every
function in the binary**, and cannot return anything else.

**Every "no strings" claim anywhere in the database is currently resting on that.** Eight documents
carry one. They are not wrong — repos-9e re-established the largest of them with a byte-level
scanner and a passing positive control, across fourteen functions at depth 0 and depth 1, and found
**genuinely no authored string**. They are *unsupported*, which is a different and cheaper problem:
the corrected scanner is in `work/repos-9e/` and needs a control each time.

**Two withdrawals attach to this, and both belong on the record.** The explanation first published
for the zero — that `-noanalysis` left Ghidra without references or typed strings — is retracted by
its author: the references half is false, the packed parent carries prior analysis, and their own
`DATAREF_CONTEXTS.tsv` holds 378 reference-derived rows. **I adopted that explanation without
testing it and had already retracted my adoption; the originator has now retracted the original.**
The scoping correction holds and extends further than I scoped it: `getMemory().getBytes()` in the
clone scan is unaffected and its empty result is a **true negative**, `ScanUnresolvedQualifiedSymbols`
is half-broken, and `DumpUnresolvedIncomingOwnerRefs` uses `getReferencesTo()` and is **unaffected —
I was wrong to include it.** One broken, one half-broken, two real negatives.

And one method note worth more than the finding it nearly produced: grepping `s_[A-Za-z0-9_.]+`
appeared to turn up a defined string `s_ResolveRuntimePointer`, which was a substring match inside
`ImageAddress_ResolveRuntimePointer`. **An unanchored regex is not a symbol search.**

### What `audit.passes` cannot distinguish

`the-largest-unclassified-functions.md` carried **eleven recorded amendments and no recorded
attack**, and both claims that broke under pass 1 had survived all eleven. Nine of the eleven were
the author extending their own reading.

> **Self-extension is not self-attack, and one counter cannot tell them apart.**

That is the same conclusion the scorer fix reached from the metric side, arrived at independently
from the document side. Five documents still claim `passes > 0` with no recorded state; four of them
need their claim checked before it is believed. The fifth, `vtable-method-index.md`, is the awkward
one — the owed table records it DISCHARGED after four real attacks, so **only the stamp is missing**,
and it is the one case where the strengthened check is right to fire and wrong about the document.

### Follow-up — the claimed passes were checked, and two of three had never happened

The strengthened metric said five documents claimed a pass with no recorded state. That is a claim
about frontmatter; the question is whether the *passes* were real. Checked by content rather than by
counter:

| document | claimed | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `vtable-method-index.md` | `passes: 6` | **REAL.** `AUDIT-LOG.md:7152` records DISCHARGED after four attacks. Only the stamp was missing — now `four-attacks-survived-discharged-GN158`. |
| `generated-float-table-builders.md` | `passes: 1` | **NOT RECORDED.** No pass section; zero `SURVIVED`/`OVERTURNED` findings in the whole text. |
| `audio-bank-and-controller-family.md` | `passes: 1` | **NOT RECORDED.** Same. |
| `dyngeo-instance-family.md` | `passes: 1` | Under attack now; stamped by its attacker mid-check. |

The two that had never been attacked now carry `last_pass_state: null` **with the reason inline**, so
the absence is stated rather than silent. Their `passes` counters are left alone: they are a truthful
count of amendments and always were. The field was never lying — **it was answering a different
question from the one the scorer asked it.**

> **The counter was honest and the reader was wrong.** That is worth separating from the ordinary
> case where a figure is simply incorrect, because the fix is different: not a correction, a second
> field.

### The mask pairing: reported, held blanked, verified, applied

The reversed `dwStatusMaskMode*` pairing was **held blanked for one tick rather than flipped**, on
the grounds that adopting a peer's mapping untested is the failure this log recorded twice on
2026-09-02. The reporting session then supplied a byte-level derivation, and the bytes were re-read
independently from the certified program before anything was restored:

- `0030E88C` → `e7e41e00 fde41e00 13e51e00 26e51e00 43e51e00 57e51e00` — six image-relative dwords,
  matching the report exactly.
- `0030E4E7` → `8b 4e 64 85 f9 …` — mode 0 reads `+0x64`.
- `0030E526` → `8b 4e 64 85 f9 0f 85 fc 02 00 00 85 7e 38 …` — mode 3 reads `+0x64` **and tests
  `+0x38`**, the only arm with two different reads.

Applied: `Mode0_3` = `+0x64`, `Mode1_4` = `+0x3C`, `Mode2_5` = `+0x38`.

**The strongest route in that derivation is the one that needs no decompiler.** The jump table
partitions the six modes `{0,3} {1,4} {2,5}` — **not** the `{0,1} {2,3} {4,5}` a reader would guess —
and the three GFZ names are `Mode0_3`, `Mode1_4`, `Mode2_5`. A naming convention agreeing with a jump
table on a *non-obvious* partition is real corroboration between two independent artefacts.

> **A name is confirmed by the structure it fails to be a restatement of.** Had the partition been
> the obvious one, the agreement would have carried almost no information; it is the counter-intuitive
> grouping that makes the match evidence rather than coincidence. This is the inverse of the false-
> corroboration entries above, and belongs beside them.

Carried out of the naming question as a finding in its own right: **mode 3 guards on a different mask
from the one it writes** — it refuses if the bit is set in `+0x64` *or* `+0x38`, while modes 4 and 5
guard only their own field. `+0x38` is also the one mask the `0x80000003` retire gate ignores. A
cross-mask exclusion unique to one mode is the thread for naming the third mask.

### Instrument limitation recorded: caller counts and the thunk blind spot

A function with zero callers in `edges.tsv` is not necessarily uncalled: `00377BA0` is reached from
four functions in three subsystems through a 5-byte tail-call thunk at `00320160` — which the ledger
**already names** `thunk_FUN_00377ba0`. Second instance after `00313F60`. **Every document asserting a
caller count is exposed, and so is `check_consistency.py`, which checks caller counts.**

The cheap fix is available and uses information already in the dump: `functions.tsv` column 6 is a
thunk flag, so a caller census that unions a target's callers with the callers of every flagged thunk
pointing at it gets both known cases right. The residual gap after that — tail calls with no thunk
flag — needs a `call`/`jmp rel32` instruction census.

### `check_denominators.py` — the mechanizable half of "one stated population per table"

A parallel session observed that **three of ten findings across two of its falsification passes were
the same shape**: a correction or an exclusion applied to one number and not to the number printed
beside it. A census refreshed while the figure next to it went stale; a scan correction applied to a
distinct-function count and not to the slot counts on the same line, understating `.data` slots
~15-fold; and an exclusion of 3,891 exception funclets that four separate figures depend on and no
caption declares. In every case **both numbers were published side by side and nothing compared
them.** Their rule:

> **Re-derive every number in a table from one stated population, and fail the table if any row
> needs a different one.**

A script cannot re-derive a count from the binary, but it can do the percentage — because a
percentage *is* a numerator over a population. `check_denominators.py` takes every `N … P %` pair,
finds which certified population reproduces `P`, and asks whether the document names that population
anywhere near the claim. Undeclared denominators are reported; declared ones and local populations
are silent. It ships `--self-test`.

**First run: 22 hits across 4 documents, every one of them the undeclared 34,270** — the
funclet-excluded population — which is precisely the exclusion the reporting session found undeclared
in *its* document. Two independent routes, one systemic defect: **the funclet exclusion is the
project's most-used and least-stated population.**

**Then the tool failed the way its own targets do, and that is the entry worth keeping.** Half the
hits were false: at a ±4-line window it reported `vtable-method-index.md`'s partition table, whose
caption says *"Partitioning all 34,270 functions"* **five lines above the first row**. A table
caption sits above a header row and a separator row, so **caption-to-last-row distance grows with the
table's height** — a fixed line window cannot see the top of a tall table. Fixed by walking up to the
first non-table line and searching from there. **22 → 11.**

> **A checker with a fixed window is making a claim about document layout, and that claim needs
> testing like any other.** This is the third instrument this session to manufacture disagreements
> out of its own formatting assumption — after a name-length cap that truncated the names it then
> called mismatched, and a peer's census regex that matched only `0x`-prefixed displacements and so
> could not see `[rax + 8]`. **All three were found by suspecting the tool, and none by suspecting
> the document.**

Of the eleven survivors, the sharpest was `vtable-method-index.md`'s *corrected* partition — whose
four rows sum to **exactly 34,270** and whose caption never said so. **The table's own rows prove the
denominator the caption omits**, and a reader taking "of all" to mean all 38,161 reads every
percentage in it about 11 % too high. Declared in place; **11 → 7**, the rest in ledger rows.

### A claim contradicted by the document's own adjacent section

Three findings across three passes are now the same shape, and it is a shape no checker looked for:

- `vbf-archive-and-st2e-tables.md` declared a *complete* forty-entry set and then spent §7 on
  `word.bin`, which is not in it — along with four other files it analyses in detail.
- `the-largest-unclassified-functions.md` §13 stated the region at `022D94B0` has **no writer
  anywhere in `.text`** — while **§12, one section earlier, documents a setter writing that same
  region through literal RIP addresses.** Eight of the sixteen referencing functions write to it.
- The same document's §14 wrote down that a `0xB` is a bound on a *second argument* and then titled
  the subsection *"an 11-entry table"*, carrying 11 into its summary diagram. The table has **32**
  entries: base `02EBE5E0` to end `02EBEBE0` at stride `0x30`.

`check_consistency.py` compares a document against other documents. `check_answered_not_established.py`
compares it against the ledger. **Nothing compared a document against itself** — which is where a
heavily-sectioned document is weakest, because the correction gets written where it was discovered
and the original claim stays where it was.

`check_self_contradiction.py` now does, for the one case whose vocabulary is narrow enough on both
sides: an absence-of-write claim, joined by address to a positive write claim elsewhere in the same
file. It ships `--self-test`.

**It found four hits. All four were its own fault, and the three defects are worth more than the
check.**

1. **`only read` was in the no-write vocabulary.** It matched *"`022CB726` is read only by
   `003603C0` and written by three functions"* — a sentence stating both halves correctly in one
   breath. **"Only read by X" scopes the reader set; "only read" denies the writer set. One
   substring covers both.**
2. **A write verb under a negation counted as a writer.** *"never initialises either: mapping the
   whole frame of `00234AF0`"* was read as positive evidence of a write, because the verb matched
   and the `never` three words earlier did not. **A verb is not a claim.**
3. **An address in a line about writing is not an address being written.** *"`02091098` has exactly
   one writer image-wide | 1 WRITE (`00249FC0`), 3 READs (`00249C60`, …)"* was reported as evidence
   that `00249C60` is written. It is in the **READ list of a sentence about a different address.**

**4 → 1 → 0.** The database has no live instance of this defect, because the two real ones were
corrected by the pass that found them. So the honest report is: **the checker found nothing, and its
value is that it is now regression-proof against the next one.**

> **Fourth instrument this session to manufacture disagreements out of its own pattern assumptions,
> and the first to do it three separate ways in one sitting.** The pattern across all four is now
> unmistakable: a checker's regex is a claim about how the database is written, and it needs a
> control exactly as much as a claim about how the binary is written. **Every one was caught by
> running it and reading the rows — not by review of the pattern.**

### Two ways to mistake something for a falsification pass

The two documents whose claimed passes were checked by content turned out to be unattacked for
*different reasons*, and the distinction is worth keeping:

- **Pass 103 mistook careful authoring for a pass.** Its scope line reads "new document
  `dyngeo-instance-family.md`". It declines address adjacency explicitly and carries a "Not claimed"
  paragraph — which is *why* it reads like an audit and is not one.
- **Pass 104 mistook verification for falsification.** It did include independent re-verification of
  four load-bearing claims before publication, by a second session. That is real work and it is why
  `audio-bank-and-controller-family.md` turned out as accurate as it did. **But nobody tried to
  destroy anything.**

> **Verification is the more seductive error, because it genuinely reduces risk — which makes it feel
> like it should count.** Re-deriving a claim and finding it holds is precisely what the evidence
> standard warns is not enough: anyone can assemble evidence agreeing with a reading they already
> hold.

### Convergence applied to a structural claim

`audio-bank-and-controller-family.md` §2's *"**every** controller's slot 7 is an adjustor thunk, and
**all four** are the same two instructions"* is **a claim about a family evidenced by a table of
four, in a family of five.** `StreamAudioController`'s vtable is the same length as the base's — no
slot 7, no secondary base.

The result is stronger than the correction: **Stream is the odd member on four independent counts** —
no slot 7 (this pass); `0xB8` with one bank method against Seb and Sep at `0xE0` with 10 and 9;
constructed fifth but stored at `+0x18`, *before* Shout at `+0x20`; and never selected by the play
call's fork, which reaches only `+0x08` and `+0x10`. **None is derived from any other.** That is the
convergence test the Gi document uses for an identity claim, applied to a structural one.

Everything else in that document held, including the seven object sizes 7 of 7, six banks 6 of 6, and
the taxonomy chain end to end with a positive control on the string scan. The attacker declared a
conflict of interest — they wrote the audio boundary document, which shares five addresses — and
**re-derived those five from the image rather than from either document.**

### Recorded from the same passes

- **A census is a claim about a predicate; publish the predicate.** §15's shift census says "a small
  `CMP`" and never defines *small*. At `imm <= 0x20` the same sweep returns **59 sites in 47
  functions** against a published 29 in 19. Not a refutation — without the threshold **neither figure
  is checkable.** The conclusions survive; the *exclusivity* of the `0024Cxxx–0024Fxxx` cluster does
  not.
- **A count disagreement is a question about two populations** — for the second time in one session,
  and the same resolution. 13 against a document's 16 for functions referencing `022D94B0`; widening
  from the base address to the table's full 768-byte extent gives 16, because three functions reach
  it at a non-zero offset. The document was right and the window was one address wide. The attacker
  now treats this as **the expectation rather than the surprise**, which is the right adaptation.
- **A good heuristic over-stated becomes a false claim.** "In a region where the data cannot be read
  statically, the accessors are the schema" is sound; it was over-stated into "nothing writes the
  region". **The accessors are the schema *and* several of them are writers** — reading only the
  readers is what produced the error.

### A checker a magic token could satisfy

`audit_crossrefs.py` reported a document as ignoring the script-VM subsystem while that document was
**dispositioning script-VM callers of two hubs, in the ledger's own vocabulary.** The alias list for
that subsystem is `["scriptvm", "script vm", "ebp", "native bridge", "01-script"]`, and the ledger's
own spelling — `Script_VM_Native_Bridge` — matches none of them. `InputGameplay` had **no entry at
all** and passed only by accident, via the substring `input` inside a function name.

**The normalisation that was supposed to prevent exactly this had already been written, and stopped
one step short.** Its comment reads: *"Normalising both sides prevents a document that DOES discuss a
subsystem from being reported as ignoring it — a false finding that trains readers to distrust the
tool."* It normalises the **keys** on both sides and never adds the ledger's spelling to the
**values**. Same shape as the half-applied corrections logged above: the fix went to one side of the
comparison and not the other.

**And the consequence is worse than a false finding.** The reporting session cleared two findings by
rewriting `Script_VM_Native_Bridge` as *"script VM / native bridge"* — the substance was unchanged,
and they noted they were one careless step from "fixing" a document by pasting a keyword.

> **A checker that a magic token can satisfy teaches authors to insert the token.** A false negative
> costs one missed defect; a token-satisfiable check corrupts every document written afterwards by
> an author who has learned what the tool wants to see.

Fixed by **deriving the aliases from the ledger that produced the labels** — every owner string
contributes its own spelling, its underscores-as-spaces form, and its underscores-removed form. A
hand-maintained list drifts from the ledger it describes; a derived one cannot. Verified with a
positive control: `Script_VM_Native_Bridge` now accepted, `InputGameplay` accepted on its ledger
spelling, and a document mentioning neither still correctly reported.

### C-12 answered, and a function invisible to both censuses

The "separate subsystem" around `DAT_01E0C2B4` / `DAT_020927E0` is not a subsystem. It is
`InputGameplay_ArbitrateDigitalInputAndModalState` (`00253C70`, Input, 1,599 B) — **one input
arbitration function's private modal state.** A full-body rip-relative sweep finds *all* 4 sites of
`DAT_01E0C2B4`, *all* 5 of `DAT_020927E0` and both of `DAT_020927E4` **inside that single function**,
with a positive control on `DAT_02F97360`, which really is shared and returned all 6.

**Why nothing had found it:** it reaches the predicate **twice** — directly at `00254067` and through
the thunk at `00254232` — making it one of only two functions in the image using both routes. **The
direct census and the thunk census each saw half of it.** That is the tail-call blind spot logged
earlier, in its most instructive form: not a function hidden from one instrument, but a function
*split across two* so that neither saw a whole caller.

The mechanism: `DAT_020927E0` is a two-state gameplay toggle, flipped once per input edge with
`DAT_020927E4` as the edge latch and `DAT_01E0C2B4` as a sticky override — **and a bit-15 field
record forces it off.** What the toggle *is* remains unnamed, and the session stopped there
deliberately because naming it is another category's work. Recorded as **substantially closed**: the
question as asked is answered, the label is not.

### Disposition discipline, applied by an author to themselves

Of six crossref findings, three were hub neighbourhood, and they were dispositioned three different
ways for a stated reason:

- `WorldTransition_GetActiveOrPendingFieldId` — **deferred by reference** to the hub document, valid
  because that document's §2 does contain the census (49 callers, 11/11 subsystem rows verified).
- `Resource_SubmitRequest` (38 callers over 7 owners) and `MapRef_GetPersistenceGroupId` (19 over 5)
  — **stated inline**, because no hub document enumerates them.

> **"A deferral is not a disposition" is easy to apply to someone else's document.** Here an author
> applied it to their own, and the test they used is the right one: point at a census only when the
> census is actually there.

### The fix for the one-step-short defect was itself one step short

The alias fix above — deriving `audit_crossrefs.py`'s subsystem aliases from the ledger — was
committed as a change that could only *loosen* the check. It was not.

`doc_accounts_for` falls back to the individual words of a subsystem label **only when the key has no
alias entry**. Registering a derived key therefore **switches that fallback off**. Two owners had no
entry:

| owner | previous fallback | derived forms |
|---|---|---|
| `PlatformOnlineAchievements` | `platformonlineachievements` | identical — no change |
| `RNG_Random_Selection` | `random`, `selection` | `rng_random_selection`, `rng random selection`, `rngrandomselection` |

**A document discussing RNG in ordinary prose would have started being reported**, because none of
the three derived forms is a phrase a human writes. Fixed by keeping the word-split forms alongside
the derived ones; verified with six cases including two negative controls, and no subsystem is now
stricter than before.

> **A change that only adds accepted spellings cannot produce new findings. A change that also
> switches off a fallback can — and this one did both while being described as only the first.**

**The shape is the one this session has logged five times tonight, committed while fixing an instance
of it**: the correction went to one side of the comparison and the other side moved without anyone
noticing. It was caught because a peer asked a single question about a change to *their* documents —
*"does deriving aliases from the ledger mean a document can now be reported for a subsystem whose
ledger spelling nobody would write in prose?"* They had the direction of the risk inverted, and
asking anyway is what surfaced it.

> **A question about a change is worth answering even when the questioner's model of the risk is
> wrong.** The answer here was "no, it can only loosen" — which was false, and would have shipped
> unexamined if the question had not been asked. **Checking a peer's wrong worry against the code is
> cheaper than the false findings it prevents.**

### The residual category's flagship example has an admissible reference

`the-unresolved-158.md` §11 held `002AAE40` up as *"the purest example in the database of why a
call-context classifier cannot touch these"* — three incoming references, all exception metadata, all
banned, therefore **"no admissible reference of any kind — no caller, no vtable, no dispatch table."**

**It has one.** `00916518` in `.rdata` holds the qword `0x00000000002AAE40`, and that slot carries a
**base relocation**. Re-read from the certified program before correcting anything:
`00916518` → `40 ae 2a 00 00 00 00 00`. A relocated absolute function pointer is **tier-8 evidence,
squarely admissible.**

**The slot is absent from the reference dump entirely**, and the cause is the one already on this
log: `DumpUnresolvedIncomingDataRefContexts` reports the references *Ghidra holds*, and Ghidra holds
none from a data slot never typed as a pointer.

> **An instrument that can only return what the database was told, asked a question about the image.**
> Third time tonight, and this is the expensive one — the previous two cost a "no strings" claim and
> a count. This one is **the source of a category's founding claim**: *"96 % of the incoming
> references to these 158 are exception metadata."* That census counts only the references the
> database happens to contain, so the 96 % is an upper bound on banned-ness measured over the wrong
> population. §11 and the category README are corrected and qualified in place.

**The base-relocation move is the durable part**, and it converts a conceded limit into a certified
count. §3's limits block had conceded that a coincidental integer can match a function entry. It need
not be conceded: **every genuine absolute pointer in a PE carries a base relocation, or ASLR breaks
it.** Intersecting candidate slots with the 114,962 `DIR64` entries settles each one exactly, with
the 1,172-slot table at `008C31D8` coming back 1,172-of-1,172 as a control.

    .rdata   29,000 slots -> 27,202 real,  1,798 coincidental (6.2 %)
    .data     3,015 slots ->  3,015 real,      0 coincidental
    _RDATA        8 slots ->      0 real,      8 coincidental (100 %)

**The `_RDATA` eight were never real.** All eight qwords are `0x00800000` — simultaneously a valid
function entry and the IEEE-754 smallest normal float — sitting among `0x7F000000`-type neighbours in
a block of float bit patterns, and nothing relocates them. **The document reported 8, an independent
audit reproduced 8, and both were wrong because both used the same method.** The shared-source rule
logged earlier tonight, caught this time inside a *corroboration* rather than inside a claim.

### Two withdrawals, one of which I propagated

The session that produced the `.data` census withdrew two of its own claims, and I had repeated the
first back to it and to the user before it was caught:

1. **`.data` slots are NOT "the runtime-built dispatch tables."** `.data` spans `01DF0000`–`02F97530`
   virtually, but its **raw image covers only `01DF0000`–`01F7E400`**. All 3,015 slots are inside the
   raw range and relocated, so they are **statically initialised in the file**. The runtime-built
   regions (`022D9000`, `02AEE000`) lie far past raw, where a static scan cannot see them at all.
   **Two parts of one section conflated.** The corrected reading is sharper than the wrong one: a
   pointer statically initialised into a **writable** section is one the engine intends to be
   *replaceable*.
2. **"Nothing has been read from it" was wrong — 75.7 % was already documented.** Measured against
   the spans other documents state: **1,740** slots are ScriptVM native dispatch family 0, **339**
   the battle action handler table, **202** the combat formula step table; of the 734 outside those,
   **501 point at ScriptVM-owned functions**. Genuinely undocumented remainder: **~233 slots.**

**The coverage instrument that produced the wrong 2 was itself the finding.** Keyed on *"is any
address within 64 bytes of this run cited"*, it reported 1,959 of 1,977 runs uncited — nonsense,
because **a 1,496-record table cites its base, not its rows.** The battle action document had already
done the identical run analysis (*"226 and 62 slots. They are one table; the runs break at null
entries"*) and the test could not see it.

> **A coverage test keyed on citation distance measures how documents are written, not what they
> cover.** Fifth instrument this session to manufacture a result from a formatting assumption.

### Modder-facing, from the undocumented remainder

`malloc`, `free`, `calloc` and `realloc` are stored as function pointers in a **writable** section at
`01F41CF8` and `01F44CE0`. **That is the cleanest allocator interception point in the image — swapping
it needs no code patching at all.**

### Still open

- `PROPOSED-repos9e-12` — **who overwrites these slots at runtime.** All 3,015 are statically
  initialised; whether anything replaces them is untested, and that is the entire point of a writable
  section.
- `PROPOSED-repos9e-13` — re-census incoming references for the 158 as `.reloc`-certified data slots
  plus the existing scan.
- The `.rdata` side is now certified at **27,202 slots and unread** — nine times larger than `.data`,
  and the same relocation method applies to it unchanged.

### A correct census of the wrong population, under the right population's name

Two sessions found this independently within one tick, in unrelated documents. It is a **new shape**,
distinct from the truncation class logged earlier: there, a list was correct on every member it
contained and merely stopped short. Here **every number is correct and the set is wrong**, and the
name on the table is the name of a *different* set.

**Case 1 — `generated-float-table-builders.md`.** The document profiles "the six largest builders".
Not one of the six is a builder: none is called by either hub, and all six sit among the 131
functions the startup chain never reaches. They are the six **largest functions in an address
range**, reported as the largest members of a **functional set defined by being called from the
hubs**. Every size in that table is exact. Three of the document's failures follow from that one
substitution:

- *"The code is scalar float math"* — true of the six measured, **false of the builders.** All 65
  real builders together: 4,518 instructions, **83 % `mov`**, 1 % touching `xmm`/`ymm`, **39 scalar
  and 25 packed float operations in total.** The profiled non-builders run 42–73 % `xmm` with
  hundreds of `movss`/`mulss` each.
- *"522 KB of startup work"* — the builders total **32,848 bytes**; transitive closure reaches 66 of
  197 functions and 32,854 bytes, **6.3 %**. The 522 KB is the **address range**, attached to the
  routines.
- The characterisation went into the **title**.

> **Name the predicate that selected the rows, next to the rows.** A table caption names the
> population; nothing names the selector, and when the two differ every correct number in the table
> is evidence for the wrong claim.

**Case 2 — the `.data` function-pointer slots.** The claim *"which matters because `.data` slots are
runtime-built dispatch tables rather than static vtables"* is not merely unsupported, it is
**backwards**, and the same session proved it from the image: `.data` runs `01DF0000`–`02F97530` with
raw size `0x18E400`, so it is file-backed only to **`01F7E400`** — **91.2 % of `.data` has no file
image** and is zero at load. **All 3,015 counted slots lie below that boundary**, so every one is
statically initialised in the file. A genuinely runtime-built slot is zero in the file and
**invisible to that scan by construction** — the audio registry singleton `01FD36A0`, the audio gate
`02091098` and the transform workbench `022D8F00` all sit above the boundary and contribute
**nothing** to the 3,015.

**The fact that settles it was already in the database when the claim was written** —
`the-shared-transform-workbench.md` §8 derives the same `01F7E400` boundary from the same PE fields.

**And a failing positive control is what exposed it.** The session seeded its scan with `02EAD0B8`,
an audio function pointer it had proven in an earlier block, and it came back **absent**.

> **The control failing was the finding.** Had the control been drawn from inside the file-backed
> range, the scan would have looked sound and the framing would have been inherited whole. A control
> chosen from the same region as the expected answer tests nothing.

### An assignment generated from a document's claim inherits that document's errors

**This one is mine.** I routed a session onto the `.data` population using two claims — *"runtime-built
dispatch tables"* and *"nothing has been read from it"* — that I had taken from a peer report and
repeated without testing. Both were wrong, and the receiving session spent its opening minutes
discovering that rather than working.

Their process note is now standing practice:

> **Run the neighbour check before *accepting* an assignment, not only before attacking a document.**

The premise was checkable in about two minutes. **Most of that population had already been read**: a
380-entry table at `01EEC460` and a 202-slot run at `01EFA5C0` are both fully documented, in
`battle-action-handler-table.md` (same base, 341 live entries, the same 249 sharing one handler, both
consumers read, already survived a pass) and `combat-formula-step-table.md` (same base, same 202,
**the same 42 no-ops**, with the `ret 0` body quoted).

**The sixth catch by the cross-document check, and the first to prevent an entire duplicate
document.** I have been describing that check as a way to find errors. It is also the cheapest
defence against *doing work that exists*.

### Three instrument errors, all from one assumption

- **Skipping zero slots fragments a table with null entries.** Run-clustering split one 341-entry
  table into 37/16/226/62 because 22 entries are NULL. **A run boundary is not a table boundary.**
- **A contiguous run is not necessarily a table.** A 202-slot run looked like a bank of
  individually-called slots from 24 `call [rip+d]` sites — but those reach only **11 distinct slots**
  of 202, and **none of the 11 holds the stub.** The nearly-published claim "42 of these calls do
  nothing" would have been false.
- **A span walked outward over-extends.** A 380-entry span ran past the end into floats — and
  `battle-action-handler-table.md` §5 already records correcting *"an earlier attempt over-extended
  the table to 380 slots by walking outward"*. **A previous session's error, reproduced exactly, with
  the fix sitting in the document the neighbour check had already pointed at.**

### The count disagreement, third pass running

487 sites / 88 callers against a published 142 / 45. §3 says *"Reach from **outside**"*; restricting
to callers outside the range gives **exactly 142 / 45**, the other 345 being intra-region. Same
resolution three passes running — and this time it was used *forwards*: the session checked whether
`26 + 40` versus `75` could be a population difference **before** reporting it, and established that
it could not, both figures being the document's own in the same code block.

> **A count disagreement is a question about two populations — and once that is a habit, it also
> tells you when a disagreement is *not* one.**

### Decided, not yet actioned

`generated-float-table-builders.md`'s **title names the characterisation this pass overturned.** The
builders are generated-table **writers**; the float code in that address range is something the
startup chain never calls. The rename is correct and is a Phase E move — deferred only because a
rename touches 988 resolved links while other sessions hold the file, not because it is in doubt.

**The highest-value follow-up is now an extraction rather than a question.** `00485390` reads
`memset(obj, 0, 0xDC0)` — the object size as an immediate — then a long run of `mov [obj+off], imm`
with `0x3f800000` (`1.0f`) stored as an **integer** immediate. So *"the data has no file image, so
every value in it is computed rather than read"* has a right first clause and a wrong inference:
**"no file image" was measured on the destination and asserted about the source.** Each builder's
`memset` immediate gives its object's size — `0xDC0` = 3,520, **which is the largest inter-target gap
the document had already observed and not connected** — and the store run gives the contents. **The
66 objects are decodable from the executable without running it.**

### 156 of 158 — the residual category's barrier was never the evidence

The re-census of incoming references for all 158 unresolved functions, run as `.reloc`-certified data
slots plus verified `LEA` decoding plus the call graph:

| incoming evidence | of the 158 |
|---|---:|
| direct caller in the call graph | 143 |
| verified RIP-relative `LEA` | 12 |
| relocated data slot pointing at the entry | 1 |
| relocated data slot pointing into a body | 0 |
| **at least one admissible reference** | **156** |
| **no admissible reference of any kind** | **2** |

The 15 without a direct caller match §10's caller-less count **exactly**, which is the internal check
this census did not claim and passes.

> **The barrier was never the evidence. It was the census.** For **13 of the 15** caller-less
> functions the classifiers had admissible evidence available and the instrument did not surface it.
> **Exactly one function in the residual was ever genuinely without a handle.**

**The flagship claim survives with a different subject, and the new subject is better.** §11 built
its case on `002AAE40`, which turned out to have a relocated pointer. The two with nothing are
`0020AC30` and `00392A10`, and they are not equally dark: `0020AC30` has **no incoming evidence but
strong outgoing** — `.json`, `spc_`, `sum_` directly, and one call deeper `JsonData/CutScenes/`,
`mDofFocusDistance`, a `plan_master\…\event\` regex. **`00392A10` (707 B) has neither, and has never
been mentioned anywhere in this database.** §11 and the category README are updated.

**This is what a fixed population and a published predicate buy.** The task was routed to the session
that found the original defect, over its own objection that it would be extending its own reading.
The distinction that made it safe holds up: **the population was enumerated by someone else, the
predicate was published before the scan, and the answer landed where the author would not have
steered it** — the function the category's case rested on turned out not to be the dark one, and the
actual dark one is a function nobody has ever mentioned. **Self-extension could not have produced
that.**

### An instrument that both omits and invents

The two earlier defects in this family were about **absence** — references Ghidra was never told
about. This one is **presence**. Of the 16 rows the dump credits as real code references, **two are
not references at all.** Both decoded from the image and re-read here byte for byte before the
correction was applied:

```
0023F06E   48 89 83 20 01 00 00           mov [rbx+0x120], rax
                                          the STORE of an address the previous instruction loaded --
                                          one address-taking counted as two references
002A756C   81 8b e8 03 00 00 00 20 40 00  or dword ptr [rbx+0x3E8], 0x402000
                                          an immediate BITMASK that equals a function entry
```

So *"16 across 13 functions"* is **14 across 12**, and **`00402000` is not address-taken in code at
all** — its only credited code reference is an OR-mask constant, and it keeps admissible status
solely through a direct caller.

> **An instrument that both invents and omits cannot be corrected by moving the number in one
> direction.** The category's founding figure is an upper bound on banned-ness **and** a lower bound
> on admissibility at the same time. The README qualification written earlier tonight had only the
> first half.

**And the way the two bogus rows surfaced is the method worth copying.** Control 1 — *recover the
dump's own 16 rows* — **failed**, on exactly those two. The session diagnosed before adjusting
anything, decoded both sites from the image, and only then changed the control's expectation.

> **A failing control is a question about which side is wrong, not a defect in the scanner.** Had
> that control been skipped, the published result would have been "12 code references" against a
> stated 13, with a quiet assumption that the new scanner was lossy — **the correct answer discarded
> as instrument error.**

**Predicate and blind spots published with the number**, per the rule adopted earlier: the scan
matches the `LEA` form only — a `mov reg,imm64` address-taking would be missed, and none of the 16
uses that form, which is not proof none exists — and it is restricted to the file image, where 91 %
of `.data` does not live. **So 156 is a floor and "2 of 158" is a ceiling. The number can only move
one way**, which is the property a census needs before anyone builds on it.

### A fix that reproduces the defect it fixed, at a scale that looks like broader confirmation

**New class, and the most dangerous one recorded tonight**, because the reproduction *feels* like
stronger evidence than the original.

`scriptvm-native-dispatch-table.md` had already corrected an over-extended table extent once — the
familiar walking-outward error. The extent adopted to fix it re-entered the same defect **307 records
deep into a different table**:

```
1,496 records : 1,739 slots   +0:1234  +8:276  +16:229  +24:  0   ScriptVM / Movement / Party
1,960 records : 1,941 slots   +0:1285  +8:327  +16:279  +24: 50   + CombatFormula 160
```

At 1,496 records **nothing occupies `+24`** — which is precisely that document's own *"no record
carries four handlers"* correction, **reproduced by an instrument that had never read it.** At 1,960
the `+24` slot fills and 160 `CombatFormula` pointers appear, because **`01EFA5C0`, the combat
formula step table's base, is exactly record 1653 of that frame**: `(0x01EFA5C0 − 0x01EED720) / 0x20
= 1653.00`.

> **The 1,960 sweep felt stronger than the 1,496 one precisely because it covered more — and
> covering more is what broke it.** A wider population reads as a more thorough measurement, so a
> defect that scales with the window arrives wearing the clothes of extra confirmation.

The `+24`-is-null result **stands**; the frame it was verified in does **not**. Corrected in place
with both censuses shown, so the next reader sees why the extent matters rather than only a smaller
number. This is not the false-corroboration family — the figures are not derived from each other —
it is a **fix that regenerates its own defect one table over**.

### The residual lead, bounded and given a structure

**Of the 158, exactly one has a relocation-certified `.rdata` pointer.** The other 157 have none —
**a single admissible lead, not a class of them.** That bound is as valuable as the finding, and it
was missing from the original flag.

`00916518` is **index 11 of a 12-entry sparse table at `009164C0`**, re-read from the certified
program before recording:

```
009164C0  002A9980  002A8C50  002A9F00  002A9980     idx 0-3
009164E0  002A8C50  002AA800  00000000  00000000     idx 4-7
00916500  00000000  00000000  00000000  002AAE40     idx 8-11
00916520  00000001  0000000A  ...                    power-of-ten table begins
```

Seven populated slots, five distinct targets, five NULL holes, and three `.text` sites taking the
table's address — `002ABEFD` and `002ABF4D` (→ `009164C8`), `002B393C` (→ `009164C0`).

**So `002AAE40` gains a structural identity without any claim about what it does**: entry 11 of a
dispatch table shared with five named functions, reached from three named sites. The power-of-ten
table next door is recorded as a **layout fact only** — adjacency is banned and was explicitly not
offered as evidence of purpose, which is the correct handling of a suggestive neighbourhood.

### The ScriptVM population is both, and the fourth face of one instrument error

**1,685** certified slots fall inside the documented table; the earlier *"1,535 singletons"* was
**run-clustering fragmenting 32-byte records** — the same assumption that split a 341-entry table
into 37/16/226/62 and over-extended a span to 380. **Four faces of one instrument error, all from
treating a run boundary as a structural boundary.**

**502 slots fall outside**, in 8 clusters — largest `01F28D30`–`01F2A140` at 187 slots, then 89 / 83
/ 77 / 28 — **all targeting `0050Dxxx`, and described nowhere.** Correctly handed over as a lead with
**no claim that they are a table**: the record structure is not established.

### Predicate, published

A slot is certified iff **P1** 8-byte aligned and inside the section's **raw** extent; **P2** non-zero
qword; **P3** the value is a known function entry; **P4** the slot carries a `DIR64` base relocation.

**P1 is the limiting clause** — `.data` is file-backed only to `01F7E400`, so the census is blind to
**91.2 %** of it by construction. Every count is *"statically initialised slots"*, never *"slots"*.
Reproduced exactly at 27,202 / 3,015 / 0 from 114,962 `DIR64` entries, with two controls: **7 of 7**
structures derived in earlier blocks recovered blind, and `_RDATA` returning 0.

### Five ScriptVM command tables, enumerated from the bound the code enforces

All three accessors — `003DC270` begin, `003DC240` poll, `003DC2A0` result — execute
`cmp edx, dword ptr [rcx]` against **the table's own first dword** before indexing. **The extent is a
value the code reads on every access**, so it never had to be inferred.

```
family 0   01EED700   1,496 records   ids 0x0000-0x05D7   1,741 non-null callbacks
family 3   01F281B0     147           ids 0x3000-0x3092     153
family 5   01F29418       1           id  0x5000              2
family 7   01F29440     104           ids 0x7000-0x7067     131
default    01F26720     212           ids 0xN000-0xN0D3     250   (shared by the other twelve)
                     = 1,960                              = 2,277
```

Verified here: `01F281B0` → `93 00 00 00` = **147**. **1,960 is the total that document already
stated, reached from five independent counts rather than from the same source.**

~~**The four tables abut exactly.**~~ **CORRECTED within the hour by an independent enumeration,
and the base was wrong too.** Both re-read here from the certified program:

- **The default table's base is `01F26720`, not `01F26728`.** `01F26720` -> `d4 00 00 00` = **212**,
  the count, exactly as at the other four bases; `01F26728` -> `60 d6 50 00` = `0050D660`, **a
  function pointer** — record 0's `+0x08` field. Taking `01F26728` as the base reads a count of
  **5,297,760**.
- **The tables do not abut.** Laid end to end the extents leave **16, 8 and 8 bytes of slack**:

```
default   01F26720 -> 01F281A0    next base 01F281B0    gap 16 B
family 3  01F281B0 -> 01F29410    next base 01F29418    gap  8 B
family 5  01F29418 -> 01F29438    next base 01F29440    gap  8 B
```

**The conclusion survives and the reason changes.** "No gap at all" was offered as the
*explanation* for why a contents walk cannot find these edges. The gaps exist — they are simply
**too small and too irregular to read as terminators.** The boundary is still the declared count
and nothing else.

> **An explanation is a claim and needs the same evidence as the finding it explains.** The
> finding — that the extent comes from the consumer's bounds check — was proven from three
> accessors. The explanation attached to it was asserted from a glance at the addresses,
> published inside the same paragraph, and was wrong in the one direction that made it more
> persuasive.

**And the independent enumeration adds a result neither version had.** No family uses the `+0x18`
field — **0 occurrences across all four installed tables, each swept only to its own declared
count.** That turns *"no record carries four handlers"* from a claim verified in one guessed frame
into one verified in four declared ones, and it retires the 1,960-record extent cleanly: **with
real extents there is no over-run to produce phantom `+0x18` pointers.**

`VMNativeCommandDispatch_InitializeFamilyTables` installs four bases into an array indexed
`[array + family*8]`, so the destination globals give the family numbers directly: **0, 3, 5, 7 —
families 1, 2, 4 and 6 are never installed**, which is why the accessor null-checks before touching
the pointer.

> **This is the cleanest demonstration yet of why the consumer has to be asked.** A contents walk
> cannot find these edges, because there is nothing at the edges to find. Every earlier instance of
> this rule involved a boundary that was merely *hard* to see; here there is no boundary in the data
> at all, only in the code.

**The id encoding, proven from the consumer.** `VMNativeCommand_ExecuteLifecycle` (`002621D0`, 461 B)
is the sole caller of all three accessors and splits before calling: `sar r12d, 0xc` /
`and r15d, 0xfff` — **family = id >> 12, index = id & 0xFFF**, a 4-bit family and 12-bit index.
Confirmed from the far end by prior spawn work: authored primitive `0x3053` → family 3 index `0x53`,
result callback `thunk_FUN_0023a520`, **reached from the script side without knowing this frame.**

**The 501 resolves as an attribution difference, not an extent one.** The four tables hold 536
non-null `.text` pointers, 500 of them `Script_VM_Native_Bridge`-owned, against a census figure of
501 — one slot. The ~233-slot genuinely undocumented remainder is untouched.

### The author's own rule did not protect the author

Enumerating family 3 disproved the same session's earlier spawn document, **in both of the classes it
has spent this session finding in other people's work**:

- *"the primitive table lives at `01F281D0`, 252 records of `0x20`"* — **`01F281D0` is not a base.**
  It is `01F281B0 + 0x20`, the **result-callback column**. The count is the dword at `01F281B0` and
  it is **147**. The 252 came from walking while entries looked like code-or-null, **running 105
  records past the end into the abutting family 5 and 7 tables** — which is exactly what "abut
  exactly, no terminator" predicts will happen to a contents walk.
- **The frame was one column off**, the same defect §12 of the dispatch document records for family
  0. Every handler named was a **result** callback, with begin and poll null.

No mapping changed — the highest index used is `0x06C`, well inside 147, and all nine were re-verified
in the correct frame. Both corrections recorded in place and attributed.

> **They wrote *"do not infer an array's extent from its contents when the code that walks it is
> available"* as the lesson of the VBF pass, and had already broken it two blocks earlier in their own
> document.** Their summary is the entry: *the rule I proposed was correct and stating it did not
> protect me from it. What caught it was doing the same kind of work again on an adjacent table — not
> review, not a checker, and not care.*

**That is the strongest argument yet for the falsification programme over any amount of checking.** A
rule is a thing you apply to the work in front of you; it does not reach backwards into work already
published. **Only redoing the work does that.**

### `check_generator_artifacts.py` — every gate was green with code in the prose

Two patch scripts mixed `'''` and `\"\"\"` conventions in one file and **leaked the delimiters into a
published document** — a literal `''' + EM + u'''` in live prose. **`check_links.py`,
`verify_doc_addresses.py` and `check_consistency.py` were all green with it there.** They check
links, addresses and cross-document agreement; **none of them looks at whether the text is text.**

> **A generator that produced something other than what it meant to leaves no trace any
> content-level checker can see.** The whole database is written by scripts appending markdown, so
> this is a permanent exposure, not one session's slip. It was caught by reading the rendered
> output — which does not scale and does not run in CI.

Now checked: triple quotes, prefixed literals, quote-adjacent variable concatenation, unexpanded
format calls, literal `\\n` and `\\x` escapes — skipping code fences and inline spans, where quoted
code is the document doing its job. Ships `--self-test`. **Database sweep: clean.**

**And it manufactured a false positive on its first run, which is now the fifth instance of that
pattern.** `\+\s+[A-Z_]+\s+\+` matched *"image-base + RVA + index, and absolute"* — ordinary prose
describing an address computation. Tightened to require an adjacent quote, since **it is the
delimiter that makes it code**.

> **A pattern for "code in prose" that matches arithmetic has not understood the difference between
> the two.**

### Schedule passes by mechanism adjacency, not category balance

A refinement to the falsification-over-checking entry above, from the session whose self-report
produced it — and it bounds the claim in a way I had not:

> **Redoing the work caught my error because the second piece of work was adjacent enough to force
> the same question. If I had gone from the spawn tables to an audio document, nothing would have
> surfaced it.**

So the rule is **not** "redoing work catches your errors". It is **"work that re-asks the same
question does"** — and that is a scheduling instruction, not an observation. **Where a session has
just published a claim about a *shape*, route its next block at another instance of that shape**, not
at whatever keeps the category counts level.

Tonight's evidence is unambiguous, and it is the same mechanism every time:

| session | published a claim about | met the same shape again | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| spawn tables | table extent from contents | ScriptVM family 3 | **own error found**, 105 records over |
| `.data` slots | run boundaries | ScriptVM records | **own "1,535 singletons" found** to be fragmentation |
| dispatch extent | over-extension, already fixed once | combat formula table | **fix found to regenerate its own defect** |

**Three self-catches, all from mechanism adjacency, none from review and none from a checker.**
Category balance would have prevented all three.

### A second routing collision, and the cause is the same as the first

I assigned two sessions overlapping work: one was routed onto 502 uncharacterised slots while the
session holding the adjacent question was enumerating the tables those slots belong to. It resolved
as a **one-slot attribution difference**, not an extent difference — the clusters *were* the tables.

**Both collisions tonight have the same cause: I routed on who had capacity rather than on who was
already inside the mechanism.** The first shipped a withdrawn premise as an assignment; this one
handed a session a lead another session was already closing.

> **Mechanism adjacency is not only how self-catches happen — it is also how collisions happen.** The
> same property that makes a session likely to falsify its own claim makes it likely to reach a
> neighbouring question first. A coordinator who ignores adjacency gets neither the catch nor the
> deconfliction.

Not wasted, and worth recording as the consolation: the cluster boundaries derived **from the data
side** landed exactly where the record counts split the tables — an independent arrival at the same
partition, by a session that could not see the bounds checks. **Two routes, one partition.**

### Recomputing a remainder whose predicate moved

The ~233-slot "genuinely undocumented remainder" is claimed, with the right first step: **recount it
before characterising it.** Its definition is *"outside every documented span"*, and **536 slots
acquired a home in the last hour**, so the population the figure names is not the population it was
measured over.

> **A remainder is defined by a subtraction, so it changes whenever anything else is documented — and
> nothing in the figure announces that.** It is the one quantity in this database that silently goes
> stale on someone else's success.

### The residual has one honest exception, and it is a dead nine-patch box renderer

`00392A10` — the only function of the 158 with neither incoming nor outgoing evidence — is read. It
is a **resizable bordered box drawn as a 3×3 patch**: four fixed corners, a stretched middle row and
column, tinted by a bilinear gradient built from four corner colours.

```
colWidth[1]  = totalWidth  - rightColumnWidth - leftColumnWidth;
rowHeight[1] = totalHeight - bottomRowHeight  - topRowHeight;
```

**Complete, coherent, and unreachable by every static route** — four of them, each controlled:

1. call graph: zero incoming edges. **Verified here against `graph/edges.tsv`: 0 as target, 6 as
   source.**
2. every `E8`/`E9` in `.text` decoded: none reach it. *Control:* the same scan recovers the three
   known edges **out of** it. PASS
3. every RIP-relative `LEA`: none targets it — **and the `MOV r64,imm64` blind spot published in the
   re-census predicate is empty for this binary.** The form occurs 1,413 times in `.text` and **not
   one carries a base relocation**, so none encodes an image address; MSVC under `/DYNAMICBASE`
   materialises code addresses with RIP-relative `LEA`.
4. the 8-byte and 4-byte encodings of its address occur **zero times anywhere in the file**.

> Stated as **"unreachable by every static route"**, not "never executes". Static analysis cannot
> establish the latter, and the document says so rather than letting the stronger phrasing stand.

**Route 3 is the important one beyond this function.** A blind spot was published honestly in an
earlier predicate — *a `mov reg,imm64` address-taking would be missed, and none of the 16 uses that
form, which is not proof none exists.* It has now been **closed for this binary by measurement**: the
form is present 1,413 times and never relocated. **A declared limitation, retired by testing it
rather than by arguing it away.**

**It is the root of a dead island: five functions, 4,090 bytes** — verified from the ledger as
707 + 589 + 2,194 + 268 + 332. `00392CE0`, `002DC7F0`, `002DD1E0` and `002DD090` are each called
**only** by `00392A10`; **3,490 bytes of the island sit inside the residual.**

**The dead code calls live code; nothing live calls the dead code.** Two callees are not dead —
`002DC290` (11 callers, the cell drawer the game actually uses) and `002DD4B0` (10 callers) — and the
dead renderer's own fallback path routes into `002DC290`, **which is exactly why half of it looks
unremarkable on a first read.**

**A vacuous control caught one step earlier than last time.** The first version of route 3 required
the relocation up front, matched nothing at all, and would have produced a zero indistinguishable
from a finding. Re-run without that requirement the matcher fires 1,413 times, so **the zero became a
measurement.** Same species as the `_RDATA` eight — **caught before it reached a claim rather than
after.**

**Do-not-confuse, correctly not over-claimed:** `002D6990`
`ThreeByThreeAtlasPatchGeometryBuild` is a **different, live** 3×3 mechanism with two callers and a
disjoint callee set. The engine has a working 3×3 patch system *and* this dead one; whether one
superseded the other is **not claimed**.

**Modding fact:** the middle extent is computed by subtraction with **no clamp**. A box narrower than
`left + right` yields a negative centre column and the loop draws with a negative size rather than
skipping.

> **The residual now has zero functions that are unexplained in a way that is a statement about the
> binary rather than about our instruments.** Every one of the 158 either has admissible incoming
> evidence, or — in this single case — has been shown to have none *because nothing calls it*. The
> category's premise has moved from *"the evidence has run out"* to *"the evidence was there and the
> census could not see it"*, with exactly one honest exception, now documented.

### R2 toggles force fight mode, and a town pins it

The two-state toggle left unnamed earlier is identified — **not by guessing from the button, but by
chasing the value into its writer.**

`R2 held` → `InputGameplay_ArbitrateDigitalInputAndModalState` flips `DAT_020927E0` once per press →
`FUN_00252B60` re-decides it against the capability mask → `FUN_00252C80` writes `01E0C2B8`, which is
**force fight mode** — the flag this database already documents from the game's own script verb
`setforcefightmode`.

**The input is nailed by lookup, not inference.** `FUN_0017DE10` calls
`GetBinding(profile 0, group 0, slot 9)`, and the name table at `01DF11E0` gives group 0 slot 9 =
**R2**. The binding document's own finding — *"the name's index is the slot's index"* — is what makes
that a lookup. **And the signature was not taken on trust:** `00197710`'s complete 99-byte body was
re-derived (`r8b` selects one of three tables at `+0x00`/`+0x40`/`+0x60` off base `01F80F90`, `dl`
scales by `0x1C` dwords, `r9b` indexes) and matches both the documented signature and that document's
worked example `GetBinding(0,2,0) = Speed1`. **Had it not matched, "slot 9 = R2" was wrong and
everything above it with it.**

**The polarity is inverted, and this is the part to protect.** In `FUN_00252C80`, `state == 0`
**sets** the flag and `state != 0` **clears** it. So **the button's job in the field is to clear force
fight mode, and a town restores the engine's default.** `force-fight-mode.md` already warns about its
predicate's polarity; **this is a second inversion one level up**, and reading the toggle as "the mode
is on" gets it exactly backwards.

**The pin has two independent routes to the same outcome** — the release path's direct
`FieldRecordBit15()` test, and capability policy row 2 bit 10, which the same field-record bit drives.
**That is why holding the button does not defeat it.**

> **Follow the output, not the input.** The tempting route was to reason from R2 to a plausible
> feature. The route that worked was the opposite: chase the value into its writer, find it writing a
> global the database had already named **from authored script vocabulary**, and let the name come
> back up the chain. **The button was the last thing identified, not the first.**

**And the on-screen label is still not claimed.** The output is identified; what the mode looks like
to a player is not, the document is PARTIAL because of it, and the FFXII-shaped candidates that could
have been reached for are exactly the suggestive-evidence trap.

**Two closures filed for another category's owner rather than edited** — AN-2 (`FUN_00252C80` is this
toggle's applier, complete 134-byte body) and AN-5 (**it cannot**: the final store is `enable ? 1 : 0`
exactly like the setter's; the only window is inside `003BA2E0`, which reads only its two byte globals
and never the flag; cross-thread observability filed as a question rather than claimed either way).

**A count that is right twice over:** a *"15 consumers"* row is correct as **call sites**; the
distinct-function count is **13** (7 direct + 6 through thunk `0030C0D0`), because
`BattleLocomotion_ComputeStepDistance` calls it more than once — and that document's own pass already
says *"8 direct E8 sites"*, sites not callers. **Both numbers correct, answering different questions.**
Fourth instance of the population rule tonight, and the second where nothing was wrong.

**Four body sizes were wrong in a first draft and caught by checking each row against
`functions.tsv` before publishing** — rather than by BODY DRIFT afterwards. Two of those functions

### The loop is the schema

Five consecutive blocks have ended the same way: **a consumer stated an extent nobody had asked it
for.** The generalisation that has been forming is bigger than arrays, and this is its final form:

> **Where a structure is built or walked by a loop, the loop is the schema.** Bounds, stride and
> field offsets all fall out of one function, and reading it is cheaper than any amount of inference
> from the data.

`InventoryRuntime_RebaseClassDescriptorsAndClearDerivedState` (`0030B6A0`) proves it in **195 bytes**:

```
lea r8,[01EEBCC0]  …  lea rbx,[01EEC1E8]  …  add r8,0x58  /  cmp r8,rbx
0x528 / 0x58 = 15 exactly
```

Fifteen inventory class descriptors of 88 bytes — **and the rebaser hands over the record layout for
free**: three rebased offset→pointer fields, an element count at `+0x3C`, a running cumulative index
at `+0x40`, and the two callbacks at `+0x48` (mutate) and `+0x50` (query), which are **precisely the
slots the census had been counting as loose pointers.** The pairs are `InventoryPackedCountClass_*`
and `InventoryBitsetClass_*` — **two storage classes shared across fifteen descriptors**, which is why
the same addresses repeat down the table.

**Extent *and* layout, from one function.** Every previous instance of this rule delivered only the
extent.

### An owner-keyed estimate of a span-keyed quantity is systematically low

The undocumented remainder recounts to **198**, not the estimated ~233 — and the 35-slot gap is **not
arithmetic, it is a predicate mismatch.**

```
family 0 / battle action / combat formula        1,740 / 340 / 202
default / family 3 / family 5 / family 7           250 / 153 /   2 / 130
inside a documented span                         2,817
REMAINDER                                          198
```

**535 slots acquired a home — 34 more than the 501 the estimate anticipated.** The estimate subtracted
by **target ownership** ("slots pointing at `Script_VM_Native_Bridge`-owned functions") where the
remainder's own definition subtracts by **span membership**. Those four tables hold **35 callbacks
pointing at functions owned by other subsystems or by nobody** — a command table is perfectly entitled
to call out of its own subsystem.

> **So the estimate was low by exactly the cross-subsystem callbacks — which are the interesting rows
> in any dispatch table.** It was biased in the direction that hides the thing you would most want to
> find. **A proxy predicate does not merely approximate the real one; it fails on precisely the cases
> that differ, and those are rarely the boring ones.**

The instrument was confirmed before the recount rested on it: **114,962 `DIR64` relocations and 3,015
certified `.data` slots, both reproduced exactly on an independent implementation.**

### The gates are not atomic against concurrent edits

A `NAME` disagreement appeared on one `check_consistency` run and was gone on the next: another
session was mid-write. **With several sessions writing, a single red gate result is not evidence
until it is re-run.**

Recorded in the inbox README. It is the cheapest possible defence against the worst outcome — a
session "correcting" a document to satisfy a gate that was never really red, which is the
token-satisfaction failure in a new costume.

### The proxy-predicate bias, measured

The prediction — *wherever this database has used an owner tag to stand in for a span, the misses
should concentrate in cross-subsystem edges* — is checkable against the call graph directly, so it
has been checked rather than remembered.

Over all 88,468 edges with both ends in the ledger, restricted to the **14,267 where both ends carry
an owner**:

```
same owner          10,918   76.5 %
CROSS owner          3,349   23.5 %
```

> **Owner-keyed proxies for span membership miss about one edge in four.** That is the size of the
> bias, and it is not a rounding error — it is the difference between "this table belongs to
> subsystem X" and "this table's callbacks all belong to subsystem X", which are different claims
> that look identical in prose.

**The base rate predicts the specific finding that raised the question.** The four ScriptVM command
tables held **35 callbacks pointing outside their own subsystem**, and the top cross-owner directions
image-wide are:

```
Presentation             -> CoreRuntimeScheduling    418
Script_VM_Native_Bridge  -> ActorEntity              233
Script_VM_Native_Bridge  -> Movement                 230
Presentation             -> Resource                 148
Movement                 -> ActorEntity              122
```

**`Script_VM_Native_Bridge` is the second and third largest cross-subsystem caller in the image.** A
command table whose whole purpose is to invoke engine behaviour on behalf of scripts is *structurally
guaranteed* to point out of its own subsystem — so an owner-keyed census of a script dispatch table is
biased **exactly where that table is doing its job.**

**83.9 % of edges have at least one untagged end**, which is worth stating beside the ratio: the 23.5 %
is measured over the tagged subset and is a claim about that subset. It is the population where an
owner-keyed proxy would actually be used, so it is the right denominator for this question — but it
is not "23.5 % of the call graph".
