### A census whose instrument undercounts its own denominator

The first partition returned **14.4 %** in vtables. The cause: the type-descriptor regex required the
mangled name to begin with a letter, **silently dropping every template class** — names beginning
`?$` — and recovering 640 of 2,335.

**What caught it was that 640 contradicted a figure already on file** (~2,350 RTTI markers ship in
this image) — **not** that the partition looked wrong. **At 14.4 % it read as an interesting finding
about how little of `.rdata` is vtables.**

> **A census whose instrument undercounts its own denominator produces a plausible number, not an
> obvious failure.** Same shape as the printable-byte filter that returned zero diagnostic strings and
> the `0x`-prefix displacement regex that lost one vtable slot in twenty. **Three instruments tonight,
> three plausible wrong numbers, every one caught by a figure from outside the instrument rather than
> by the result looking odd.**

That is the operational form of the rule: an instrument cannot be validated by whether its output is
interesting. It needs a number it did not produce.

### The database has outgrown its own index

Three assignments in a row were premised on a population being unread, and **all three turned out to
be mostly documented**: `.data` (75.7 % covered), the 502 (entirely), `.rdata` (99.02 %).

> **This is not a routing failure. The database has grown faster than its own index of what it
> contains, and the cross-document neighbour check is currently the only thing detecting it.**

That check has now caught seven things, and **four of them are "this already exists"** rather than
"this is wrong". It is doing two different jobs and only one of them was designed for.

**Consequence for coordination:** a target is not a task until someone has asked whether it is already
written down, and **that question is cheaper than the work it replaces** — about two minutes against
several hours, three times over tonight. It belongs at assignment time, which is where the standing
practice now puts it.

### The registrar is the schema, when there is no loop

`01F32xxx` closed, and the pre-published hypothesis — base, stride `0x80`, five records — was wrong
in the way its author flagged it might be, **but not for the reason predicted.** There is no array,
no stride, and no loop.

Five **individually declared descriptors**, each beginning with a `char *name`. Verified here:
`01F32110` → `00D8D6C8` → `"Skin\0"`, immediately followed by `"SkinLocal\0"`.

```
01F32110  Skin              +40 006D5CC0   +48 006D5DF0
01F32190  SkinLocal         +40 006D5B60   +48 006D5DF0
01F32210  SkinLocalTangent  +40 006D5B60   +48 006D63D0
01F32290  SkinVertex        +40 006D5CC0   +48 006D6AC0
01F32310  SkinVertexLocal   +40 006D5B60   +48 006D6AC0
```

**Five named skinning variants — the mesh-deformation paths a character model goes through.** And the
two callbacks are **orthogonal discriminators**, shown by which pointers repeat rather than by reading
either function: **`+0x40` selects space** (`006D5B60` for every `…Local` name, `006D5CC0` for the two
without), **`+0x48` selects output kind** (plain / tangent / vertex). Five of six combinations exist.
**A structure recovered entirely from repetition.**

**The registry never learns a record's size.** `FUN_006D5A60` (132 B) is a linked-list insert keyed on
the name — refuse if null, refuse on duplicate, else `record->next = head; head = record`, head at
`02E9FD60`. So a record is `{char *name; Record *next; …}` and **records of two different sizes go
through the same registrar.**

> **"Stride" was the wrong question, not a question with a wrong answer.** The loop-is-the-schema rule
> has a precondition — a loop — and when it fails the answer is not "unbounded", it is **look for
> whatever else states it.** Here it is the registration sites: `FUN_006C45F0` performs 14
> registrations, `FUN_006C4750` the matching 14 unregistrations. **Fourteen established**, of which
> five are the Skin family and nine are a different record type at `02E9FEF0 + k*0xD0`.

**The author's own pre-stated dichotomy was too narrow** — it allowed for *"a loop states it"* and
*"nothing states it"*, and missed **"something else states it."** That is the more useful correction
than the hypothesis being wrong, because the dichotomy is what a reader would have inherited.

### A remainder run can be a fragment of a mostly invisible population

**Why only five of fourteen reached the census:** `.data`'s raw extent ends at `01F7E400`. The five
Skin records are **below** it — statically initialised, relocated, file-backed — so their callbacks
satisfy the five-condition test. **The nine are above it in the zero-filled tail**: no file image, no
relocations, names null in the file, built at run time.

> **A run appearing in a remainder may be a fragment of a population that is mostly invisible to the
> test.** That is different from a run being the whole of something small, **and nothing in the run
> says which.** Anyone treating a remainder run as a complete object needs to establish which they
> have. Here the instrument could see 5 of 14.

### Prefer instruments that produce named output

A registration-site scan counted `call` and reported **13**. The fourteenth is a **tail jump** —
`lea rcx,[01F32310]` / `add rsp,0x28` / `jmp 0x6d5a50` at `006C4734`.

**Third time tonight the tail-call-as-sink effect has cost something**, and this instance is the one
that matters: the same session had written up two other tools' tail-call blind spots earlier in the
session, **and then built the same blind spot into its own scan.**

> **A census of call sites that does not count tail jumps is not a census of call sites — and having
> said so twice did not help.** Second instance of *a rule protects the work in front of you and
> nothing else*, now from the same author who supplied the first.

**What actually caught it was a semantic regularity: four `Skin*` variants with an obvious fifth
missing.** Not the rule, not a checker, not review.

> **The cheapest general defence is not more rules but preferring instruments that produce NAMED
> output. A gap in a name series is visible; a gap in an address series is not.**

That is the strongest methodological claim of the session, and it explains several earlier catches
retrospectively — the missing `GiPrim` reserve site, the template classes dropped from an RTTI regex,
the `Skin` variant. **All were found because something had a name and the name had a hole in it.**

### A cutscene is cinematically focused because someone named its asset so it would be

`0020AC30` records which cutscene asset occupies each of five slots and decides **from the name**
whether that scene gets a depth-of-field sidecar:

```
found("sum_")  ->  load "<name>.json";  if found("0001") then flagA = 1
else if found("spc_")                                    flagB = 1
```

`001C5750` composes `JsonData/CutScenes/<name>.json` and reads **`mDofFocusDistance`** and
**`mDofApertureFnumber`** — focus distance and aperture, the two parameters a depth-of-field effect
needs.

**So the film-camera look on a cutscene is two numbers in a text file beside the scene data, switched
on by a naming convention.** That is a cheap modding lever: no code change gives a scene the film
camera. A change guard compares length then `memcmp` and **skips everything if the name is
unchanged**, so reloading the same scene re-reads nothing.

An asymmetry that is in the code and not a simplification: **`0001` is tested only when the name
contains `sum_`, and `spc_` only when it does not.** What `sum_` and `spc_` denote is **not claimed**
— eight `sum_?0001` entries invite an obvious story and the bridge that would settle it is authored
data in the VBF, not code.

### Two holes in `audit_crossrefs`, both found by a session dispositioning its findings

**1. The substrate test was applied to the neighbour and never to the cited side.** A document citing
`0016D6A0` — `_guard_check_icall`, which every indirect call in the image passes through — imported
its **2,479 distinct callers across 16 owner subsystems** as unaccounted neighbours. That produced
**8 of 20** findings against `15-Input`, **not one of them an input relationship**; enumerating them
would have said only that the executable uses CFG.

> **A substrate function is uninformative as a subject for exactly the reason it is uninformative as
> a neighbour.** The asymmetry was invisible because the findings looked like real cross-subsystem
> edges. Fixed with an explicit `is_substrate`, verified: `0016D6A0` →
> `CompilerRuntime.ControlFlowGuard` → skipped as a subject.

**2. A third alias mismatch, and it survived the fix aimed at its own class.** The ledger writes
`PlatformOnlineAchievements` with no separators; the curated key is `Platform/Online/Achievements`.
Normalising `/` and space to `_` gave `platformonlineachievements` and `platform_online_achievements`
— **which never met**, so the curated aliases `platform` and `achievements` never applied and a
document writing the subsystem out in prose was still reported as ignoring it. Keys are now
canonicalised to alphanumerics only. **Seven cases pass, both negative controls still fire.**

### `crossref_clean` had drifted in both directions and nothing machine-checks it

Before this pass, one document claimed `crossref_clean: true` while carrying **3** findings, another
claimed true with **10**, and a third claimed **false with 0**.

> **This is the COVERAGE rule — a hand-maintained summary of machine-checkable facts must be
> machine-checked — applied to a field that has no checker. And it is the field the AUDITED bar
> depends on.** Same shape as `audit.passes` counting amendments: a status field asserting something
> a tool could settle, trusted because it is written in the frontmatter where facts live.

All four corrected to what the checker reports. A checker for the field itself is identified and not
yet built; it needs a full `audit_crossrefs` run per document, which is the reason it has never
existed.

### Dispositions worth keeping

- **Save/Load is a second writer of the capability policy table.** That document says *"different
  subsystems own different rows"* and documents only row 2; `SaveStorageQueue_ControllerStateHandler`
  and `SaveLoad_ControllerLifecycleHandler` call both the set and clear primitives — which is exactly
  what a save system needs a capability row for. **Which row and bit is not established**: a backward
  liveness census over all 72 call sites gives 14 CONST, 24 DYNAMIC, 34 UNKNOWN, with all four
  Save/Load sites in the dynamic buckets and one computing the row as `add rax, rcx`. **The
  discriminator abstains rather than guessing.**
- **Party reads the raw analog input history**, so that buffer is not consumed only by Input — **a
  change to its format would surface as a movement bug rather than an input one.**
- **A disposition pass created two new findings**, by citing a 180-caller hub by address in a
  one-line aside. Resolved by **removing the hex and keeping the name**: the claim did not need the
  address, and the address would have needed a census. **A citation is a commitment to account for
  what it drags in.**

### The `.rdata` residue was the RTTI-less corner

The four largest uncharacterised runs are **one mechanism**: a statically-linked audio library at
`0088E000`–`00895000` — **42 functions, 29,042 bytes, 32 Audio-owned — and no function outside that
range calls into it directly.** No `E8` edge reaches it.

> **That is why every caller-census technique is blind to it**, and why its tables surfaced as
> "uncharacterised residue" rather than as anything. **A library reached entirely through function
> pointers is invisible to the call graph by construction** — the same shape as the two-thirds of
> uncalled unowned code reached through data-table pointers, now with a name on it.

**`01CEB618` is an allocator hook table, not a dispatch table.** Verified here — four consecutive
qwords, all pointing into one tight cluster of small adjacent functions:

```
01CEB618 -> 00861FBC      01CEB628 -> 00861F2C
01CEB620 -> 00861F32      01CEB630 -> 00861F26
```

**242 `call qword ptr [rip+…]` instructions** from Audio-owned functions in the block target two of
the four. That is the standard shape of a portable library's replaceable-allocator table, wired in
this build straight to the CRT: **every allocation this library makes goes through those four
pointers.**

**Flagged carefully rather than sold:** `.rdata` is read-only at runtime, so this is a **link-time
seam, not a live hook.** The distinction matters because the earlier `malloc`/`free`/`calloc`/
`realloc` pointers found in `.data` *are* writable — **two allocator tables, one patchable and one
not, and only the section tells you which.**

**`01CEB070` is the library's own dispatch table** — twenty slots, every entry inside the block, **no
RIP-relative consumer at all.** It is reached through a single pointer at `01CDCF68`, and the one
instruction taking that address is *inside the block itself*. In `.rdata` it is preceded by float
constants rather than a complete-object locator: **a vtable-shaped table for a class compiled without
RTTI.**

> **Which is exactly why the 94.7 % RTTI partition could not see it. The residue was not random — it
> was the RTTI-less corner.** A partition built on RTTI leaves behind precisely the code that opted
> out of RTTI, and that residue will look like noise while being the most structurally coherent thing
> in the section.

Three further runs in the same region with the same owner mix are **almost certainly more of the
same — consumers not traced, so not claimed.**

### A correct instrument, misread by its reader

The locator found the pointer to `01CEB070` **correctly on the first try — and printed its address in
decimal.** Converted to hex by eye it became `01CDF3A8`; it is `01CDCF68`. That wrong address was
then read, float constants were found there, and **a coherent and entirely fictitious account of "the
structure that points to run A" was one step from being written up.**

> **A radix mismatch between a tool's output and its reader survives every check aimed at the tool.**
> Positive controls, controls from outside the instrument, round-trips — **all of them pass, because
> the instrument was right.**

What caught it was that **the follow-up read disagreed with the search that produced it** — the same
self-inconsistency test that caught the `+0x008` displacement regex.

**Third distinct way a session has been given a wrong answer tonight while its instrument worked as
designed:**

| failure | where it lived | what caught it |
|---|---|---|
| undercounted denominator | the selector | a figure from outside the instrument |
| boundary assumption | the interpretation | meeting the same shape again |
| **misread output** | **the reader** | **a follow-up that disagreed with its own source** |

Only the first is addressed by validating instruments. **The other two need the work to disagree with
itself somewhere a person will notice** — which is the case for chasing every disagreement rather
than filing it, and for preferring output that carries names and units over output that carries bare
numbers.

### The 88 single-slot runs do not exist

They were an artifact of the grouping rule that produced them. **Regrouped as arithmetic progressions
instead of contiguous runs, 88 becomes 19.**

```
                        contiguity   progression
groups                         113            34
slots in a group                 —           179
TRULY ISOLATED                "88"            19
```

**The mechanism is arithmetic and complete:** a table whose record contributes **exactly one** pointer
can never produce a contiguous run, because consecutive pointers are one **stride** apart, not 8. **So
every such table shatters into as many "single-slot runs" as it has records.**

> **A grouping rule is a hypothesis about the data's shape, and reporting its output as a population
> asserts that hypothesis.** *"88 single-slot runs"* reads as a fact about the engine and was a fact
> about `step == 8`.

**The check is cheap and was not run on the author's own number: regroup under a different rule and
see whether the population survives.** It did not.

**And the warning sign was already inside the same section.** §17 says *"contiguity is the wrong
shape"* about the Items runs — and then publishes a residue computed by contiguity. **The diagnosis
was written and not applied to the author's own remaining figure**, one section apart.

**Fourth face of the run-boundary assumption in this document's history — nulls, then stride, now
adjacency — and the first where the fragmenting instrument belonged to the person reporting it.** The
tell that should have caught it: the §17 inventory descriptors and the §18 Skin descriptors
**reappear among the singletons** wherever a record's second callback is null. **Two tables already
identified by the same author, reported again as loose pointers.**

### The largest group is a 128-record authored-command table

```
0041E097  lea r13, [rip -> 01EFFAF0]        ; base, hoisted out of the loop
0041E0C6  and eax, 0x7f                     ; index MASKED -> 128 records
0041E0C9  shl rax, 4                        ; stride 16
0041E0CD  cmp byte ptr [rax + r13 + 8], 0   ; +0x08 enable byte
0041E117  call qword ptr [r9 + r13]         ; +0x00 handler
```

`01EFFAF0`–`01F002F0`, consumers `PresentationEmbeddedRecord_ExecuteCommand` / `UpdateCurrent` /
`ExecuteDeferred`. **Only 73 of 128 records hold a certified pointer**, the rest `ICF_FoldedRetStub`
fillers — which is why the contiguity rule saw 73 singletons where there is one table.

**The index is masked rather than validated** — `and eax, 0x7f` — **the same clamp-don't-check pattern
recorded at `022D94B0`.** Second instance, and worth watching for as an engine-wide habit: an
out-of-range command id does not fail, it aliases onto another record.

### What the remainder now is

**A floor on structures, not a count of loose pointers.** Nine tables account for **179 of 198**, and
the 19 are **not established as lone callbacks — only as slots this grouping could not place.**

> **Whether this engine dispatches anything individually rather than through tables is still
> unanswered, and the population that would answer it is 19, not 88.**

That is the honest form of a residue: a bound on what remains, with the method's reach stated, rather
than a number that inherits the shape of the tool that produced it.

### The "float table builders" are constructors that stamp a header and register the object

The assignment premise — *each builder's `memset` immediate gives its object's size, so all 66 are
decodable* — **is true for a quarter of them.** Only **18 of the 65** call `memset` at all, yielding
**17 recovered sizes**, and they verify hard: **17/17 are ≤ the gap to the next data pointer, and 9
are exactly equal to it** — consecutive objects with no padding. `0xDC0` = 3,520 is both a `memset`
size and the largest inter-target gap the document measured; **they are the same object**,
`02AE21B0`.

**Chasing what the other 47 call instead produced the mechanism the "builder" framing was hiding.**
Two hot helpers both write a **common object header**:

```
008631D0(obj, dx)         15 B   word[obj+0]=dx ; byte[obj+3]=0x10 ; dword[obj+4]=0
008631E0(obj, rdx, r8d)   84 B   byte[obj+3]=0x30 ; word[obj+0]=1
                                 n = *(u32*)02EB37B0                    <- global counter
                                 *(u32*)(02EAF930 + 16*n)     = r8d | 0x4A000000
                                 *(u64*)(02EAF930 + 16*n + 8) = rdx
                                 *(u32*)02EB37B0 = n + 1
                                 dword[obj+4] = FUN_0020E620(...)       <- id stored back
```

Split: **18 `memset`, 40 header-init, 29 registration, 15 none of the three.** The objects share a
header — `u16` at `+0`, a **kind byte at `+3`** (`0x10` plain, `0x30` registered), and a `u32` at
`+4` that is zero for the plain kind and a **returned id** for the registered kind. **29 of the 66
publish themselves into a runtime registry at `02EAF930`**, tagged `0x4A000000`, counted by
`02EB37B0`.

> **These are constructors that stamp a header and register the object, not writers of float
> tables.** An earlier pass established what they are *not*; this establishes what they are. **The
> instruction not to inherit the title's framing was load-bearing** — the alternative was hunting for
> table writes and finding header stores that made no sense.

**Not claimed, correctly:** the 48 objects without a `memset` size are **bounded above by their gap
but not determined**, and gaps are not quoted as sizes — **8 of the 17 measured objects are strictly
smaller than their gap**, so the bound is demonstrably not tight. Also unclaimed: what `02EAF930` is
a registry *of*, and the meaning of the `0x4A000000` tag.

### A control that a wrong answer also passes is not a control

The first extractor took the first `mov r8d, imm` followed by any call and returned **36 sizes — 22
of them `0x0`.** The zeros were `xor r8d, r8d` feeding a different callee entirely.

**The control passed.** *"Size ≤ gap"* is **trivially satisfied by zero.** What caught it was that
**22 identical zeros is not a plausible size distribution** — not the control. Fixed by resolving
`memset` by name and reading `r8d` only at its call sites, taking the count from a fictitious 36 to a
real 17.

This is a **fourth** way a session has been given a wrong answer while its instrument ran as designed,
and it belongs beside the other three:

| failure | where it lives | what caught it |
|---|---|---|
| undercounted denominator | the selector | a figure from outside the instrument |
| boundary assumption | the interpretation | meeting the same shape again |
| misread output | the reader | a follow-up disagreeing with its own source |
| **control too weak** | **the check** | **an implausible distribution in the output** |

> **A control must be able to fail.** The first three are instruments that were wrong; this one was an
> instrument that was wrong **and a check that could not have said so.** When designing a control,
> the question is not "does the right answer pass" but **"what wrong answer would also pass".**

### The cutscene naming convention also changes script pacing

`PROPOSED-repos9e-18` answered, and the answer reaches a second subsystem. The two flags set from the
asset name feed `WorldActor_UpdateRuntimeAndScriptExecutionState`, a per-frame loop over `0x28`-byte
script entries:

```
if ( ( result != 0
    || ( FUN_001ed130() && (worldState - 1u) < 2 && flagB() == 0 )    // states 1,2
    || ( worldState == 3 && flagA() != 0 )                            // state 3
    || DAT_022C7F84 != 0 )
   && FUN_00357770() == 0 )
        entry[0x16] = 1;
```

**The two flags act in opposite directions and in disjoint states.** Flag B must be **clear** for the
state-1/2 arm, so a `spc_` scene **suppresses** that stop condition; flag A must be **set** for the
state-3 arm, so a `sum_…0001` scene **enables** one that otherwise never fires there.
`(worldState - 1u) < 2` is unsigned, so it is exactly states 1 and 2 — disjoint from `== 3`.

`entry[0x16]` is a one-shot stop marker the same loop consumes next pass: **a script runs a step and
stands down until the next frame.**

> **So the cutscene's name changes both how the scene is focused and how often actor scripts stand
> down during it.** Two unrelated subsystems keyed off the same substring test, and neither was
> visible from the naming function alone.

**Bounds stated:** one consumer of three read for flag A, one of four for flag B; the five gate
predicates treated as opaque.

### A possible second dead island, handed over rather than absorbed

`0034CF90` and `0034D790` — **137 bytes each, adjacent, both consuming these flags, and zero callers
by graph or bytes.** Verified here against `edges.tsv`: **both are 0 incoming / 6 outgoing**, the
identical signature the dead nine-patch renderer had.

**And they are not in the residual 158** — they are classified functions with no caller. **If they are
dead, dead code is not confined to the unclassified tail**, which is a different and larger claim than
the one dead island already documented.

The session that found them **did not check, because it was outside what its question asked** —
handing over the lead rather than quietly widening scope. That is the right call and the reason the
lead is legible enough for someone else to take in twenty minutes.

### Contiguity is right for `.rdata` and 5.3× wrong for `.data`

The database-wide sweep for populations produced by a grouping rule came back **section-specific**,
which neither branch of the question anticipated:

```
section  slots    contiguity(step 8)          arithmetic progression      singletons surviving
.rdata   27,202   2,465 runs /   404 single   2,849 groups /  482 single   119 %
.data     3,015   1,977 runs / 1,678 single     574 groups /  316 single    19 %
```

> **The defect is not "contiguity is wrong". It is "contiguity is wrong for `.data`."** `.rdata`
> holds **arrays of pointers** — vtables, which genuinely are contiguous — so contiguity is the right
> rule there and regrouping makes it marginally worse. `.data` holds **records with a pointer
> field**, where consecutive pointers are one stride apart. **The same rule is correct in one section
> and 5.3× wrong in the other, and nothing in the phrase "N single-slot runs" says which you have.**

**That is a better answer than either "the document was unlucky" or "the practice is unsound",
because it is actionable:** the check needs running on `.data`-side run analyses, and `.rdata` run
counts can be left alone.

The `.data` figure of 1,977 runs is the census's own — the *"1,959 of 1,977 runs uncited"* line. Under
progression those same slots form **574 groups.**

### Claims flagged, with the confidence each deserves

1. **`why-the-unowned-code-has-no-owner.md`, the `.rdata` residue** — *"266 slots form 192 runs, 166 of
   them single."* It is `.rdata`, the safe section, **but 86 % singletons against an `.rdata` base rate
   of 16 %.** The residue behaves like `.data` — consistent with what it turned out to be: **a library
   reached entirely through function pointers, with a vtable-shaped table for a class compiled without
   RTTI**, i.e. precisely the part of `.rdata` that is *not* an array of pointers. Owner alerted; one
   regroup settles it.
2. **`rtti-vtable-object-model.md`** — *"3,639 of 3,953 unnamed runs are a single slot."* Its
   population is explicitly *pointer runs in data carrying no locator*, **which is exactly where
   contiguity fails.** The reporting session **did not reproduce the figure** and makes no claim it is
   wrong — only that the instrument behind it has a measured 5.3× singleton inflation on the closest
   population they could rebuild. **A stated inability to reproduce, offered as a reason to check
   rather than as a finding.**
3. **`the-unresolved-158.md`** — *"14 connected clusters plus 109 singletons."* That is a
   **connectivity** rule, not contiguity: a different hypothesis, **not covered by this measurement.**
   Flagged as unchecked rather than at risk.

**Distinguishing "at risk", "not reproduced", and "not covered" is what makes a sweep usable.** A
sweep that reports everything it touched as suspect is a sweep nobody acts on.

### Two instruments caught before they reported

**A mixed-population figure, one probe before publishing.** The first run combined both sections and
gave *"36 % of singletons survive"* — **one number averaged over two populations with opposite
behaviour.** Caught by splitting per section before writing up. **The exact defect the sweep exists to
find, committed by the sweep, one step before reporting on it.**

**And an over-broad selector, self-narrowed.** The first pass flagged **754** "unstated population"
claims by counting selection nouns — *callers*, *sites*, *slots*. But *"31 vtable slots"* is
**structural, not a partition choice**. Narrowing to genuinely partition-dependent nouns gives **46**.

> The over-broad version **would have been the sixth instrument tonight to manufacture findings from
> its own pattern assumptions** — and it would have arrived as 754 of them. **A checker's false
> positives scale with the corpus; its true positives do not.**

### An abstention bucket protects against UNKNOWN, not against WRONG

`argscan.py` determined which registers an instruction writes from capstone's `regs_access()`. **For
`lea` that is inverted:**

```
lea edx, [rdi + 0x15]   ->   capstone: written = ['rdi'], read = ['edx']
```

**Destination and base swapped.** A backward liveness walk therefore stepped straight **past** every
`lea` write and reported whatever earlier instruction it found — **as a CONST, not an abstention. A
confident wrong value, not a missing one.**

> **A discriminator with an abstention bucket can still lie. The bucket protects against UNKNOWN, not
> against WRONG.** 13 of 17 verdicts were UNKNOWN, which *felt* like honesty, while **two of the four
> confident ones were false.** An instrument that abstains often reads as cautious; abstention rate
> says nothing about the accuracy of the non-abstentions.

And the general form, which is the same shape as the decompiler rule already in this log:

> **`regs_access()` is a claim about an instruction, not the instruction.** Anything in the toolkit
> that walks registers must derive `lea` destinations from **operands**, never from `regs_access()`.
> `argscan.py` is fixed and carries the defect in its docstring so the next reader sees why the code
> looks that way.

**What caught it was a disagreement, not a review.** A different census printed `CONST 0` for a site
whose disassembly — read minutes later for an unrelated purpose — plainly showed
`lea edx,[rdi+0x15]`. **Two readings of the same site, one from a tool and one from the bytes.**

### The corrected census strengthened the claim it corrupted

```
first run:  4 CONST (all 0), 13 UNKNOWN
corrected:  6 CONST, 9 DYNAMIC, 2 UNKNOWN  -- ids 0, 0, 4, 5, 24, 31
```

Verified here from the image: at `00234376`, `41 b0 1f` = **`mov r8b, 0x1F`** — id **31** — immediately
before the call at `0023437E`.

**Four of the six ids now carry a native behavioural check against the help text used to name them,
and all four agree:**

- **4 = Sleep** and **5 = Confuse**, both cleared where a special sequence commits accumulated damage
  — **damage waking a sleeping or confused unit.**
- **24 = Invisible**, touched as a standard action advances — **acting breaking invisibility.**
- **31 = Vanished**, REMOVED when an area initialises — **clearing an irreversible removal state at
  area load, the only sane time to clear it.**

**None was sought; each fell out of the corrected census, and the naming predates all of them.** A
correction that converts an authored-text identification into a behavioural one is worth more than
the claim it replaced.

**What died:** *"status 0 is the only status id any native call site passes as a constant."*
**What survived:** no native site **adds** 1 or 31 by constant — which is what the argument actually
rests on. Status 1 has no native constant site at all, and the single constant use of 31 is a
**removal**.

**Proven rather than repeated:** the two mis-read sites are the authored direct-command bridge —
`statusId = command - 0x51` on the add path, `command - 0x71` on the remove path. A GFZ comment
asserted a `0x4051..0x4070` / `0x4071..0x4090` family; **that arithmetic is now read from the
binary.**

### Save/Load owns row 1, bit 21 — confirmed from the consumer side

All four sites hand-read, two set and two clear:

```
005823F8 clear / 0058252C set    xor edi,edi … lea edx,[rdi+0x15] / lea ecx,[rdi+1]
005828B4 set   / 00582F1B clear  mov edx,0x15 / lea ecx,[rdx-0x14]
```

**The second handler computes the row from the bit** (`row = bit - 20`); the first passes both as
offsets from a zeroed register. **Different idioms, same pair** — which is itself evidence, since a
transcription error would not survive two encodings.

**And the confirmation is from the consumer, not a restatement of the writer.** `00229AF0` (Audio)
reads the aggregate, tests bit 21, and **on that path calls the per-row reader with argument 1.** A
consumer that sees bit 21 goes on to read row 1. **Writer and consumer agree and can fail
independently.**

**What the bit does is not established and was not guessed.** Bit 21 has **no entry in the UI-request
projection**, so it is consumed directly rather than by refusing a UI request. The two handlers are
named for controller state and controller lifecycle, which is consistent with an inhibition raised
while a save is in progress or a controller is lost — **but naming behaviour from handler names is
the trap**, and it was declined.

### The dead-code candidates are live script verb handlers

`0034CF90` and `0034D790` — 137 bytes each, adjacent, **0 incoming / 6 outgoing by graph and by
bytes**, and not in the residual 158 — are **not dead.** Searched against every ScriptVM command
table by its own declared record count:

```
0034CF90  <- family 0, record    0   field begin / +0x08   slot 01EED708
0034D790  <- family 0, record 1493   field begin / +0x08   slot 01EF91A8
0034DCC0  <- family 0, records 0 and 1493, field poll / +0x10
```

**They are the begin callbacks for script call IDs `0x0000` and `0x05D5`.** So the larger hypothesis
this pair was raised to support — *dead code is not confined to the unclassified tail* — **does not
follow from them.** It may still be true; these two do not support it, and the hypothesis is
withdrawn to unsupported rather than carried forward on a hedge.

**And the reason they looked dead is documented in the very census that produced them:**

> **"0 incoming, N outgoing, not in the residual" is not the signature of dead code. It is the
> signature of *reached through data*** — the majority case in this binary, where two thirds of
> uncalled unowned code is reached through a pointer in a table and an `E8`-based edge list is blind
> to all of it by construction.

**The dead-renderer signature and the reached-through-data signature are identical in the call graph**
and are told apart only by a data-pointer search. The relocation-certified census answers it in one
step, so **that check is now the gate on this entire class of hypothesis** — run it before nominating
any candidate, not after.

Incidental, for whoever holds verb dispatch: **records 0 and 1493 share one poll callback while
having different begin callbacks.**

**And the answer took one step because the family-table extents from an earlier block were still in
context.** That is the concrete case for reporting structure rather than conclusions: **the extents
were a by-product then and they were the whole answer here.**

### The `.rdata` residue: 166 singletons become 22

```
contiguity, step 8                           192 groups   166 singletons (86 %)
progression, stride 0x8-0x100, >=3 members    52 groups    22 singletons (42 %)
```

Strides: `0x10` ×14, `0x8` ×6, `0x18` ×4, `0x30` ×3, `0x20` ×2, `0x60` ×1. **The residue is not
fragmented — it is mostly 16-byte record tables**, and contiguity had hidden its two largest
structures: 27 members at `01CCB168` and 22 at `01CCA3F8`, both stride `0x10`, in a family of
`01CCAxxx`–`01CCExxx` tables that are **all unowned and none characterised.**

> **A better target than the singletons ever were — and one nobody would have looked at, because 27
> members were sitting in the table as 27 separate "single slots".**

**The rule discriminates correctly in both directions:** `01CEB070` stays a stride-8 array of 20
because it genuinely is one. **The fix is not "prefer progressions" — it is that the grouping rule has
to match what the section holds.**

### AS-4: the figures reproduce, the inference is half wrong

An independent rebuild under that section's own definition: **3,957 runs / 3,643 singletons against
its 3,953 / 3,639** — four runs apart, **both derived percentages identical to the decimal.** Same
population, so what follows is about the numbers rather than a near-miss.

```
.rdata  3,202 slots | 1,976 runs / 1,963 single | 1,836 groups / 1,807 single |  92% survive
.data   3,015 slots | 1,977 runs / 1,678 single |   572 groups /   301 single |  18% survive
```

*"A one-slot run is an individual stored function pointer, not a table"* **holds in `.rdata` and fails
in `.data`**, where 82 % of singletons are members of progressions. **1,533 of 3,643 (42 %) are not
individual stored pointers.** The population straddles both sections almost equally — 3,202 against
3,015 — **which is why one inference could not cover it.** Qualified in place; the figures are
untouched.

**And the instrument bounded itself.** Greedy longest-progression search is itself a hypothesis: in a
dense region it merges slots from different structures, and two reported `Script_VM_Native_Bridge`
progressions at strides `0xC0` and `0xA0` **span the `0x20`-stride command tables and are search
artifacts.**

> **So 301 is a lower bound, not a measurement: the true `.data` singleton count lies between 301 and
> 1,678.** The direction is not in doubt. **Reporting 301 as exact would repeat, one level down, the
> defect this check exists to find** — and a bounded interval that can be defended beats a clean
> number that cannot.

### The failure table, reordered

The fourth row belongs first for a new session:

> **"What wrong answer would also pass?" can be asked before running anything. The other three only
> bite after you already have a number.**

### The script stand-down gate, every term named

`00357770` is **seven bytes**, verified from the image: `8b 05 12 08 f7 01 c3` —
`mov eax,[rip+0x01F70812]` / `ret`, and `0x00357776 + 0x01F70812` = **`022C7F88`**. It returns one
global and nothing else.

Its partner `00357760` **clears that global immediately before each bytecode step**, and the gate
tests it after — **so it reports what happened *inside* the step, not standing state.** That single
observation is what turns a mystery predicate into a protocol.

**Thirteen of its fourteen writers are ScriptVM native command handlers**, located in the dispatch
table at `01EED720` — commands 45, 46, 47, 48, 641, 1018–1021, 1056, 1304, 1305, 1415.

*Control:* the table's own census reproduces the documented figure exactly — **1,234 records with a
non-null field `+0`**, matching `scriptvm-native-dispatch-table.md` §4. **A wrong base or stride would
not land on that number**, so the membership claim rests on a table that was verified rather than
assumed.

**Eleven of the thirteen write from field `+0x10`** — the slot that runs while a command is still in
progress rather than at its start.

> **So the flag means "a native script command signalled during this step that it has not finished",
> and it vetoes the stand-down outright.** The engine is not deciding whether a script *may* pause; it
> is asking the script whether it is done.

**The third arm is an authored bracket.** `DAT_022C7F84` has exactly two writers, both ScriptVM
commands: **1485 sets it, 1486 clears it.** A paired set/clear on consecutive command ids is scripted
data switching the behaviour on for a region and off again — **so a scene author can force the
stand-down without touching code.**

**And `001ED130` wires straight back to the cutscene slot setter**, reading `DAT_01DFE40C` — the
current-slot marker that function publishes — and the same per-slot flag array:

```
return !( fieldVar == 0x19 || (fieldVar == 0x10C7 && perSlotFlag[currentSlot] == 5) );
```

**Two hard-coded carve-outs.** `001ED180` requires three unrelated predicates clear **and** the
transition field id to be one of `0x2F4`, `0x2E9`, `0x27B` — **so the state-1/2 arm is dormant except
during three specific world transitions.** `001EDDA0` and `001EDE80` test the same two globals on
opposite polarity — two faces of one runtime mode — and `001EDDA0` has **50 callers**, making it a
general engine-mode question rather than local to this gate.

**The gate is now legible end to end:** the VM's own result, three narrowly gated situational arms,
and a hard veto from any command that says it is mid-operation. **Nothing in it is opaque except the
second rank behind it, which is listed rather than left implicit.**

regardless of arguments. **`--db` is not parsed.** Every invocation in this project passes

> **A selector nothing reads is worse than no selector, because it tells the caller a population was
> chosen.** Same defect class as the audit counter that counted the wrong noun — and this time in the
> gate every session quotes at the end of every block.

It surfaced the way these always do: a **live session's scratch file** in `Tools/work/<session>/`
turned the gate red. Those are working notes and staged rows; their links point at wherever the
author was standing and are **not database links**. Under the non-atomic-gates rule that cost a
diagnosis before anyone could act on the real result.

Fixed on both counts: `work/` and other scratch directories are skipped, and `--db` now **selects the
root or exits with an error** on a path that does not exist. Verified in all three modes.

**And with the noise removed the gate immediately found a real defect that had been sitting behind
it.** `weather-apply-and-environment-materialization.md` linked a **sibling** file as
`../weather-probability-and-transition-roll.md`. Reproduced across two runs before acting, per the
non-atomic rule, then corrected — **1,030 links, all resolve.**

> **A gate with a known-noisy channel does not fail loudly; it fails into the noise.** The broken link
> was not hidden by a bug in the link logic — it was hidden by everyone's willingness to glance past a
> red line they had learned to expect from scratch files.

### 143 Lua standard-library functions, named by the name Lua exposes them under

The `01CCAxxx`–`01CCExxx` family is the Lua standard library's **registration tables**. The records
are `luaL_Reg { const char *name; lua_CFunction func; }` — 16 bytes, name at `+0`, function at `+8`.

Verified here from the image:

```
01CCB160   name -> 01CCB320   func -> 00818A80
01CCB320   "abs\0acos..."
```

**`FUN_00818A80` is `math.abs`.** A packed string table, and the first record of the largest array.

**Twelve arrays, 145 records, 143 distinct functions:**

```
01CCB160  27  math          01CCC0B0  11  io
01CCA3F0  22  base (_G)     01CCC2E0  11  os
01CCC6C0  16  debug         01CCC170   9  io file methods
01CCAD50  14  string        01CCA950   6  coroutine
01CCAFF0  12  bit32         01CCAA90   6  table
01CCB3E0   8  loadedlibs    01CCB470   3  preloadedlibs
```

**Two of the twelve are not libraries** — they are Lua 5.2's own bootstrap lists from `linit.c`.
`01CCB3E0` is `loadedlibs` (opened at startup) and `01CCB470` is `preloadedlibs` (left for
`require`). **Stock 5.2 opens all of them at startup, so this build moved `bit32` and `math` out of
the startup set.** `string` appears in both lists — **recorded, not explained.**

**This answers R-6** — the exact boundaries of the Lua library in the address space — with the named
functions spanning `00814xxx`–`0081Cxxx`, and it **independently confirms the version**: `bit32`
exists as a library only in 5.2, agreeing with a version banner the document already had **from a
different source.**

**Not claimed:** this names the standard library, **not the interpreter core** — `lua_*` API functions
and the VM carry no `luaL_Reg` entry. And **registration is not reachability**: it says nothing about
which of these the game's own scripts can call, **which is the sandbox question and a different job.**

### The discriminator is the content of the gap, not the regularity of the spacing

The grouping had been **offset by 8** — grouped on the *function* field, so the real base sits eight
bytes earlier. What settled it was asking **what sits between the members of a stride-`0x10` group:**

- For the two headline groups, **every in-between slot is a relocated pointer to a string** — real
  16-byte records.
- For the **largest** group found in the region, 53 members at `01CD6268`, the in-between slots are
  **certified function pointers**. Its true stride is 8, and the rule had taken **alternate entries of
  a pointer array.**

> **A rule that only ever merges will manufacture structure. The discriminator is the content of the
> gap, not the regularity of the spacing.**

**Both outcomes came from the same test**, which is what makes it trustworthy rather than a rescue —
and **all three headline groups were checked, not the two that supported the conclusion.** That is
the distinction between a control and a confirmation, applied by the author to their own result.

So the corrected residue reading stands **with a measured caveat**: stride-`0x10` grouping is right
where the gaps hold non-function pointers and wrong where they hold function pointers.

### The residual clustering survives — and the sweep's three different verdicts are the result

The 158's clustering was the third flagged population, and it is the one that **holds**. Residual list
taken from a self-verified checkpoint, SHA matching the certified value.

```
rule                                        clusters 2+   singletons   largest
A  call only, residual-internal (theirs)             14          109        13
B  call OR TAIL JMP, residual-internal               14          109        13
C  shares a callee of fan-in <=5, or a caller        24           71        11
   C at cap 10 / 25                              21 / 13      56 / 42   34 / 76
```

**Rule A reproduces exactly, and rule B gives the identical partition.** That second line matters more
than the first:

> **The variant was chosen because it was the one most likely to break — the tail-call defect has cost
> this fleet three findings tonight — and it did not apply: no residual reaches another residual by
> tail jump.** A survival under the attack most likely to succeed is worth more than a generic pass.

So *"109 singletons"* is **not** an artifact. **109 residuals genuinely neither call nor are called by
another residual.**

**But it overstates isolation.** Rule C asks a different defensible question — *"are these used
together?"* rather than *"do these call each other?"* — and at a conservative hub cap only **71 of 158
are isolated.** Six sibling clusters of 3+ contain functions no call cluster holds, the clearest being
**four residuals totalling 3,635 bytes with zero overlap with any call cluster**, joined by shared
low-fan-in callees. **Their consecutive addresses are explicitly not offered as evidence** — adjacency
is banned and would be circular here.

**And the 13-function cluster is corroborated, not undermined.** Rule C independently produces a
10-function cluster **sharing 8 members with it.** Two rules that disagree about the population
agreeing about that core is support for the reading two sessions have already acted on — **the
opposite of what the sweep was braced for.**

### Three items, three different verdicts

```
.data run analysis      COLLAPSED   88 singletons -> 19
AS-4's 3,953 runs       SPLIT       sound in .rdata, fails in .data
the 158's clustering    SURVIVES    reproduces, and survives the variant most likely to break it
```

> **A sweep that returned the same verdict three times would have been measuring the sweep.** These
> came out differently on the same test, which is the strongest available evidence that the test
> measures the documents rather than the expectations of the person running it.

**And the caution travels with the number.** Rule C's singleton count moves from 102 to 31 as the hub
cap goes 2 to 100. **71 is reported at cap 5 because it is conservative, and any single number from
rule C is a choice of cap** — the same class as the 301-vs-1,678 bound on the `.data` figure. Two
bounded intervals delivered tonight in place of two clean numbers that could not be defended.

### A stale board is a collision waiting to happen

Third near-collision of the session, and the cause is no longer the one I diagnosed at the second.
Routing by mechanism fixed *choosing* the wrong target; it does not fix **publishing a free list that
is accurate when written and wrong when read.** A session picked a task from a board that had gone
stale inside one tick.

> **A board is a snapshot, and a snapshot handed to four parallel readers is a race.** The fix is not a
> better board — it is that a claim must be confirmed against the current state at the moment of
> claiming, by the coordinator, before any work starts.

### `setmapwind` — a name recovered from the game's own vocabulary

`002E3D40`, listed only as *"field runtime parameter derivation (zero-mode path)"*, has exactly two
Script VM callers and **they are authored verbs that name it:**

```
0x0481  setmapwind      3 args  handler 0034B6C0 -- pops exactly THREE ints, then jmp 002E3D40 mode=1
0x0482  defaultmapwind  0 args  handler 0034BD10 -- pops NONE, zeroes all four args, jmp 002E3D40
```

**Both arity-verified against the catalog**, which is the bar the Script VM category requires. So
`002E3D40(mode, a, b, c)` is **the engine's map-wind entry point**: mode 1 with three script arguments
sets it, mode 0 resets it to the field default — **and the "zero-mode path" is the default-wind call
the weather apply path tail-enters when a field's environment is materialised.**

> **Same route that named `setforcefightmode`: the name arrives from authored script vocabulary, not
> from a reading of the body.** Two names recovered this way tonight, both for globals whose behaviour
> was already documented and whose *identity* was not.

### The documentation was right in the wrong words

Five findings named `RNG_Random_Selection` as an unaccounted neighbour — **and they are the Weather
transition roll**, the subject of a document that names MT19937 **thirteen times.** The checker could
not see it because those documents never write the word *"random"*; they use **the algorithm's name.**

**And the natural experiment was already in the data:** the one Weather document containing the word
*"selection"* — once, in an unrelated sentence — **is the one Weather document with no RNG finding.**

> **An alias list is a claim about how a subsystem is written about, and it was written from the
> ledger's vocabulary rather than the authors'.** A document that names the algorithm instead of the
> category is being *more* precise, and the checker punished it for that.

### Three more alias/hub defects, all now fixed and measured

**1. A fifth alias case, structural rather than a bad row.** The two taxonomies spell the same
subsystem differently — the ledger's PrimaryOwner is `Save_Load_Settings` (87 functions) while the
CodeDomain path head is `SaveLoad`, which exists **only** as a domain. `subsystem_of` falls back to the
domain head for an unowned function, **so the checker can report a subsystem under either taxonomy
while the alias table knows only one.** That recurs for every unowned neighbour whose domain head
differs in spelling from its owner counterpart — **not one row to add.** Fixed by registering domain
heads and merging alias lists across canonical-prefix relations in both directions.

**2. A hub the substrate test could not catch.** `ImageAddress_ResolveRuntimePointer` (`0020E600`) has
**815 callers across 18 owners** and is runtime infrastructure in exactly the sense the CFG stub is —
but it carries a real `PrimaryOwner`, so `is_substrate` returns false. **It alone produced four of five
`CoreRuntimeScheduling` findings in one category.**

**Threshold measured rather than guessed**, over the 19,995 functions with at least one caller:

```
p50=1   p75=2   p90=5   p95=9   p99=46   p99.5=76   p99.9=461   max=2479
>100 callers = 74 functions = 0.37 % of called functions
```

**`>100` sits far out on the tail, captures both known hubs, and leaves ordinary shared accessors
alone.** Six cases pass including two negative controls.

### A reference to a census someone else holds is not a citation

Six documents describe one system from different angles and cite the same neighbourhood, so the census
was **stated once and deferred to by reference** from the other five — correct, and the standard's own
rule against duplicating a census across files that will rot.

**The counter-example arrived in the same pass, twice.** A shared disposition paragraph named an
accessor a document had never cited, **drawing three Movement and five UI findings that had not
existed.** It was replaced with text citing a resolver **by address**, which took that category from 5
findings to 10 — pulling in ActorEntity, Audio, CombatAI and CombatAction. **The second mistake was in
the paragraph warning against the first.**

> **Write the name, not the address — the address is a commitment to account for everything it drags
> in.** The enumerating document is protected by its own census; **the referencing document must not
> re-cite the address.**
>
> **Boilerplate is the specific hazard: shared disposition text makes the same commitments in every
> document it is pasted into, including documents that never made them.**

### "Press X to continue" — the flag means a script command is still waiting

All 23 handler bodies behind the 15 located command ids read, 1,184 bytes. **`DAT_022C7F88` does not
mean "something happened". It means a script command is still waiting.**

| family | cmds | shape |
|---|---|---|
| wait for a button | 45–48, 1018–1021 | poll an input mask, raise while not pressed |
| wait for a condition | 641, 1056 | build a state mask from the actor, raise while zero |
| wait N frames | 1415 | countdown, raise while counting |
| produce a value, yield anyway | 1304, 1305 | write an int result, raise **unconditionally** |
| authored bracket | 1485 / 1486 | set / clear `022C7F84` plus two matched helper pairs |

> **A cutscene script pausing for a button raises the flag every frame it is still waiting, and the
> gate then refuses to stand the script down — so the wait is re-polled on the very next frame. That
> is why a cutscene prompt responds the instant you press it.**

The eight button waits are **one routine against two banks of four accessors** — a *history* bank and
an *actor-state-aware* bank at the same four offsets — and nine commands share a secondary handler
that pops the mask off the VM value stack. **An authored wait-for-button is one command id plus one
integer.**

**The protocol, stated exactly:** field `+0x10` is the poll handler; a command returns true to stay
active **and** raises the flag on the same path. **The return value keeps the command alive, the flag
tells the frame loop not to stand the whole script down — two consumers, one fact.**

### Three unrelated approaches converged on one mechanism

The four actor-state-aware accessors behind the button waits are **exactly the four that
`the-unresolved-158.md` §11 named as readers of the eight-slot actor registry at `0209C4D0`.**

> **The cutscene stand-down gate, the ScriptVM wait commands and that actor registry are one
> mechanism — reached from three unrelated directions across the session, none of them looking for
> the others.**

That is the strongest kind of corroboration this project can produce, because no step of any of the
three routes was chosen with the others in view.

### Scripted waits run at double rate during three world transitions

Command 1415's frame countdown **decrements a second time** when the same three-world-transition
predicate from §11 is true. **So every scripted frame-wait runs at double rate during those three
transitions.**

> A predicate that was one term in a stand-down gate turns out to **halve scripted timing**. If the
> archive read names those three transition ids, this becomes a statement about **three specific
> places in the game where cutscene pacing differs** — which is exactly the kind of fact a player
> would have noticed without ever being able to name.

**New question `-24`:** a small function tested against `actor[0x15]`, used by two of the wait
families, that **ends the wait regardless of the condition.** It is the escape hatch on every scripted
wait in the game and it is one small body — the highest-value single lookup left in the thread.
