### ~~`/OPT:ICF` folds vtables, not only functions~~ — RETRACTED WITHIN THE HOUR

`01CD6268` is **not a 53-slot array and not Lua.** It is a **three-slot vtable that the linker merged
across 26 different Input classes.** Verified from the image:

```
01CD6260 -> 01D4DF60   a .data pointer -- the boundary
01CD6268 -> 0086CE50   scalar deleting destructor
01CD6270 -> 0016D6A0   ICF_FoldedRetStub, a bare ret -- a no-op virtual
01CD6278 -> 00861EC6   _purecall -- a pure virtual never overridden
```

Non-function pointers on both sides, so the table is **exactly three entries.**

> **ICF folds vtables, not only functions.** The `0016D6A0` story so far has been one 3-byte `ret`
> with ~273 folded bodies and 2,479 callers; **this is the same mechanism one level up**, and a worked
> instance of it.

**The 26 classes each keep their own 66-byte deleting destructor and all install this same table**, on
a regular 80-byte pitch, and their `mov edx, <size>` immediates give the object sizes: **`0x28` ×20,
`0x40` ×4, `0x38` ×2.**

**Two defects, and the second hides the first.** Slot 0's sized branch passes `0x28`, so a virtual
`delete` through this table carries **the wrong size for the six classes that are `0x38` or `0x40`.**
ICF merged the tables because their contents were byte-identical — **and they are identical precisely
because the size lives in the destructor body rather than in the table.** But all 26 route bit 2 to
the ret stub, **so the size is never used and the wrong-size dispatch has no observable effect.**

> **One defect is hidden by another**, and neither is visible from either one alone.

These are **26 concrete, sized instances of BQ-27**, which narrows that question usefully: whatever the
runtime answer is, it now applies to a family whose **object sizes are known** rather than to 1,606
anonymous destructors.

**And the document carries an explicit warning not to read the shared vtable as a type
relationship** — they share it because three entries are byte-identical, **which is a linker outcome.
The only thing the sharing proves is that none of the 26 overrides slot 1 or slot 2.**

> **RETRACTED 2026-09-03, by its author, and re-verified here before the retraction was
> accepted.** There is **no shared vtable**. There are **26 distinct four-slot vtables** at
> `01CD6268` on a `0x20` pitch running to `01CD6588`. Read from the image:
>
> ```
> 01CD6268  0086CE50 dtor | ICF_FoldedRetStub | _purecall | -> 01D4DFE8
> 01CD6288  0086CF40 dtor | 00874080          | 00873170  | -> 01D4E078
> ```
>
> **Only the first has the ret stub and `_purecall`; the other 25 override both slots with real
> implementations** — the exact opposite of what was published. `01CD6268` is a **base class with
> two pure virtuals** and the other 25 are derived classes that implement them. Slot 3 of each
> points to a per-class `.rdata` structure.
>
> **What survives:** all 26 destructors write `01CD6268` into the object and free with their own
> size (`0x28` x20, `0x40` x4, `0x38` x2), and all 26 route the sized branch to the ret stub — so
> **the 26 sized instances of BQ-27 stand.** But the explanation is **textbook, not a defect**:
> restore the *base* vptr, free the *derived* size is what MSVC emits for a derived class adding
> no destructor body. **The "wrong-size dispatch" reading was an artefact of the same error.**

#### Why the measurement was right and the reading was wrong

The scan recorded, for each destructor, the target of its `lea rax,[rip+…]`. **All 26 returned
`01CD6268`, and that was read as "26 classes, one vtable".**

> **In MSVC a destructor's vptr store names the class whose destructor runs *next*, not the class
> the function belongs to.** The measurement was correct; the inference was not.

The check that settles it costs one command: **where does each destructor's own address appear in
`.rdata`?** Twenty-six distinct answers on a regular pitch is a vtable array; one answer would have
been a shared vtable.

> **A scan that reads one field of a structure will describe that field faithfully and the
> structure wrongly.**

**This is a fifth entry for the wrong-answer table and it is unlike the other four:** the
instrument was right, a control would have passed, the distribution was plausible, and the output
was read correctly. **The error was entirely in what the field was taken to mean, and nothing
internal to the measurement could have caught it — only looking at a different field.**

**And my own verification failed in a way worth recording.** I read `01CD6260`–`01CD627F`, saw a
`.data` pointer before the three entries, and concluded *"non-function pointers on both sides, so
exactly three entries"*. I never read the next eight bytes. **Slot 3 holds a `.data` pointer, which
is indistinguishable from the boundary marker I thought I was seeing.**

> **A boundary test that reads "a non-function pointer ends the table" cannot tell a 3-slot table
> from a 4-slot table whose last slot is a data pointer.** I verified the claim's *shape* instead
> of testing it, and stopped at the boundary I expected to find.

**And the author's own diagnosis of why it got through is the part I would keep:** *"this got past
me because it was interesting."* **"ICF folds vtables, not only functions" was a satisfying
generalisation of a mechanism this database already had**, and it arrived with a tidy
two-defects-masking-each-other story attached — **so it was checked less hard than things that
looked mundane.** Second time tonight the same bias produced an error rather than missed one.

**Band note, carefully bounded:** the neighbourhood is Phyre input classes — 35 named types,
`PInputSource` and subclasses among them, each referenced by one registration function on a `0xA0`
pitch. **Exactly 26 are `PInputSource` plus subclasses, matching the 26 vtables — but the registrars
install vtables in `01CD0xxx`, not `01CD62xx`, so no traced link joins a name to a vtable. A
matching count is not a mapping**, and the identification was left open.

### Proximity in `.rdata` is the same fallacy as adjacency in `.text`

**Both halves of the framing were wrong, and one half was mine.** I routed this as *"in the Lua
region, so it is the interpreter's own dispatch or something adjacent to it"* — and the address is
indeed in `.rdata` near the Lua tables, **but every one of its 27 consumers is Input.**

> **Proximity in `.rdata` to a known library is not membership of it** — the same class of inference
> as address adjacency in `.text`, which this project has banned since a branch lost 182
> classifications to it. **I wrote the ban into the routing instructions and then shipped an
> assignment resting on it.**

It nearly carried because **it arrived as part of the assignment**, which is the specific hazard: a
frame handed down by a coordinator is not examined the way a frame a session builds for itself is.
**The consumers settled it in one step**, as they have every other extent in this run.

### On the stale board

Three near-collisions while routing nine sessions from a snapshot one message old is **the expected
outcome of the design, not a lapse in it.** The fix already in place is the right one and does not
need reinforcing with more discipline:

> **State the mechanism, not the target, and let the receiving session run the neighbour check before
> accepting.** That has caught it every time — **seven catches, four of them "this already exists".**

And the trade is settled in favour of speed: **slightly-stale boards issued quickly beat accurate ones
issued slowly**, because the two-minute check on the receiving end is the only part of this that
scales with the session count.

### State the band, not the mechanism

The fix for three near-collisions was *"state the mechanism, not the target"*. That was half right, and
the session whose claims have collided least identified the missing half:

> **Stating the mechanism only helps if the receiving session can act on it. "Strided record arrays in
> `.data`" would not have deconflicted anything; "`006Dxxxx` and `008B7xxx` is where my consumers
> live" did.**

**An abstraction is not checkable and an address band is.** A coordinator holding nine sessions cannot
tell whether two mechanism descriptions overlap, but can trivially tell whether two address ranges do.
The board is now published as bands, and a claim is expected to name **where in the image the session
will be reading**.

Adopted this tick: the four-residual claim was checked against three in-flight bands — `0026xxxx`,
`0086Cxxx`/`00814xxx`–`0081Cxxx`, `002E3xxx`/`0034Bxxxx` — and cleared in one step rather than by
inference from the last message each session sent.

### Pre-commitments that make a null result reportable

The same claim arrived with two refusals **stated before any work was done**:

- **Adjacency is banned here and is doubly circular**, because same-translation-unit is a *plausible
  alternative explanation* for four functions sharing callees, not merely an inadmissible one. **A ban
  is stronger when the banned inference also has a competing explanation available.**
- **The selection rule's job was candidate generation and it is finished.** Carrying the grouping into
  the reading as a premise is how a selection rule quietly becomes a conclusion.

> **And "the sibling rule grouped a compilation artifact and the group is not a target" was declared a
> result rather than a failure — in advance.** Stating that before starting is what makes a null
> result reportable instead of looking like a retreat, and it is the cheapest possible defence against
> the pressure to find something.

**Coordinator note on the same claim.** The graph gives **eleven callees common to all four**
(`001B03D0`, `001B06D0`, `001B1620`, `001B1910`, `001B1C00`, `001B2410`, `001B2490`, `001FBD80`,
`001FBE30`, `001FBE50`, `00808C40`), three more shared by three of four, and sizes of **937 / 885 /
932 / 881 bytes** — a 6 % spread.

**That was handed over as data and explicitly not as a conclusion**, because it is exactly the
*suggestive* shape the claim pre-committed against, and the alternative it names — same translation
unit, same author, same helper set — **explains it just as well.** Four sibling routines over one
library would look precisely like this.

### A batch flag is applied to the rows that did not need it

The staged mutation batch was about to go in as two batches — ledger-moving rows, and
"re-classifications" needing `-AllowExistingTag`. **Checking rather than assuming split it into
three:** two of the six supposed re-classifications carry tags but **no `CodeDomain`**, so they take
the strict fence.

> **`-AllowExistingTag` is a batch-level flag. A batch that mixes rows needing it with rows that do
> not applies the weakened fence to rows that never asked for it — and it succeeds either way, so
> nothing in the result would say it had happened.**

Same family as *a control a wrong answer also passes*: the gate cannot distinguish the two cases, so
the only defence is not to create them. Now staged as **A (4 rows, plain, moves unresolved 158 → 154)
· B1 (2 rows, plain) · B2 (4 rows, `-AllowExistingTag`)**, to be applied strict-fences-first so an
unexpected failure lands before any weakened flag is used.

**And the reason they have not run is now stated as a condition rather than a deferral:** the cycle
changes the parent checkpoint every session imports from, and four sessions have been continuously
mid-block reading bodies.

### The escape hatch is a per-manager bitmask, and it leaves the subsystem

`FUN_00267310` is 22 bytes: `return table[managerIndex * 0x288 + 0x201]` — byte `+0x201` of a
**648-byte actor-manager record**, indexed by `actor[0x15]`.

**The array base was derived, not assumed:** sweeping `.text` for `imul r64, r64, 0x288` finds **55
sites in 46 functions** (control: form present, PASS), lowest base `02098E10` — and the one named user
of that stride works at `+0x108` of the same records. **Independent evidence that it is the
actor-manager array.**

**It is a bitmask, not a boolean** — a setter takes the bit index as a runtime argument.

**A wrong expectation, caught by a control built for a previous section.** The setter's immediate
callers were expected to be dispatch entries, as the `022C7F88` writers were. **The membership test
returned 0 of 4**, and only one hop further up did two commands appear.

> **Reasoning by analogy from the previous result would have produced "script commands set these
> bits" about a byte the engine writes on four other paths.** The check built for §11 is what stopped
> it — **the argument for building the check even when you already think you know the answer.**

**And the thread leaves its own subsystem.** **65 readers**, graph and bytes agreeing exactly,
including `World_UpdateSimulationTick` and `Movement_UpdateSteeringTowardTarget`. **The waiting
commands are one consumer among many**, so §13 is not cutscene documentation and says so.

**The modding fact:** waits test **the whole byte**, not a specific bit. **Any bit set in a manager's
flag byte terminates every scripted wait belonging to that manager** — a wait cannot opt out, and a
bit set for one purpose ends waits that had nothing to do with it.

**Player-facing, at the limit of the evidence:** a manager-wide switch that makes scripted waits stop
waiting — **which is what skipping or fast-forwarding scripted content looks like from outside.**
Which bit means what is **not established**, and naming one "the skip button" needs assignments that
sit behind the authored-data boundary.

**The cutscene thread is complete from the code side:** slot classification → DoF sidecar → the two
flags → the stand-down gate → the five predicates → the fifteen waiting commands → the escape byte.
**Every remaining question in it is authored data.**

### The suggestive shape was right about the fields and wrong about the order

`setmapwind(elevation, azimuth, preset)` — **the reverse of what the packed-field layout suggests.**
The record lists preset at offset 0, azimuth at 3, elevation at 7; a reader carrying that order into
the verb writes `setmapwind(preset, azimuth, elevation)` and is exactly backwards.

> **The suggestive shape was right about *which* fields and wrong about the *order* — so inspection
> would have felt like confirmation.** That is the most dangerous form of a plausible guess: it
> survives every check that asks "are these the right quantities".

**What settled it is a proof rather than an inference.** `002E3D40(mode, A, B, C)` is a two-source
multiplexer: it loads the three script arguments into `ebp`/`esi`/`eax`, and **when `mode == 0` it
overwrites all three from the three MWeather extractors** before tail-jumping to one consumer.

> **When one function serves a value from two sources under a mode flag, the mode that reads the
> known source labels the registers for the mode that reads the unknown one.**

**And a caveat was closed on the way up.** A document recorded that two of three field widths were
*"inferred from the offsets being 3 and 7 with a 9-bit total, not read directly"*. They are readable —
**each wrapper computes its offset from its width**, so the encoding states both: `mov r9d,3` /
`xor r8d,r8d`; `mov r9d,4` / `lea r8d,[r9-1]`; `mov r9d,2` / `lea r8d,[r9+5]`. **A tier upgrade, not a
correction** — the inference was right and is now read.

**Modding consequence:** `setmapwind` overrides all three fields for as long as the script leaves them
set, and `defaultmapwind` restores them from the record for the **current** field and Weather Slot. **A
zone script that sets wind and never resets it keeps its override across a Weather Slot change that
would otherwise have re-read the table.**

### Only four of eleven Lua libraries were ever wired up — and `io` and `os` are not among them

**`luaL_openlibs` does not run.** Lua 5.2 opens its libraries by walking `loadedlibs` and
`preloadedlibs` from `linit.c`; **both arrays are in this image and neither is referenced by any
instruction, nor by any 8-byte pointer anywhere in the file.**

**The control for that absence is what makes it a finding rather than a scan result:** of the twelve
`luaL_Reg` bases, **ten are referenced, each by exactly one function** — naming nine more openers
(`luaopen_base`, `luaopen_coroutine`, `luaopen_table`, `luaopen_string`, `luaopen_bit32`,
`luaopen_math`, `luaopen_io`, `luaopen_os`, `luaopen_debug`). **The two unreferenced ones are
precisely the two bootstrap lists.**

**The game registers four libraries from one function** — `math`, `bit32`, `string`, `coroutine` —
through a helper that **has exactly four call sites in the entire image, all four of them there.**

> **So `base` (`_G`), `table`, `io`, `os` and `debug` are compiled in and never registered.** Zero
> direct callers and zero address-takings outside the two inert arrays. **A script cannot reach
> `os.execute`, `io.open` or `debug.sethook` through this path**, because the tables that would
> install them are never walked and their openers are never called.

**For a modder that is the practical shape of it:** *this is not a general Lua with the dangerous
parts removed — it is a Lua where only four of eleven standard libraries were ever wired up*, and the
omission happens to include both libraries that touch the OS.

**Three things not claimed, and one is load-bearing.** `base` and `table` being absent is genuinely
surprising — a Lua with no `print`, `pairs` or `setmetatable` is unusual — and **the likeliest
explanation is that the script environment is built by the Phyre binding layer rather than by stock
Lua. That is not traced and was not asserted.** The five calls made before the registrations were not
read, so **four libraries is a floor, not necessarily the whole environment**; and the registration
helper *stores* the pair rather than calling it, so deferral-until-`require` is the reading the body
supports **with the list's consumer untraced.**

### Four offset and units errors, every one plausible, none caught by looking odd

The first pass at the reference census returned **1 of 12 bases referenced** — which reads as a
spectacular finding: *"no `luaL_Reg` table is referenced by anything"*. It was arithmetic: the JSON
keys were already record bases and 8 was subtracted again to "correct" them. **The single hit was a
float constant being loaded by `divsd`.**

**The control failing at 1 of 12 is what stopped it.** After the fix it reads 10 of 12, with the two
exceptions being exactly the meaningful ones.

That completes a set of four:

| error | what it produced | what caught it |
|---|---|---|
| RTTI regex dropped template classes | 14.4 % of `.rdata` is vtables | a figure from outside the instrument |
| locator printed in decimal, read as hex | a coherent fictitious structure | a follow-up disagreeing with its source |
| size extractor took the wrong `mov` | 36 sizes, 22 of them zero | an implausible distribution |
| record bases offset by 8 twice | **1 of 12 tables referenced** | **a control, immediately** |

> **Every one produced a plausible number. Not one was caught by the result looking wrong.** Three
> were caught late by something outside the instrument; only the fourth was caught by a control built
> in advance — **and it is the only one that never reached a claim.**

**And "no Lua library table is referenced anywhere" is exactly the kind of dramatic negative that
reads as a discovery.** The dangerous errors are not the ones that produce nonsense; they are the ones
that produce a headline.

### The sibling rule is vindicated, and the skip is the finding

The four-residual group is **one family**, and the evidence is in the bodies rather than in the
shared-callee statistic that selected them. Each runs the same sequence in the same order against one
global context: fetch context → reset draw state (`memset(ctx+0x3930, 0, 0x178)`, `ctx[0x3A4C] =
0x80`) → set a pair of context fields → the shared helper chain.

> **Same-translation-unit — the alternative named in advance — is insufficient. It explains shared
> helpers. It does not explain four functions driving one global context through an identical
> reset-then-set sequence with a systematic polarity discriminator.**

**The discriminator was recovered from which values repeat**, the same method that split the Skin
family: three of the four set the `0x3001`/`0x44` pair and pass `+1`; **one skips that pair and passes
`-1`.** Three enable variants and one restore/disable variant. **The skip is the finding, not a gap in
the data.**

The bodies compute packed-field unpacking and rect arithmetic — a **packed 12:12 coordinate pair**
(`and 0xFFF` / `shr 0xC` / `and 0xFFF`) and `right = (s16)hdr[4] + (u16)hdr[8]`,
`bottom = (s16)hdr[6] + (u16)hdr[0xA]`. **A drawing shape.**

**And the refusal is the part worth keeping.** One caller consults save-busy state immediately before
invoking two of the four — **which names one caller's business, not the four functions'.** The context
getter has **56 callers image-wide**, so the context is shared infrastructure rather than
save-specific, and **inheriting an owner downward from a caller is banned regardless.** A 3-hop upward
trace from all three entries returns **zero named ancestors**, and there are **no strings** in any of
the four or in any shared helper. **What they draw is not established and was not named.**

### A correction I could not confirm, and the measurement that settles it

The reading session reported that the callee lists handed to them contained three **mid-function
addresses** — `001D7C21`, `001D7C62`, `001D7FB1` — attributed to a `jmp`-as-call-edge conflation in
whatever produced them.

**Checked, and the attribution does not hold:**

- **`edges.tsv` has zero internal edges whose target is not a function entry** — measured across all
  90,525 edges, 2,057 external: **0, 0.00 %.**
- None of the three appears as an edge target anywhere, and none is a function.
- They are interior addresses of `001D7A20` (932 B) and `001D76A0` (885 B).
- The list actually sent contained entry addresses only.

> **So the edge list is clean on exactly the defect it was accused of, and the three came from
> somewhere else in that session's pipeline.** Recorded because a correction accepted without
> checking is a defect adopted — the same rule that has cost this project three retractions tonight,
> applied to a correction rather than to a claim.

**The general point in the report stands and is worth the entry anyway:** counting `jmp` as an edge is
what caught `001D7280`'s **tail jump** into the group, which a call-only scan would have missed. **The
rule earns its keep and wants an "is the target a function entry" filter, not removal** — and
`edges.tsv` already applies exactly that filter, which is why it measures clean.

### `crossref_clean` asserts something false in 21 documents

`check_crossref_clean.py` is built and run. It takes the JSON from `audit_crossrefs.py`, groups
findings by document, and compares them with the frontmatter field. Ships `--self-test` — which
includes a control that the field is read from **frontmatter only**, so a document *discussing*
`crossref_clean` in prose is not parsed as declaring it.

**45 documents disagree with the checker, and the two directions are not the same finding:**

| direction | count | what it means |
|---|---:|---|
| **claims clean, has findings** | **21** | **the dangerous one — a document is treated as audited when it is not, and the AUDITED bar rests on it** |
| claims dirty, has none | 24 | the field is not maintained |

**And the 24 must be read with a caveat I have to declare, because I caused it.** Three fixes landed
in `audit_crossrefs.py` tonight — substrate excluded as a *subject*, a measured fan-in hub threshold,
and alias merging across taxonomies. **Every one of those legitimately removes findings**, so a
document that recorded `false` honestly when it was written can be clean now through no act of its
author. **The 24 are partly my own doing and are not evidence of neglect.**

**The 21 carry no such excuse.** They assert a machine-checkable fact that the machine contradicts.

> **The field the AUDITED bar depends on has never been checked, and it is wrong in 21 places.** Same
> shape as `audit.passes` counting amendments rather than attacks, and as `--db` being accepted and
> ignored: **a claim that looks like a fact because of where it is written.** Third instance tonight,
> and the pattern is now specific — **status fields and tool arguments are the two places nobody
> looks, because both are read as infrastructure rather than as assertions.**

### 160 is not stored, and it *is* enforced

A first pass on the character-render-record document overturned one claim and produced the
consequence the document had stopped one step short of.

*"160 is not stored anywhere as a capacity — it is a consequence of the allocation size divided by
the record stride."* **True of storage, false of enforcement.** A slot allocator compares against
`0xA0` three times: refuse when the live count reaches 160, re-check after increment, and **wrap the
round-robin cursor at 160.**

**And that decodes the `0x130` tail the document had identified and left unread:** `base + 0x48808`
is the allocation cursor, `base + 0x4880C` the live record count.

> **So the document can now say *why* the pool cannot be grown: there is no capacity field to edit.
> 160 is compiled into three immediates in one function plus the allocation literal — four patches,
> and nothing in the data would tell a modder that.**

**The quotient warning cleared, and the third state was the right question.** The figure is neither
stated nor counted but **derived** — and the derivation is circular **if and only if** the stride was
itself obtained by assuming 160 records. It was not: the stride is independently established at **652
sites in 376 functions.** Two independent inputs, one quotient. **Neither of the pass's two prepared
questions would have found that; naming "it may be a quotient" as a third state is what did.**

**A clean negative on the adjacency play, and it is a full result.** Functions referencing both the
render-record array and the `001Bxxxx` draw context: **zero.** Both the array and the authored-command
table: **zero.** The draw context has **3** referencing functions image-wide against the array's
**372**. **Two separate drawing paths sharing no code** — so the four-function family does not emit
character render records, and both readings stand independently.

**A count restated with its predicate rather than corrected:** 639 references claimed, 636 sites in
372 functions measured, **three apart, and the document does not state how it counted.** Recorded as a
predicate difference in which **neither figure is refutable by the other** — the fourth time tonight
that distinction has prevented a false correction.

### The family is proven by a second quantity; the members are not, and that was not claimed

The 26 vtables are **`PInputSource` and its 25 subclasses.** Not by count — by **object size
multiset**, read from `r9d` at all 35 registrars:

```
size    PInputSource* registrars    the 26 destructors
0x28              20                      20
0x40               4                       4
0x38               2                       2
```

**20 / 4 / 2 across three values is distinctive enough that agreement by coincidence is
implausible**, and the base with two pure virtuals is `PInputSource` itself. Named by band: `0x38` is
the joypad-axis and mouse-button sources, `0x40` the joypad-button, key and mouse-delta sources,
`0x28` the base plus nineteen motion / quaternion / touch / vision-tracker sources.

**And the honest stopping point is the entry.** **No registrar contains any reference into
`01CD6268`–`01CD65A8`** — checked across all 35. Nothing joins an individual name to an individual
vtable, so **within a size band the members are interchangeable on present evidence and not one of the
26 rows is individually named.**

> **A count plus a matching multiset is enough to identify a set and not enough to map it.** Closing
> the last step by pairing sizes to names in address order is exactly the trap — the 20 classes at
> `0x28` are unordered with respect to the 20 vtables at `0x28`.

**Two more instrument slips, both caught by controls.** A registrar list generated from an **assumed
`0xA0` pitch** resolved one address of 35, because the real pitch is irregular — *"assuming a stride
is the same error as assuming a boundary"*, third time tonight, **and the fix is the same each time:
derive the set, do not generate it.** And `6F537475706E4950` was nearly filed as an unidentified
8-byte constant before being decoded as `"PInputSo"`.

### The second look has to be a different kind of look

On the retracted vtable finding, the author's comparison of the two failures is sharper than either:

> **A wrong inference from a correct field is one thing. A test that could not have returned a
> different answer is another** — and the boundary check I ran verified the shape that had been
> asserted rather than testing it.

**Between a scan and a verification the finding survived both**, because both asked the same question.

> **The second look has to be a different kind of look, not a second instance of the first.**

### A recorded instrument failure is reusable; a silently corrected one is not

The first pass on the keymap document went to **the parts its own author had previously accepted**,
and said so. The claim that had licensed an earlier identification — *"the name's index is the slot's
index"* — was attacked first. **It survives, and now proves more than was originally cited:** the
slot counter is **explicitly reset to zero per group**, and the loop-back target is the dispatch
rather than the group-counter initialisation, so the pointer-pairing runs exactly once at index 0.
**Inferred before, proven now**, and an identification resting on it is safe.

**Two corrections, both population errors rather than reading errors:**

- *"10 call sites"* is **10 distinct callers and 15 call sites** — one caller invokes it six times.
  **The document stated the number it had not measured.**
- *"The only reader that reaches group 2"* is true **only of binding getters**, and the document's own
  §4 is the evidence against it as worded. **And the chase was worth it:** group 2 is reached as
  `base + 0x60` and **not** by referencing its own address, so a second group-2 reader would be
  invisible to the very test the section cites. What closes it is the base's reference list — 8 sites
  across 6 functions, all accounted for.

**A population difference recorded rather than resolved:** 7 references from one instrument, 5 from a
rip-relative operand sweep, and the difference is **computed accesses the decompiler resolves to the
symbol** — including an indexed load that is not a reference to that address in the encoding at all.
**Both counts correct for their instrument, recorded so nobody "fixes" one to match the other.**

**And the reusable lesson:**

> **A recorded instrument failure is reusable; a silently corrected one is not.**

That document had already caught one of its own instruments failing — a linear sweep returning 0 for
every global including a provably referenced one — and **wrote the failure down instead of quietly
switching tools.** One document and one author later, that note is what told the next session which
instrument to use for three absence claims.

**Status left DOCUMENTED rather than AUDITED, with a non-empty "not attacked" list**, chiefly tier-10
rows resting on a file not re-read from disk.

> **Claiming AUDITED with a non-empty not-attacked list would be the status equivalent of softening a
> claim until the tool goes quiet.**

### The movement gate is dropped mid-session, not latched at bring-up

A dichotomy offered by the document — *"this is not a tuning switch. It is 'the actor system has been
brought up', and it reads as a guard against running the flat path during bootstrap or after a
teardown"* — **fits neither branch. Third missing third state of the session.**

Writer census over all 38,161 bodies: `02B40530` has 2 writers, one of them a **7-byte public
setter**, verified from the image — `89 0d 1a 87 78 02 c3` = `mov [rip+0x0278871A], ecx` / `ret`,
target `0x003B7E16 + 0x0278871A` = **`02B40530`**. `02B40534` has **8 writers, three of which store
0.**

**The setter's callers pass constants both ways** — six sites in five functions, three passing 1 and
three passing 0. **A value written 0 and 1 from five functions through a dedicated setter is not a
bring-up latch.**

**And the clearing has a visible purpose.** A 284-byte function clears the gate **at its head**, then
walks the actor list — resolve by packed id, get world position, per-actor work, bounded by the list
count — **and never writes it back.** Restoration is somebody else's job.

> **So the gate is dropped while the engine is mutating actor state in bulk: a consistency interlock
> over the actor list, held false for the duration of a bulk update.** The document's *instinct* is
> right — it guards against reading invalid state — and its *lifetime* is wrong. **The window is a
> runtime operation, not bootstrap-to-teardown.**

**Practical consequence: the flat path can be disabled mid-session**, so a mod assuming a startup
latch will mis-predict behaviour during whatever that bulk update serves.

### State a claim at the width you can defend, not the width that reads better

The uniqueness claim in the same document is the kind that usually breaks under a census, and it
**survives — because it was precise.** It claims *"the one function that sets **both**"*, not *"the
only writer"*. **Ten writes across the two globals, and it is still the only function in both sets.**

> **A looser phrasing of the same true observation would have been overturned by this census; the
> exact one is not.** State a claim at the width you can defend rather than the width that reads
> better — the loose version is not a simplification, it is a different and false claim that happened
> to be adjacent to a true one.

Everything else reproduced exactly: three body sizes, 33 distinct callers over 37 sites, a function
called from **exactly three** functions at four sites which are **the three the document names by
role**, both globals zero and past `.data`'s raw contents, and both selectors' bit arithmetic.

**And the document names its own prior conflation** — §2 separates three things *"because the database
has previously conflated the last two"*. **A document that records what it was previously confused
with is doing by hand what the provenance convention formalises**, and it is why this pass could
attack the distinction rather than rediscover it.

**Two never-attacked documents closed in succession: `audit_coverage` 84.21 % → 87.37 %.**

### An undispositioned false positive is the noise a real finding hides in

`how-a-sound-request-becomes-a-voice.md` carried **two continuously-red gates, both false, neither
ever dispositioned** — and **seven genuine BODY DRIFT findings sat behind them.**

**One of the two was my tool's fault and is fixed.** `BODYSIZE` ended with `\b`, which the `/` in
`24 B/entry` satisfies, **so a stride in a stride column was read as a body extent** and a compliant
data address was reported as a ghost. Now required to end its cell; verified with two controls — a
real body row still matches, the stride cell is rejected — and 68 genuine body-size rows in that
document are still recognised.

> **An undispositioned false positive is not free. It is the noise a real finding hides in.**

**And the attacking session refused to silence it by rewording** — *"writing `24-byte entries` would
silence it without changing the claim; that is a decision about the tool and I have not made it."*
**The tool was wrong, and rewording would have hidden that permanently.** Same shape as the alias
table a magic token could satisfy, seen from the document's side.

### Seven wrong sizes, and the grouping underneath them

All seven confirmed: actuals **231 / 78 / 62 / 97 / 97 / 62 / 62**. **Two candidate causes tested and
both fail** — measuring to the first `ret` gives 225/78/56/97/97/35/56, and none has a tail `JMP`.
**So they did not come from mis-measuring the current program**, and the document's provenance
sentence is not true of those rows. **Where 196/66/46 came from is the one thing the pass could not
derive, and it has been put to the author as the single question worth asking.**

**The claim underneath the sizes is the real finding.** Three claimed sizes across seven functions is
a **grouping**, and it half-survives:

| implied group | actual | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| three functions all "46 B" | all **62** | holds |
| three functions all "66 B" | **78**, 97, 97 | **breaks** |

**The base `AudioController` constructor is not the same size as the two derived constructors it was
grouped with.** And the two surviving groups came out **stronger** than the document had them — **6 of
62 bytes differing** across one trio, **12 of 97** across the pair. **Two genuine constructor families,
one specialised three ways and one twice, plus a base belonging to neither — a structural fact the
document never stated, recovered from its own error.**

### Every census figure moved one way, and that is checkable

The thunk exposure flagged at placement was real and **entirely directional**: 100 non-Audio callers
not 99; an inbound surface of **182 / 325 / 421** against a stated 168 / 305 / 401; and a previous
"168, not 174" correction that went one direction only — **174 is both an upper and a lower bound.**

**19 of the 20 omitted edges are `JMP`s from thunk functions, and the graph had zero edges the byte
decode lacked** — *on that population.*

> **~~A graph census can only under-count against a byte decode.~~ RETRACTED 2026-09-03.** That was
> true of the 177 functions it was measured on and **is not a property of the instrument.** Across
> the whole image the graph holds **384 edges a direct `E8`/`E9` decode does not** — indirect calls
> the decompiler resolved that a byte scan cannot see. On one later population: **1 graph-only, 8
> bytes-only.**
>
> **Neither route bounds the other. They see different things**, and a figure from either is a floor
> with respect to the other's blind spot, not a floor absolutely.

**I promoted that to a rule in this log and it is wrong.** Anyone who took *“the graph only omits”*
as licence to treat a graph-derived count as a hard floor would have been wrong wherever indirect
calls matter — which is most of the dispatch-heavy code this database is about.

> **A property measured on one population is not a property of the instrument.** It is the same
> error as reading six entries of a nineteen-entry table: **a boundary observed and then assumed to
> be the edge.** The corrected version is narrower and still useful — **use both routes, and say
> which blind spot each figure carries.**

### A scanner too narrow to see what it is testing

A first RIP-relative scanner **hardcoded the modrm `REG` field to 0**, so it saw only `EAX`-sourced
stores and reported a global as having **zero writers** — it would have "refuted" a true claim.

**The control that caught it was drawn from the document under attack**: requiring the scan to find
the six writers the document itself names.

> **Drawing a control from the document under attack is the cheapest guard against a scanner too
> narrow to see what it is testing** — and it is available in every pass, because a document that
> states any positive fact has handed you a known-positive set.

### The thunk document fell to its own thesis

`the-thunk-layer-and-why-call-counts-disagree.md` §2 says *"`0028FB40` is the only 19-byte member, and
its body is not a forward."* **True of the 689 `Thunk.*`-tagged functions. False of the binary.**

Scanning every ledger body for the exact shape `mov rcx,[rip+disp]; add rcx,imm; jmp rel32` finds
**five**, and the ledger confirms all five at 19 bytes:

```
0028E220  19 B  ledger thunk=true   no Thunk.* tag
0028E860  19 B  ledger thunk=true   no Thunk.* tag
0028E8B0  19 B  ledger thunk=true   no Thunk.* tag
0028FB40  19 B  ledger thunk=true   Thunk.InternalForwarder    <- the one documented
0028FB60  19 B  ledger thunk=FALSE  no Thunk.* tag
```

`0028FB60` read from the image: `48 8b 0d 19 c3 e0 01` / `48 81 c1 80 53 00 00` / `e9 0d a5 ff ff` —
`mov rcx,[rip+0x01E0C319]` → **`0209BE80`**, `add rcx,0x5380`, `jmp 0028A080`. **The same singleton
`0028FB40` loads**, with a different sub-object offset.

> **So these are a family of bound-method entry points over one global, not an oddity — and
> `0028FB60` is flagged by neither instrument the document contrasts.** Invisible to the graph census
> *and* to the tag census, while byte-identical to the one that is documented.

**The failure is the one this document exists to warn about, one level up: §2 measured the tagged
population and stated a property of the binary.**

**And there is a two-hop chain the document does not anticipate.** One of the twelve unflagged direct
tail forwarders jumps to a **flagged receiver-binder**, which jumps on again. **Each hop defeats a
different instrument:** a graph census stops at hop 1; a census that models thunk forwarding walks
through hop 2 **and never records that `RCX` was rewritten on the way.**

### The worked example reproduced the thesis during the audit

Every measurement in the document survived exactly — 689 tagged, the size histogram 568/108/12/1 on
all four, 677 flagged with the twelve unflagged being precisely the twelve enumerated, 43 incoming and
0 outgoing for those twelve.

**And its own worked example produced the document's thesis while the document was being audited.**
Its `47 / 65 / 110` is exact under a **call-only** convention. A call+`jmp` census gives
**47 / 66 / 111** — one more on each of the last two — **and the extra caller is the thunk itself**,
reaching the target by `jmp`. Remove it and both land exactly.

> **Two instruments, three numbers, one binary, and the difference is entirely whether a `JMP` counts
> as a call. Nothing was wrong in either measurement.**

**And the same convention choice was a *defect* in that session's edge scan three blocks ago and is a
*convention* here. The difference is only whether it is stated** — which is the document's own
closing line, demonstrated on the document.

### Tildes concealing a 44-function gap

Family counts *"~528"*, *"~105"* and 12 sum to **645, not 689**. The exact tag counts are **560 / 117
/ 12 = 689 with no remainder.**

> **In a document about measurement discipline, two tildes concealed a 44-function gap** — and a
> reader checking the arithmetic would have assumed the approximation, not the shortfall.

**And one more pair restated rather than corrected:** *"43 incoming edges"* counts **distinct
caller-callee pairs**; an instruction census finds **45 sites**, and **12 outgoing where the graph
records 0.** Both right, different questions — the sixth such pair tonight.

**Three never-attacked documents closed in succession by one session: `audit_coverage` 84.21 % →
88.42 %.**

### The seven sizes were estimated from decompiled line counts

**There was no tool to chase.** The author wrote those rows while correcting a different error, had run
a `functions.tsv` size lookup for an earlier batch that did not include the seven new rows, and
**filled the Body column by estimating from the length of the decompiled bodies in context.**

**The reading is testable and it holds:**

```
~6 decompiled lines  -> wrote  46   actual 62, 62, 62
~8 decompiled lines  -> wrote  66   actual 97, 97
~9 decompiled lines  -> wrote  66   actual 78
~25 decompiled lines -> wrote 196   actual 231
```

> **Decompiled length tracks source structure; body size tracks emitted bytes.** Where the two agree —
> three identical constructor shapes, all genuinely 62 — **the group held.** Where they diverge — a
> base constructor shorter in source than the derived ones but not proportionally shorter in bytes —
> **the group broke.**

**So the grouping was real signal presented in the wrong units**, and the attacking pass produced a
better statement than the document had: two genuine constructor families, **6 of 62 bytes differing**
across one trio and **12 of 97** across the pair, with the base belonging to neither.

**And the two eliminated candidates were the right ones to eliminate.** Both *had* to fail for the
answer to be "the author estimated": a tool would have produced a **consistent transformation**, and
first-`ret` measurement would have produced a **shorter** number, not a longer one.

> **Nothing findable in the binary would have reached this answer. It needed the author to say it** —
> which is an argument for asking one precise question of an author rather than a general handover,
> and for the author answering it against their own work.

### Whether the tool or the document is wrong is a decision to make, not to route around

**The author had made, an hour earlier and on the same document, exactly the mistake the attacking
session refused to make**: faced with the ghost finding they reworded `24 B/entry` to `24-byte
entries` — **turning the gate green without changing a single claim, on a row that was never wrong** —
and wrote a paragraph asserting the checker was right.

**Both are now reverted**, the wording restored and the paragraph replaced with a retraction, on the
grounds that *"a gate turning green is not evidence that anything was repaired"* is worth more in the
document than a clean scan was.

> **Whether the tool or the document is wrong is a decision to make, not to route around.**

That is the general form of the token-satisfaction rule, and it is the third time tonight the same
pressure has produced an edit: an alias table a keyword could satisfy, a status field asserting a
clean scan, and now a data row reworded to quiet a pattern.

### A one-directional error is a systematic one

On the census corrections: a graph built from `getCalledFunctions` **under-reports tail-called
thunks**, so every census run off it is low **by exactly that class** — 19 of 20 missing edges are
thunk `JMP`s with **zero** in the other direction.

> **A one-directional error is a systematic one**, and the figures were published with a positive
> control that **could not have caught it, because the control tested membership rather than
> completeness.**

That is a distinct control failure from the four already tabulated: not too weak, not too narrow —
**aimed at the wrong property.** A membership control answers *"does my instrument find things it
should find?"*; only a completeness control answers *"does it find all of them?"*

`keymap-ini-file-format-and-default-controls.md` reaches AUDITED at pass 2, all three not-attacked

**And the residue is named rather than absorbed.** Not directly re-derived: the parser's two grammar

they produce — but none was read instruction by instruction in either pass.

> **Naming them is the difference between an audited document and a stamped one.** A later reader
> knows exactly where the thinness is instead of inheriting a clean stamp. The bar was reached by
> attacking until the residue was small enough to name, **not by reinterpreting the criterion.**

### A control that cannot separate its hypotheses

The key-semantic mapping was re-parsed rather than inherited, and **all 28 of 28 shipped codes resolve
through the `-1` transform**, names matching exactly.

**But resolving *without* the `-1` still hits 27 of 28.**

> **A coverage-based check cannot separate the two hypotheses.** Anyone re-verifying by counting hits
> would have confirmed a true claim **for the wrong reason** and been right by luck.

What separates them is **semantics**:

```
LX_N 28  ->  code+1 = Key_A   |  code = (nothing)
LX_P 31  ->  code+1 = Key_D   |  code = Key_C
LY_N 50  ->  code+1 = Key_W   |  code = Key_V
LY_P 46  ->  code+1 = Key_S   |  code = Key_R
```

**One hypothesis yields WASD. The other yields C, V, R and a hole.** The document's own worked check
was the right discriminator and is now shown to be **the only one available.**

That is a sixth entry for the control table, and a distinct failure: **not too weak, too narrow, or
aimed at the wrong property — a control that passes for both the true and the false hypothesis, so
its result carries no information at all.**

Two byte-identical copies of `keymap.ini` exist on this machine — one at the game root, one under a
`<SteamID64>` directory. §2 says the path carries a Steam-id component; §8 says *"the id component is
empty when Steam is not initialised."*

> **The two files ARE that branch condition, observed from disk.** The same build wrote the same
> content down both paths. **Not sought, and not constructible** — a tier-1 observation that only
> exists because someone looked at the filesystem rather than the binary.

**With the right caveat carried:** this works only because the file here is unmodified. **On a machine
where the player has rebound anything the claim becomes UNTESTABLE, not false** — and a later reader
must not report that as a defect.

### Three independent routes per row, and the last one was closed rather than waived

The bar was set at three routes per row **before** the verdict arrived, and row 4 came back one short.

**The auditing session named the cheapest way to close it** — read `003659F0`, whose role they had
inferred from call position — **and did not close it themselves**, which would have made their two
routes look like three.

Read here, and it settles it:

```
memset(state, 0, 0x68)                        zeroes the text state block
state[0] = state[1] = state[2] = 0x3f800000   three scale fields, 1.0f
state[0xc] = 0x80808080                       colour
*(state+8) = DAT_022cbe00 + 0x1a0             the shared matrix
FUN_00203170(local_68)                        loads the identity from the 008C5F80 pool
short writes from param_5[0..3]               the box rect
*(DAT_022cbe00 + 0x238) = 0                   clears the last-glyph-record publish slot
```

> **It initialises exactly the fields the document independently describes the emitter reading** —
> scale at `+0/+4/+8`, colour at `+0x30`, the box rect. So *"setup + glyph emit, twice"* is two calls
> **whose contract is visible in the callee**, and an inference from position became a reading of a
> body.

**And it puts `00203170` — the `008C5F80` pool reader — one hop inside batch A's evidence chain**,
which makes that pool load-bearing for more than one document.

### What made the verdict trustworthy

- **A controlled negative on the absence claim.** *"Zero render or scope calls"* on the measuring
  path, with the identical scan returning **6** on the emitting path. **The instrument fires when
  render calls exist, so the zero is a measurement, not a silence** — control discipline applied
  inside a clearance somebody was waiting on.
- **Corroboration from an unused direction.** `2 + 22×4 = 90` accounts for the trailer exactly, and
  **22 cases resolving to 12 distinct targets is eleven tags plus a default** — confirming the
  document's count without touching the reasoning that produced it.
- **A bounded verdict.** The shadow *offsets*, the icon body, and one callee's role were explicitly
  **not** cleared, with the demonstration that none of the four names depends on them.
  **Separating "what I verified" from "what the row claims" is the difference between a clearance and
  an endorsement.**
- **The reported cause checked, not adopted.** `002D28E0` ends `FF`, not `C3` — consistent with a size
  taken from the wrong row of a caller listing.

### Publishing your controls should not cost audit noise

An address cited **only** on control lines is an instrument control, not a subject —
and `audit_crossrefs` was inheriting its entire neighbourhood. One document cites `00378540` exactly
once, as *"positive control 2: `00378540` → `MWeather` PASS"*, and the checker read that as a claim
about Resource.

> **We have spent the session pushing every session to name its controls in the document. The cost of
> that must not be borne by the author** — otherwise controls quietly disappear from documents to
> keep a gate green, **which is the token-satisfaction failure aimed at the evidence rather than at
> the prose.**

Fixed narrowly: an address survives as a subject if it appears **even once** on a line that is not a
control line, so a real subject that also serves as a control is unaffected.

### My correction was an over-read of the same species as the one it replaced

`008C5F80` has now been named three times and the first two were both wrong in the same way.

- The original: **"the 4×4 identity"** — named after the four rows one caller assembles.
- **My correction: "six ± axis vectors"** — named after six.
- **What it is: a compiler-deduplicated `.rdata` constant pool**, and the "missing `−X`" is not an
  anomaly.

Re-read here from the certified program:

```
008C5FE0 (+0x60)   0  1  0  1      <- not an axis vector at all
008C5FF0 (+0x70)   22 05 93 19 01 00 00 00 | 40 45 c3 01 00 00 00 00
                                   <- not float data; the pool has ended
```

**110 distinct functions touch the region and 72 of them touch exactly one row.** Different callers
take different subsets — the identity reader takes rows 0/1/3/5, and the sole reader of `+0x20` takes
0/2/4 = `+X`, `−Y`, `−Z`. The constants immediately before it are `0.02`, `0.10`, `1.5708`, `6.2832`,
`1000.0`: a generic pooled area.

> **There is no `−X` row because no function in the image needed one.** A pool contains what was used,
> deduplicated, in emission order. **The missing element is only missing relative to a structure that
> was never there.**

> **A run of constants in `.rdata` does not have to be anything.** And when the reference census shows
> **most callers taking exactly one element, that is the answer rather than a step toward one.**

**I diagnosed the original defect correctly and then committed it.** I wrote at the time that naming a
data region after the use four of its six rows are put to *"is the same species as inheriting an owner
from a caller"* — and then named it after six. **The species was right and I was inside it.**

That makes three of my own contributions overturned tonight: a vtable finding verified by a test that
could not fail, a batch size claim, and now this. **Every one was caught by a session I had routed at
the work**, which is the argument for the routing rather than for me.

### I broke the shared gate for forty minutes, and it failed the right way

The control-line filter added an hour ago used `for a in cited:` — **shadowing the argparse namespace
`a`** — so the *next* document in the walk died on `a.docs` with
`AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'docs'`. **Single-document runs passed; every
category-wide run crashed.** Two sessions could not complete a category run.

Fixed, verified with a full multi-document pass (145 findings across 57 documents, both hard classes
still empty), and the cause left in the file as a comment rather than silently repaired:

> **A loop variable is a claim about the enclosing scope.**

**And the failure mode is the one to want.** A crash is not a false clean: **the gate died loudly**, so
nobody could have been misled into believing a category was green. After a night of instruments
returning *plausible wrong answers*, a tool that stops is the cheap outcome.

**The reporting session flagged the exact line and deliberately did not patch it** — shared tooling
under someone else's authority, with an active editor in the file. **Cost: one message.** That is what
the authority boundary is for.

### The one class of claim nothing in this database re-checks

> **`audit_crossrefs` compares documents to the binary, never to each other. A claim about a
> neighbour is the one kind of claim in this database that nothing re-checks.**

Two documents were each describing the other **as it used to be**: one said a file format *"is still
unread"* when it is read and AUDITED; the other said its neighbour *"calls `01DF1738` a staging
buffer"* when that document says the **opposite**, explicitly, with the same arithmetic.

**That sentence survived two falsification passes on its own document** — because both attacked its
claims about the binary and neither attacked its claims about the corpus. **It was already stale when
it was written.**

It is a direct hit on an AUDITED stamp earned an hour earlier: criterion 10 says every claim needs a
killer, **and it was applied only to claims about the binary.** Naming that oneself, an hour after
earning the stamp, is worth more than the stamp.

**A checker is owed and is mine to build** — narrow form: resolve assertions shaped *"`<doc>` says X"*
where `<doc>` is a linked database file, and flag when the quoted claim is absent from the target.
**It will not catch paraphrase and does not need to: the failure mode is staleness, and stale claims
tend to quote.**

### A zero from a tool that did not read anything

A published evidence row read *"raw read of `01F80F90`, 336 bytes, every byte zero."* **There are no
336 bytes there** — `.data` is file-backed only to `01F7E400`, and that address is past it. The row
was reading a tool's zero-fill for a region the image does not contain.

**The conclusion survived and the evidence did not**, which is the harder case to notice — and the
consequence drawn from it was **false**: *"which is why you cannot read the game's default controls
straight out of the executable."* **You can.** The defaults are authored constants elsewhere, decoded
and matched byte for byte against the player's file in another pass.

> **A true premise carrying a false conclusion is invisible to anyone checking the premise.**

### Recusal as a measured fact rather than a principle

A session declined its own spawn document, and the reasoning is stronger than the rule:

> **That document has already been corrected twice, both times by me doing adjacent work rather than
> by review — and both errors survived my own writing of it *and* my own adversarial pass on it. My
> blind spots on that specific document are demonstrated, not hypothetical, and re-reading it is the
> activity that has already failed to find them twice.**

**And the prescription follows from the diagnosis:** route it to whoever next reads a ScriptVM command
table or a strided `.data` record array. **What found those errors was meeting the same shape
elsewhere, not looking harder at the document.**

They also flagged prior context before starting the next one — several of its cited functions appeared
in their constant-pool census an hour ago — on the grounds that *"I have seen this address before" is
exactly the state where I would otherwise carry an assumption in without noticing.*

### `check_doc_claims.py` — the cross-document gap, closed

Built and running. It finds a sentence that names or links another database `.md`, uses a reporting
verb, and quotes a backticked or quoted term — then asks whether the target contains that term.
**Hits are questions**: absent means either the claim is **stale** or the target **paraphrases**, and
the tool does not decide which. Ships `--self-test`.

**First run: 83 claims across 35 documents. After two corrections to my own instrument: 7 across 5.**

**Both corrections were mine and both were the same class.** The sentence splitter joined every line
of a paragraph before splitting on punctuation, **so an entire markdown table collapsed into one
"sentence"** and a filename in one cell was matched against a term three columns away in an unrelated
row. And `_inbox` was being scanned, where a report *about* a stale claim legitimately quotes the
stale wording.

> **A sentence splitter is a claim about how the document is laid out.** Fifth checker in this kit to
> manufacture findings from its own text assumptions, and the fix is the same each time: **respect the
> structure that is actually there rather than the prose structure assumed.**

Of the seven survivors, **two are `_index` files that quote claims as their subject matter** —
AUDIT-LOG and EVIDENCE-STANDARD exist to record defective wording — leaving **three real corpus
claims** for review.

### Two name disagreements, one real and one a range row

Reported by one session, re-run per the non-atomic rule, and **both reproduced** — so not a mid-write
artefact. Resolved from the image rather than by choosing between the documents:

```
01F2CEB8 -> name ptr 00D2BAF8 -> "ShaderParameterF2"   component count 2
01F2CED0 -> name ptr 00D2BB98 -> "ShaderParameterF1"   component count 1
```

- **`01F2CEB8` was a genuinely stale row** — still reading `ChannelSemantic_(unread)`, *"name not yet
  read (BM-1)"*, in a document whose own §10 had just **closed BM-1 and named it**. The pass corrected
  the section and left the summary table behind. **Struck, with the old value visible.**
- **`01F2CED0` is a checker limitation, not an error.** The row is a **range**:
  `| 4–7 | 01F2CE88…01F2CED0 | ShaderParameterF4, F3, F2, F1 | 4, 3, 2, 1 |`. The checker paired the
  end-address with the **first** name in the cell. The document is right — `01F2CED0` is `F1` in that
  row and in the detail table.

> **A range row states one address and several names, and a pairing checker cannot read it.** Recorded
> as a limitation rather than silenced by rewording the document — **the row is correct and the
> checker cannot see why.**

### 19 entries, not 6 — and the example was the narrowest one available

Every number in the animation document's §3 is exact. **What failed was a boundary: it read six
entries of a nineteen-entry table and described the six as the table.** Walking the document's own
stated stride from its own stated base until the name pointer breaks — confirmed here, `01F2D008`
holds a null pointer — gives thirteen more, **all nineteen referenced from `.text`**, 2–5 sites each,
none vestigial.

**And the boundary error cost a player-facing claim.** The document offers *"a shader parameter"* as
**the** example of a non-transform channel. The table also carries **light colour, intensity and
falloff; camera FOV, near, far, orthographic size; morph target weight — the channel that drives
facial expression; and four user-attribute types.**

> **One animation file can pull the camera's FOV, dim a light and change a face in the same bundle of
> curves that moves the skeleton** — staying in sync for exactly the reason the document already gives.
> **The mechanism section was right; its example was the narrowest one available.**

**BM-1 closes**, and the component count the document already had was correct — **it measured the field
it could reach and did not guess the one it could not.**

### An instrument that cannot answer the question at all

To test *"exactly one descriptor object per semantic"*, the first attempt counted **name byte-strings**:
`Rotation` 2, `Translation` 2, **`Scale` 5,167** — because *Scale* is a common English substring.

> **A test that looks equivalent to the right one and is not is worth more in the log than the answer
> it gave.** The pointer test is the right one — read each descriptor's own name pointer, find every
> aligned qword equal to it — and gives **one slot each, image-wide.**

### A clean survival, and what it takes to earn one

After four documents that each gave up a finding, the Bullet integration document gave up none: **0
overturned, 9 survived, 2 strengthened.** Every stated size exact, and two identifications matching
upstream Bullet **instruction for instruction, arrived at independently** — the
`DISABLE_DEACTIVATION`/`DISABLE_SIMULATION` pair, and `btCompoundShape` initialising its local AABB to
`+BT_LARGE_FLOAT` / `−BT_LARGE_FLOAT`. **Tier-6 corroboration that did not come from name resemblance.**

**And both strengthenings converted a hedge into a census.** *"FFXII never sets it at the call site
read here"* becomes: `btCompoundShape` has **one caller image-wide**, it passes zero, and
`btDbvt::btDbvt`'s **only caller is `btCompoundShape`**. So the dynamic AABB tree is constructed
**nowhere in FFXII** and every compound shape uses the linear child scan.

> For a modder that is the difference between *"this call site does not enable it"* and **"enabling it
> has no precedent anywhere in the shipped binary."**

The second identifies **Bullet's allocator hook table** — `malloc`, `free`, an aligned-alloc and an
aligned-free hook in four consecutive slots, each with exactly one writer and one reader — **and takes
one of the six runs off the unowned-code census's uncharacterised remainder.**

### `0x7F` is not a literal at any call site

Verified from the image at `00249C77`:

```
ba 40 00 00 00      mov  edx, 0x40          the pan IS an immediate
8b c8               mov  ecx, eax
44 8d 42 3f         lea  r8d, [rdx + 0x3f]  the volume is COMPUTED from it
```

A document states *"the values are not derived from anything at the call site; they are literals
compiled in."* **Half of that is wrong, and it is the half a modder acts on**: the same document
offers this call site as an intervention point.

> **Someone searching for a `0x7F` immediate near the play call will not find one — and patching the
> pan silently moves the volume, because the volume is derived from the pan register.** Four of the
> five other resolvable direct callers use the same `lea` idiom. **Not one call site in the image
> passes `0x7F` as an immediate.**

And the fifth caller passes a **variable** volume, which sharpens the document's own caution: not
merely *"not every sound passes through here"* but **"even the sounds that do do not all carry the
same volume."**

### An illustration is not worth a citation

A paragraph naming four callers was **purely illustrative** — the census point stood without any of
them — and citing two of them by address pulled Combat Formula and Combat Action edges into an audio
document. Rewritten to name them by owner: **folder findings 14 → 5.**

> **A citation commits the document to accounting for everything the address drags in; an example that
> could be replaced by a count never earns that.**

**Third instance of this defect tonight, by the third different route** — shared boilerplate, a
by-address reference to someone else's census, and now an illustrative list. The one citation kept was
kept deliberately and dispositioned, **because the claim it supports cannot be checked without it.**

### Auditing outward finds what auditing inward does not

The same pass corrected **its own author's other document**: a sound described as *"sound id `0x52`"*
is a **bank-local index**, since the resolver returns `bankSlot*512 + index`. So identifying that sound
needs the **runtime bank slot** as well as the authored data — the open question was understated.

> **Second time auditing a neighbour has corrected that session's own work, and neither was found by
> re-reading their own text.**

That is the mechanism-adjacency rule arriving from a third direction: not *"meet the same shape
again"* but **"read the document your own claims lean on."**

### I routed a session onto a document that had already been attacked

A session was placed on `what-the-engine-calls-to-make-a-sound.md` as *never attacked*. **It already
carried a pass** — §10, dated the same day, by another session — and its frontmatter is stamped.

**The list was correct when I built it and stale when I used it.** Third instance of that shape
tonight, after two routing collisions, and the same cause each time: **a snapshot taken once and
consulted for several ticks.**

**The session recovered it into a better pass than the one I intended**, by taking §10's own statement
of what it could not reach — *"the boundary population figures would need an independently built
census to attack rather than re-run"* — and attacking exactly that, with a census built for the

first pass on a document nobody has read.**

> **The fix is not a better list. It is to re-derive the unattacked set at the moment of placing, not
> at the moment of asking.** It costs one command.

Re-deriving a split with *"Audio caller" = owner == Audio* gives **14 / 69 / 43**, not 25 / 54 / 47.

### The audit metric was wrong a third time, and this time it under-counted

Re-deriving the unattacked set live — the fix committed to after routing a session onto an
already-audited document — surfaced a **second field name the scorer never read.**

**Eleven documents carry `falsification_passes`.** Nine of them also carry a stamped `passes` and a
recorded state, so they scored correctly by accident. **Two use the new field alone** — `passes: 0`,
`last_pass_state: null`, `falsification_passes: 1` — **and each carries a written falsification-pass
section.** The scorer counted both as never attacked.

```
audit_coverage   92.63 % (88/95)  ->  94.74 % (90/95)
OVERALL          45.18 %          ->  45.50 %
```

**`falsification_passes` is arguably the better name**, since `passes` was established tonight to
count *amendments*. Rather than legislate the name, the scorer now accepts either — **but the new one
only with a section in the body, never on the counter alone.** Verified both ways: a bare counter with
no section does not score; a counter with a section does.

> **Accepting a bare counter would be the original defect returning under a new name.** The whole
> point is that **a number in the frontmatter is a claim and only the section is evidence.**

**Third correction to this metric tonight, and the first in the under-counting direction:**

| | direction | cause |
|---|---|---|
| 86.81 → 80.22 | over-counted | `passes` counts amendments, not attacks |
| — | neither | required a recorded program state |
| **92.63 → 94.74** | **under-counted** | **a second field name nobody reconciled** |

> **A metric drifts both ways, and only one of those feels like a problem.** An inflated figure gets
> attacked because it flatters; a deflated one is read as rigour. **Nobody audits a number that makes
> them look worse** — which is exactly why this one survived two corrections to the same scorer.

And it is the fourth instance of the pattern named earlier: **status fields and tool arguments are the
two places nobody looks, because both are read as infrastructure rather than as assertions.** A field
*name* is now the third.

cmp  byte [rax + 5], 1  -> regs_access(): written = ['rax']
```

Both are reported as **writing their read operands**, which in a liveness walk **kills the register at

> **A defect found in one opcode is a reason to audit the instrument's model of every opcode it
> special-cases nothing for.** Patching the instance and stopping is how the same bug gets found
> twice.

**And the published census that depends on it was re-run rather than assumed safe.** Unchanged — 6
CONST, 9 DYNAMIC, 2 UNKNOWN — with the reason stated: **the defect can only turn CONST into DYNAMIC,
never the reverse**, and no `cmp`/`test` on an argument register sat between a write and a call in

**A second, smaller one, self-reported:** a fresh `regs_access` loop was written **while a corrected
`written_regs` sat in the same directory**, and two runs were spent debugging a zero its own docstring

**What the zero did right:** it was a **loud** wrong answer — 0 sites including one read by hand — not

The claim — *"`BattleLocomotion_DecodeOrderGoal` is one of the 82 functions testing that byte"* — is

003127EB  0f 85 e3 02 00 00      jne  bail

Five instructions, one basic block, no intervening write — **the tightest possible form of the cited

> functions"* — and never enumerates, **so it cannot support a membership claim about any particular
> function.** The claim needed the site, not the count.

**A structural gap that will recur:** either that document carries its member list, or every document
naming a member cites the site directly. **A count can never be cited for membership**, and nothing
but this checker was ever going to say so.

same rebuild, loose filter            115      85         11
unfiltered [reg+5] scan               258     187          -

**Function count and subsystem count reproduce exactly.** The 3-site difference is on the finer figure

### Two ways a result escapes checking, and they cover most of what a session produces

From the session that produced both:

> **The vtable fold got past me because it was interesting; the seven fabricated sizes got past me
> because they were boring.**

**A flattering result is checked less because checking it risks losing it. A dull one is checked less
because nobody is watching.** Together they cover most of a session's output — and the only defence
that works on both is the one already standing: **make the second look a different *kind* of look.**

That is also the general form of the metric asymmetry logged an hour ago: **nobody audits a number
that makes them look worse**, and nobody audits one that makes them look better either, for the
opposite reason.

### An absence claim rescued rather than refuted

EASTL: **nothing overturned, one completeness gap filled** — and the absence claim needed its support
replaced.

*"There is no short-string optimisation."* **A 24-byte string is not evidence of that** — modern
EASTL's SSO layout is *also* 24 bytes, a union whose inline buffer occupies exactly the three
pointers' space. **Had the claim rested on the size, it would have been unsupported.**

It rests on the constructor's control flow, and that holds:

```
001FF7A6  cmp  eax, 1                  eax = strlen(src)+1
001FF7A9  jbe  short                   the ONLY branch on length
001FF7BC  call qword ptr [rax + 0x10]  allocate -- taken for every n >= 2
001FF7D7  lea  r14, [rip+...]          -> 02EBA2E0, the shared sentinel
```

**One branch, at length 1, and both arms write the same three qwords.** No second threshold, no inline
buffer. The support was rewritten to rest on the branch structure.

> **The size would have been the wrong reason for a right answer** — and a right answer with a wrong
> reason survives every check aimed at the answer.

**And the gap strengthens the document.** The allocator names **five** container kinds, not one —
`basic_string`, `vector`, `set`, `list`, `map`, the complete set of `EASTL `-prefixed literals in the
image. A build shipping a name-tagging allocator with five distinct tags **can attribute allocations
per container kind**, which is what the class name implies and which the document had inferred from
the name alone. Independently corroborated: **the allocator constructor has 230 distinct callers
against 17 for the string constructor.**

**Both B1 rows were already classified. The batch is retired, not deferred.**

The second row failed identically — `already classified 002F7380` — so **the whole of B1 was obsolete
and only the gate knew.** Two applies attempted, two clean refusals, nothing written.

> **The same stale dump that made a document's census wrong by two functions made a mutation's
> eligibility check wrong by 100 %.**

**And the reason it survived my own audit of that dump is worth stating exactly.** This morning I
checked whether the stale dump had corrupted `progress.py` and found it clean — because the scorer
reads only **addresses and sizes**, which are properties of the binary. **Eligibility reads *tags*,
which are precisely what the dump is stale about.**

> **I audited the instrument that reports a number and not the instrument that decides an action.** A
> number gets checked because someone quotes it. **A decision gets checked by whatever it collides
> with** — and here that was a gate, which is the good case. There was no guarantee of one.

Standing consequence recorded in the batch directory: **no row may be staged or applied on the
strength of `graph/functions.tsv`. Eligibility is a property of the live project and only the gate
knows it.**

**Both files retired rather than deleted**, so the proposed domains survive: if either is better than
what the project now carries, that is a **re-classification** needing `-AllowExistingTag` and a fresh
comparison — **not the strict-fence batch they were staged as.** `batchB2` is unaffected; its rows
were *known* to carry an existing tag, which is why they were separated.

With the live dump installed, `unresolved` is still reported as **158** — and **four of those 158 are
