### `final_audits 0 / 30` is a gate, not a backlog

The terminal protocol requires `unresolved = 0`, every system documented, and `OPEN-QUESTIONS.md`
empty. **Current state: 154 unresolved, 492 questions open.** So the zero is the condition being
correctly gated — **not thirty passes nobody has started** — and it is worth saying, because a `0/30`
next to four rising bars reads as neglect.

**And the protocol's own rule is the one this session has been living all night:**

> **When an audit disproves something, you do not change the information to make the audit pass. You
> re-derive the truth from the binary and write what you can prove.**

Tonight produced that failure mode three times and it was refused three times: an alias table a
keyword could satisfy, a data row reworded to quiet a pattern, and a status field asserting a clean
scan. **The protocol names it exactly** — *"a claim weakened to survive an audit must be marked as
such and re-proved from scratch"* — and adds the sharper form: **narrowing a claim's scope to dodge a
counter-example is the same error wearing a smaller hat.**

**Nine of the thirty passes are now partly or wholly mechanised**, mapped into the protocol document:
addresses, body extents, classification currency, data-vs-function, arithmetic (percentages only),
unaccounted neighbours, contradiction sweep, link integrity, status honesty.

**Pass 28 — the contradiction sweep across documents — had no tool before today**, and it is the one
the corpus was demonstrably failing. **Every falsification pass this project has ever run attacked
claims about the binary; none attacked claims about the corpus**, which is why two documents each
describing the other *as it used to be* survived multiple passes.

**Three cautions were written in beside the map, because each will bite whoever runs the thirty:**

- **Every one of these checkers has produced false findings from its own assumptions** — a
  name-length cap, a fixed line window, a sentence splitter, a `\b` that matched `24 B/entry`, a term
  matcher blind to `0x` prefixes. **Run each against a known-positive before believing a zero, and
  read the rows before believing a count.**
- **A crash is not a false clean, and it is the good failure.**
- **Pass 5 — fresh-import reproducibility — is the only pass that re-validates the parent every other
  pass is measured against.** It is numbered fifth and should run first.

### Route 4 is wrong the same way in two documents by the same author — that is a habit

The cutscene document's escape-route table reads *"8-byte / 4-byte encoding in the file : 0 / 0"*.
The **RVA** form of `0020AC30` — `0x000EAC30` — appears twice. Verified here at VA `01D62730`
(RVA `1C42730`):

```
01D62730   30 ac 0e 00 | ff ff ff ff | 91 ac 0e 00
           RVA 0EAC30    -1 (filter)   RVA 0EAC91
```

A `__C_specific_handler` scope record, `0x40` past that function's own unwind info. **This image has
no `.xdata`, so unwind data lives in `.rdata`.** Both hits are `.pdata`/unwind — **inadmissible rather
than absent.**

**The conclusion is untouched; the sentence is wrong. The right claim is "no *admissible* RVA entry".**

> **This is the identical defect, in the same table shape, in the sibling document by the same
> author** — corrected in the nine-patch renderer an hour earlier. **Two instances is a habit, not a
> slip.** The escape-route table is a good instrument; its route 4 has twice been written as a
> stronger claim than it measures. **A third document with that table will have it too**, which makes
> this worth telling the author rather than only fixing.

### A count that is nearly right and a split that is not

`01DFE40C` has **23** referencing functions, not 24 — and **seven of them write it**:

```
read only 16 · write 7 · both 2 · total 23
```

> **The count is tier-11 corroboration and one off is not worth much. The reader/writer split is.**
> *"24 readers"* reads as a flag something else sets; **a marker with seven writers across the image
> is a different object.**

### The population claim came back whole, and the reason it was attacked is the finding

Re-derived from scratch by byte-decoding every `E8`/`E9` across all 38,161 bodies rather than
re-reading the figure: **143 in both · 0 graph-only · 1 bytes-only · 14 neither. Exact.** All 14 body
sizes exact.

**And the attacker said plainly why they went after the body-size table:**

> **I fabricated seven body sizes myself earlier today and wanted to know whether this author had done
> the same thing. They had not.**

**A session's own failure made it suspect a class of error, and the suspicion was wrong here.** That
is the most useful way an error can propagate — as a hypothesis rather than as a habit — and reporting
that it *did not* reproduce is worth as much as finding that it had.

**They also produced a false mismatch and kept it in the write-up** rather than dropping it: a
caller-count pattern attributed "50 callers" to a **data global** when the sentence attributes it to a
function.

> **A phantom mismatch reported as a finding costs the next reader a re-derivation.** Two were
> generated this session and both were caught by their authors before publication.

I relayed three known-weak points — a shadow-offset reading, an unread icon path, an unseparated
`+0x04` field — to the session taking the **cutscene** document. **All three belong to the glyph
document.** Same author, adjacent subject, and I did not check which file they were about.

cost would have been a search for claims that were never there, and the author would not have
recognised their own stated doubts.

> **A handover of "what I doubt about my work" is scoped to a document, and I forwarded it scoped to
> an author.** Fourth routing defect of the session, and the first that was not staleness: **this one
> was a category error about what the information was attached to.**

**A caution to carry across the transition, since every rule logged tonight was learned on

animation document thirteen of its nineteen channels — and it is invisible to every checker in the
kit, because nothing it says is false.

### 95 of 95 — and what the number does not mean

The last unattacked document closed with **nothing overturned** and two of its own claims coming out
**stronger** than it had them.

**The load-bearing step was read from the bytes rather than from the body that computes it.** The
binding names at `01DF11E0` are **UTF-16LE**, and all sixteen read in DualShock order — Select, L3, R3,
Start, Up, Right, Down, Left, L2, **R2**, L1, R1, Triangle, Circle, Cross, Square.

> **The document cites slot 9 alone, where a single name could be an indexing coincidence. All sixteen
> in order cannot be.** No off-by-one or mis-based read produces that table.

**And the instrument note nearly went the other way:** an ASCII reader truncates every one of these at
the first byte, and the first run **reported slot 9 as `'R'`.**

> **`'R'` is not obviously wrong** — it is consistent with R1, R2, R3. **Plausible-but-wrong output
> from a correct search, one encoding away.**

**Two bare `FUN_` names identified as audio gates**, and the second is the payoff: `003603C0` reads the
byte at `022CB726` — **the audio boundary document's second gate, the one that makes the play call
return 0.** So the toggle consults the same gate the play call consults, one level earlier. **That
fell out of the neighbour check on a document that needed no correction** — 53 addresses shared with
21 documents — which is the clearest case yet of that check paying for itself when nothing is wrong.

**Two documents in a row where an author's own failure produced a hypothesis that did not
reproduce.** Body-size tables attacked first, specifically because that session had fabricated seven
sizes earlier in the day; neither author had done the same.

> **95 of 95 attacked. Every document has survived one recorded pass; none has survived a second, and
> eight of tonight's passes overturned something.** A first pass is where the cheap errors die —
> fabricated sizes, mis-scoped absences, counts right for the wrong population. **The errors that
> survive a first pass are what a second pass is for.**

### A known false positive, left in the log and not in the tool, cost two sessions

`check_consistency` reported `01F2CED0` as named both `ShaderParameterF1` and `ShaderParameterF4`
inside one document. **It is neither a contradiction nor new:** the row is a **range** —
`| 4–7 | 01F2CE88…01F2CED0 | ShaderParameterF4, F3, F2, F1 | 4, 3, 2, 1 |` — four addresses, four
names, in order, and a pairwise matcher takes the **end** address with the **first** name.

**I diagnosed this hours ago and recorded it in this log. Two sessions have since re-flagged it, and
both were right to.**

> **A limitation recorded in the log but not in the tool is a limitation that gets rediscovered.** And
> **a known false positive left in place is not free — it is the noise a real finding hides in**, which
> is the same rule that cost one document seven real `BODY DRIFT` findings behind two permanently-red
> gates.

Fixed in the checker: table rows whose address cell states a **span** are excluded from pairwise name
extraction. Verified both ways — two plain rows naming one address differently still fire; a range row
does not.

### The narrowest-example failure, refined by the session it was handed to

The caution sent across the phase transition — *"the narrowest available example presented as the
mechanism"* — came back sharpened:

> **It is a claim wider than its evidence wearing the opposite costume.** The evidence is one channel,
> the claim is one channel, and **the over-reach is in the implicature that the one channel is
> representative.** Not a new species — the same species in a place no gate looks, which is why it
> survived.

**And that makes it findable after all.** The operational form:

> **"How many instances does this generalisation rest on?" is answerable, and if the answer is one, it
> is worth saying so in the document.**

Plus the reader-facing test, which no tool has: **not *"is this claim true"* but *"would someone
looking for the other things this does find them here"*.** Different questions, and only the first one
has a checker.

### audit_coverage 100.00 % — and the rule that came out of it

**95 of 95 documents have survived a recorded falsification pass.** The constraint that opened the
session at a falsely-inflated 86.81 %, was corrected down to 80.22 % when the counter was found to be
measuring amendments, and has been climbing on real work ever since, is closed.

**Three of tonight's instrument defects were the same defect in one session's matcher, and they have
been written up as one entry rather than three corrections:**

| where | missing form | what caught it |
|---|---|---|
| audio pass | modrm **REG** hardcoded to 0 — reported a global as having **zero** writers | a control requiring the six writers **the document itself named** |
| spawn pass | `BT` family only — a 64-bit bit test as `mov r64, imm64` was invisible | a **partial positive in the same body**: bit 26 appeared, so the absence of 45 and 49 was suspicious rather than conclusive |
| cutscene pass | **`MOVSXD`** (`48 63 05`) — sixteen readers invisible, reporting 7 functions against a true 23 | a **known positive already read by hand** |

> **The lesson is not "add more forms".** An x86 form list is never complete, and **all three looked
> complete while they were in use.**

The rule that works, and it costs nothing:

> **Every absence claim from an instruction matcher needs a known-positive control chosen before the
> scan runs — and the cheapest source is the document under attack, because any document stating a
> positive fact has handed you a set the scan must find.**
>
> **A scan that finds nothing has told you nothing until it has found something you already knew was
> there.**

**All three were caught that way. None by inspection.** And it generalises past one session: **three
more of tonight's fleet-wide instrument defects were absence claims from matchers**, and a control
drawn from the target document would have caught each at the moment it was built rather than a pass
later.

**The route-4 correction closed the same way** — verified per hit rather than by shape, with each
banned class nameable individually: `.pdata` `RUNTIME_FUNCTION` records, `.rdata` words within `0x200`
of an unwind RVA, one adjacent to a `-1` filter word.

> **Being able to say *which* banned class each hit belongs to is what stops the next reader
> re-litigating it.**

### 97 questions the fleet raised had never reached the ledger

Seven parallel sessions opened **97 `PROPOSED-*` questions** during the audit run and **not one had
reached `OPEN-QUESTIONS.md`.** They were staged correctly — sessions do not edit `_index/*.md` — and

> **A question nobody can see is a question that gets re-derived.** And the ledger's denominator
> excluded everything the run had opened, so `questions_closed` was reported against a population that
> did not include the session's own output.

**All 97 are merged**, grouped by originating session, with the text as raised.

**They keep their session ids rather than being assigned lettered ones.** Assigning a letter is
**triage** — it asserts a question is new, distinct from every existing row, and worth a permanent id.
**None of that has been done**, and doing it silently during a merge would be the same defect as a
status field asserting a check that never ran.

**And the merge itself dropped eleven and reported eighty-six as if complete.** The extractor took the

> **A merge that silently drops 11 of 97 is a merge that reports 86 as if it were the number.** Same
> shape as a count reported without its selector — and it was caught by comparing the merged set
> against the raised set, which is a check that costs one command and that **I only ran because

Recovered by widening to the following line, with the text as found and the shortfall recorded.

**Note on the metric:** merging these barely moved `questions_closed`, because the scorer counts
checkbox items (`- [ ]` / `- [x]`) and these arrived as table rows. **The visibility problem is fixed;
the counting one is not, and pretending otherwise by reformatting them into checkboxes would be
manufacturing a denominator.**

Seven `''' + EM + '''` fragments appeared in **hand-written prose** — a patch-script habit bleeding

### Where the remaining value is

**226 independent arms in one function, each a few instructions, none of them read.** The distribution
is measured; the individual targets are not.

> **It is the single richest catalogue in the binary of which addresses the developers thought were

### The extraction found what no single arm could

Taking the **extraction** rather than a slice was the right call: all 282 console rows are catalogued,
and the finding is one only the whole set shows.

**The arms touch 97 distinct `.data` addresses and 86 of them fall in one span** — `02CB7FD0`–
`02CB8438`, 1,132 bytes, **81 of the 85 gaps exactly 4 bytes.** A densely packed 4-byte array in the
zero-filled tail, built at run time.

**And it is not the console's scratch space: twenty-eight functions reference that span.**

> **So the commands adjust values the engine is already reading elsewhere. That is what makes this a
> tuning console rather than a debug display** — and it is unreachable from reading arms one at a
> time. The hottest single address is nudged by **18** different commands.

### A column handed over labelled unreliable, with the tell

**`kind` is sound** — it rests only on whether `addss`/`subss` appears, and reproduces the
independently published 110/63/56/32/21.

**`step` is not, and the author said so with the evidence.** It takes the first float operand and signs
it by mnemonic, so an arm loading one constant and stepping by another is mis-valued. Confirmed here
from the file: **58 rows read `-0.01` and not one reads `+0.01`**; only 3 of 88 nudged addresses show
both directions.

> **That is not plausible for a console with up/down pairs. It is a limitation of the extractor, not a
> fact about the data** — and the pairing is almost certainly there.

> **A handoff artifact that overstates itself is worse than none.** Labelling the column unreliable
> costs the next reader one re-derivation; leaving it clean-looking costs them a wrong catalogue built
> on it. The work order now says so above the slice table, so nobody meets the column before the
> caveat.

**The catalogue is the deliverable**, and it answers questions nobody could previously ask:
**depth of field is the largest family at 63 techniques, with a separate Bokeh family of 40 on top** —

**A number a scene author typed into a text file arrives here as a shader parameter.** Labelled a
**name correspondence, not a traced dataflow**, because no code path between them was followed.

### A printable-only string filter is not neutral

**Fourth narrow matcher from the same session, and the sharpest.** A `[\x20-\x7e]` string scan
returned 364 hits — **and the five it dropped were the five that name the function**, because each
ends in `\n`.

> **A printable-only filter selects against log messages, which are the most identifying strings there
> are.**

Caught by the rule from that session's own §14: **the GFZ's own comment quoted a string the scan did
not report, and the known positive disagreeing with the scan is what sent them to look.** That rule
has now caught **four** of their defects and **none was found by inspection.**

**And a second limit stated because it touched a number:** a linear `E8` decode found 37 apparent call
targets, **13 of which are not functions** — `E8` bytes inside other operands. Excluded; per-helper
counts are sound, **a raw target count would not have been.**

**The generalisation audit was run and written down**, per the phase-transition caution: the suffix
grammar rests on **325** names; the count-as-multiplier reading on **four literals at two of seven
helpers**, explicitly not established for the other five; the `fParam_FocusDistance` link on **one**
name pair. **All three carry their support rather than reading as equally solid.**

> **And the honest limit on the whole thing: 325 names recovered, zero techniques explained.** The
> shader bodies are in the `.pso`, not the executable. **No byte-offset map was published** either,
> because the handles are qword indices and no byte layout was verified.

The first pass on the console document went to the **extraction** before the document, and the reason
is the coordination finding:

> **Nine slices were about to be built on `console_arms.tsv`, and that extraction has a defect its own
> author flagged. Taking a slice would consume the suspect data; attacking it first protects the other
> eight.**

**And the defect is worse than "a column labelled unreliable".** Measured on the file:

```
step column:  97 negative,  7 positive,  ZERO +0.01
document:     0.01 is the MOST referenced constant in the function, 88 times
```

> **A hand-tuning console with 58 decrement arms and no increment arms is not a console anyone could
> use** — one command to lower a value and none to raise it. **The asymmetry is structural, not
> statistical.**

**Slices B–I are on hold** pending an independent re-derivation from the binary. **Slice A is
unaffected** — it read its 32 arms directly, found only `1` and `-1`, and used a known-positive
control chosen before the scan.

> **This is the first time a session has stopped a work programme rather than a claim.** The rules
> logged tonight are about not believing a number; this is about **not multiplying one by eight before
> it is checked.**

### Slice A reframed the catalogue, and the span figure needed its population

**The arms tune fields of a settings object through `rdi`, not globals** — `add dword ptr [rdi+0xDA0],
ebp` with the direction from `test bl,bl ; cmovne`. Measured across all 282 rows:

```
with a data_touched value   112  (40 %)
without one                 170  (60 %)
rows touching 02CBxxxx       86
```

> **So "86 in one span" is 86 of the 97 distinct addresses and 86 of the 112 rows that touch data at
> all — not 86 of 282 arms.** Sixty per cent touch no global whatever. **The finding stands; its
> population needed stating**, and it had two plausible denominators.

**And what a row is worth changed with it:** `field · width · step · bound`.

> **The bound is where the authored intent survives not knowing what the field is.** `WRAPS AT 3` is a
> three-state mode cycle whether or not the mode can be named; `CAPPED AT 0x12` is nineteen positions.
> **Twenty-six offsets with their bounds is the catalogue.**

**The settings object is not identified and slice A says so** rather than working around it — `rdi` is
the console's own context pointer and nothing in that slice names its type.

### A work order is an instrument that decides actions

My own slice table mixed *entry starts* with a *byte extent* and said "nine slices of 31–32 ids" when
eight are 32 and one is 26. Caught before anyone claimed a slice.

> **A document with a bad row misinforms a reader; a work order with a bad row misdirects nine.**
>
> **The instrument that decides an action needs more checking than the instrument that reports a
> number, not less** — and a work order is exactly such an instrument. Same shape as auditing the
> scorer and not the mutation-eligibility check.

### Why the unraised-question class was the most dangerous of the three

> **An answered question is visibly present; an unraised one is invisible by construction.**

That is why 97 proposals sat in staging for a whole run with nothing to notice — **no gap, no red
gate, no inconsistency.** It was found only by grepping for the id pattern, and the merge's own
shortfall was found only by comparing the merged set against the raised set. **Neither check is one
anybody would think to run unprompted.**

**Chasing the RTTI turned up a class layer nobody had looked at: 32 `*Obj@@` render-command classes**

### A broader pattern returning fewer results than a narrower one

`Obj@@` returns **32**. `\.\?AV[A-Za-z]+Obj@@` returns **0** — and the narrower
`\.\?AV(Enable|Shadow|AO|Dof|IBL)[A-Za-z]*Obj@@` returned **2**.

> **A superset pattern that matches less than its subset is an instrument defect, not a result.** Had
> the broad form been run alone, "there are no `*Obj@@` classes" would have been a clean, plausible
> zero — the same shape as the printable-only string filter, the `0x`-prefix displacement matcher, and
> the four narrow matchers already logged.

**Caught by the ordering only:** the narrow queries were run first and returned matches, so the broad
zero was visibly impossible. **Running the general query first would have ended the search.**

### The control that would have inverted the answer

The render-settings identification rested on finding the block's **consumers**, and the values are
floats.

> **An integer-only form list finds almost nothing in this block — and it would still have found the
> console, because the arms use `addss`.** It would have missed every consumer and **supported the
> opposite conclusion: that the block is console scratch.**

The control was the 91 arms the extraction lists as touching the span: they must appear, and they do.

> **A form list blind to the consumers but not to the producer does not return nothing. It returns a
> coherent wrong answer.**

**One disagreement flagged rather than smoothed:** the work order says **28** referencing functions,
an independent scan finds **25**. **Take 25 as a floor** — that scan's form list is not exhaustive and
a register loaded by an earlier `lea` is invisible to it. The qualitative claim is unaffected.

**And `01F82D20` was characterised and explicitly not identified:** 61 referencing functions spanning
the console, the debug menu, `InputManager_*` and a large audio-driver cluster, every access a `MOV
r32` read. **A global read by audio, input and UI alike is not a render setting**, and the honest
answer is that nobody knows what it is.

### An arm does not have a step — it has a step and its inverse

**The console is symmetric. The asymmetry was an extraction artefact.** A constant census over the
function, with a positive control:

```
addss  +0.01  x58   ->  step = +0.01
subss  +0.01  x30   ->  step = -0.01
addss  -0.01  x28   ->  step = -0.01
```

**`0.01` is referenced 88 times exactly as the document says, and `-0.01` exists as a separate
constant 28 more. Totals for the pair: 58 positive, 58 negative — exactly balanced**, which is what a
hand-tuning console must be.

> **The step's sign lives in `(mnemonic, constant)` jointly, never in the constant alone.** A `subss`
> of `+0.01` is a decrement; an `addss` of `-0.01` is also a decrement.

**And the mechanism explains the artefact exactly.** An extractor reading **one signed value per arm**
cannot represent an arm that contains both directions; whichever it saw last wins, and with `subss`
typically emitted after `addss`, **a symmetric function produces an overwhelming negative bias.**

> **In neither the float arms nor the integer arms does an arm have "a step". It has a step and its
> inverse**, selected at run time — `addss`/`subss` on one constant, or `test bl,bl ; cmovne`
> choosing `+1`/`-1`. **A row that records "a step" has already lost the thing that makes it a
> console.**

The work order's row shape is corrected to **`field · width · step MAGNITUDE · direction mechanism ·
bound`**. **The magnitude is the invariant; the sign is not a property of the arm.**

**Three things about how this resolved are worth more than the answer.**

**The alarm was raised structurally, not statistically.** *"A console with 58 decrement arms and no
increment arms is not a console anyone could use — one command to lower a value and none to raise
it."* **Nothing in the data said the column was wrong; the impossibility of the thing it described
did.**

**The resolving session had the decoder warm and used it rather than waiting** — and **slice A was
unaffected for a stated reason rather than by luck**: it never consumed the extraction, decoded the
table itself, and reported id 26's constants **without assigning a step sign**, which is the one
thing that would have been wrong.

**And they bounded their own result before anyone asked.** *"This is a census of constant references
inside one function, not a per-arm attribution. 58/58 refutes the asymmetry; it does not establish
that 58 arms step up."*

> **The hold is lifted to *pending confirmation*, not cleared.** The session that raised the alarm is
> re-deriving independently, and **their hypothesis was half right in a way the result makes precise**
> — the sign comes from the operation *and* the constant can itself be negative, so **the two sources
> compose rather than one overriding the other.** Confirming that independently is worth more than
> accepting it.

### Two instruments, no shared code, the same three cells — and the walk found what the census could not

**Confirmed independently, instruction for instruction.** A constant census over the function body and
a walk of the 282-entry dispatch table into its 227 arms both measure **`addss +0.01` ×58,
`subss +0.01` ×30, `addss -0.01` ×28.** The composition rule holds from both directions: a step is
negative if the mnemonic is `subss` **or** the constant is itself negative, with `+0.01` at `009002BC`
and `-0.01` at `009002F4` as separate floats in the pool.

**And the table walk supplied the thing a census structurally cannot reach:**

> **58/58 is FIFTY-EIGHT ARMS, not 58 raise-commands and 58 lower-commands.**

```
001D1FB0  movss xmm0, [02CB8140]   ; the parameter
001D1FB8  test  bl, bl             ; the direction flag
001D1FBA  je    0x1d1fd1
001D1FBC  subss xmm0, [008F30E8]   ; 0.05 -> decrement
001D1FD1  addss xmm0, [008F30E8]   ; the SAME 0.05 -> increment
```

**102 of 102 stepping arms have this shape.** So **the command id names the parameter, not the
direction** — and *"each command adds or subtracts a fixed step"* reads as separate raise/lower
commands and is corrected. **The corrected reading fits the document's own "hold a button and watch
the value creep" better than the original, because holding it the other way walks the value back.**

**Two extractors with complementary blind spots, and neither alone is complete.** 102 against 110, the
walk's set a strict subset — **and the 8 extras are real nudges of a different shape**: one loads
`±1.0` **into the register** and does a single `addss` against the parameter (the operand roles
reversed), another **computes** its step by dividing an integer by 5 and scaling. **Together they
account for all 110; neither alone does.**

**And a correction that changes how every slice reads its own data:** `001D4BFA` is the target of 56
unimplemented ids **and the common tail 212 of the 226 real arms jump to when they finish.**

> **A reader told only that it is the no-op target will misread 212 jumps as 212 commands doing
> nothing.**

### The rules this produced

> **An extraction feeding N consumers should be attacked before the first consumer, not after the
> Nth.**

**And why it was findable at all**, which is the part that transfers:

> **The asymmetry looked like a finding about the console — developers who only tuned downward —
> rather than a fact about the extractor. What made it visible was asking whether the artefact made
> sense *as a tool*: a console with a command to lower a value and none to raise it is not usable, so
> either the data or the reading had to be wrong.**

**Slice A being unaffected is the same discipline from the other side:** it decoded the table itself
and **declined to assign a step sign** — refusing to record the thing that was not a property of the
arm, before anyone knew that was the defect.

**Hold cleared. Slices B–I are open**, with the corrected row shape, the per-arm magnitude table, and
the common-tail warning in the work order.

**New open item:** what supplies the direction flag. The register differs between arms — `bl`, `sil` —
**so it is an argument to the console rather than a global**, and the caller was not traced.

### I held the pack for hours on a constraint that did not exist

Batch A has been applied and unpacked since the mutation landed, and every `progress.py` run since has
warned that `unresolved` is four too high. The stated reason for waiting was **"all four sessions
idle"**, because a pack *"redistributes the parent every session imports from."*

**Reading the script settles it: that is not what it does.**

> **`Pack-GfzCheckpoint.ps1` writes a NEW `.gzf` to a path the caller chooses. It overwrites nothing.**
> Sessions keep importing the existing certified parent until `GfzEnv.ps1`'s lineage block is updated
> to point at the new one — **which is a separate, deliberate step.**

So the disruptive act is **updating the lineage**, not packing. **Packing is safe at any time**, and I
had conflated the two for hours across four separate ticks, reporting the delay as a cost of
coordination when it was a cost of not reading the tool.

> **I audited the scorer, the eligibility check, the dump and the gate — and never the wrapper whose
> behaviour the whole schedule was built around.** The same shape as auditing the instrument that
> reports a number and not the one that decides an action, one level up: **this was a decision built
> on an unexamined belief about a tool, and the belief was checkable in forty lines.**

**And the cost was not zero.** Four ticks of user-facing reports carried `unresolved = 158` when the
project holds 154, with the provenance warning firing every time and the explanation being *"waiting
for a window"*. **The warning was correct, the number was wrong, and the reason given for both was
wrong.**

Packing now. The lineage update stays gated — **that one really does change what every session
imports**, and it wants the fresh-import re-certification the wrapper's own closing line demands
before anything points at it.

**Packed.** `PACK_PASS`, target reporting `open=false busy=false changed=false canSave=false`, output
**82,118,788 bytes**, sha256 `fb9b5e7ea002c1626a53d47da0b0b69a2443e246f7ce2b64329be4e034a2d3f7`.

**The size is itself a check nobody asked for:** the previous parent is 82,114,525 bytes, so the new
pack is **4,263 bytes larger** — consistent with four rows of added tags and comments and nothing
else. **A pack that had gained or lost megabytes would be a different artefact wearing the right
name**, which is exactly what the wrapper's `MinBytes` floor exists to catch and why it is a floor
rather than an equality.

**Fresh-importing into a completely new project now** — the certification the wrapper's own closing
line demands, and **protocol pass 5**, which re-validates the parent every other pass is measured
against. **Nothing points at the new pack until that clears.**

### Naming a dispatcher after its callees

Two documents in one folder disagreed about `001D1660` — `DevConsole_DispatchCommand` against
`DebugConsole_CommandArms`. Caught by `check_consistency`, settled from the image:

```
001D1673  41 0f b6 f0                movzx esi, r8b   ; arg 3 -> sil
001D1677  0f b6 da                   movzx ebx, dl    ; arg 2 -> bl   (the direction flag)
001D167A  48 8b f9                   mov  rdi, rcx    ; arg 1 -> rdi  (the settings object)
001D167D  41 81 f9 19 01 00 00       cmp  r9d, 0x119  ; ids 12..293
001D16A3                             mov  r9d, [table + id*4]
001D16AB                             add  r9, rcx     ; RVA -> VA, then jmp
```

**Rebase the id, save three arguments, bounds-check, index a table, jump. That is a dispatcher**, and
the arms are what it jumps *to*. Corrected; `check_consistency` back to zero.

> **Naming a dispatcher after its callees names the function after the thing it is not.** The arms do
> live inside the same body — **which is exactly what made the wrong name plausible** — but *"every
> command arm lives inside it"* is a fact about the **layout**, not about what the function is.

**And the same prologue closed an open item for free.** `bl` and `sil` are **arguments 2 and 3**, so
**nothing in the console supplies the direction — the caller does**, and the register differing
between arms is only which argument that arm consults. Two further confirmations fell out: the id
bound is the code's own `cmp r9d, 0x119`, and `add r9, rcx` is **why** the table holds RVAs rather
than a convention someone asserted.

> **Eleven instructions answered a question, settled a name, and confirmed two figures that had been
> taken on the document's word.** The prologue of a dispatcher is the cheapest thing to read in any
> function of this shape and it was read last.

### The known-positive control covers absences and not inflations — and I have been promoting it as if it covered both

**A site-count inflation, from double-matching one instruction.** `F3 0F 10 05 …` matched a `MOVSS
load` form at the `F3` byte **and** a `MOVUPS` form at the `0F` byte — same target, two different site
addresses. REX-prefixed integer forms did the same at the `48` and at the opcode.

```
001D1660   337 -> 254
001CD0E0   158 ->  79
006084B0    14 ->   7
00186CD0     9 ->   7
```

Fixed by advancing past each matched instruction rather than by one byte. **Function counts were never
affected** — a doubled site still names the same function — and no string-based identification is
touched.

**And this defeats the guard that caught the other three matcher defects:**

> **Those were absences — a form the scan could not see — and a known-positive control catches those,
> because the scan fails to find something you know is there. An over-count finds the positive
> perfectly.** No control drawn from a document would have fired here.

**What caught it was internal consistency between categories:** `MOVSS load` and `MOVUPS` reported
**82 and 82** in one function, **78 and 78** in another, **5/5** and **1/1** elsewhere.

> **Two independent instruction forms do not land on identical counts four times.**

So the rule as written is half a rule, and it has been given to every session tonight in that form:

> **For an absence defect the tell is a disagreement with the world. For an inflation defect the tell
> is a suspicious agreement inside your own output.**

**A known-positive control tests reach, not discipline.** It answers *"can this scan find what is
there"* and says nothing about *"does it find it once"*. The second question needs a different check
entirely — **cross-category agreement, and the suspicion that two independent measures agreeing
exactly are not independent.**

### A fix that changes nothing is evidence about the fix

**The first attempted fix deduped by site address and produced identical numbers** — which reads as
*"no bug after all"*.

> **The two matches have different site addresses, so site-dedupe cannot help.** A fix aimed at the
> wrong mechanism leaves the output untouched and looks like a clean bill of health.

> **A fix that changes nothing is evidence about the fix, not about the defect.** It was only
> re-examined because the 82/82 pairing was still sitting in the output — **the original tell
> survived the failed repair, which is the only reason the repair was recognised as failed.**

### `engine_explained` rewards breadth by two orders of magnitude, and the fleet should know before it optimises

Measured across all 103 documents:

```
distinct functions cited            6,507
mean per document                    69.0

vtable-method-index.md              4,276   <- 66 % of everything cited
phyre-script-object-accessors.md      747
embedded-lua-and-phyre-object...      171

post-processing catalogue (844 lines)   16
the-282-command console (516 lines)     13
what-the-console-tunes (304 lines)      11
```

> **One RTTI catalogue accounts for two thirds of the entire `engine_explained` numerator. The three
> largest documents of the writing phase — 1,664 lines between them, naming 325 shader techniques and
> 226 console commands — moved it by forty functions.**

**That is not a criticism of those documents.** They are the best work of the run. **It is a fact about
the metric**, and it needs saying before the fleet starts optimising against a number I built:

> **`engine_explained` counts distinct function entries cited. It cannot see 226 arms inside one
> function, or 325 shader techniques that are not functions at all.** A document can explain a whole
> subsystem and move the figure by thirteen.

**And the uncited mass is shaped for breadth:**

```
uncited            27,763 functions   5,796,359 bytes
of those <=200 B   21,159 functions   1,371,030 bytes
                   = 76 % of the count, 24 % of the mass
```

**Three quarters of what remains uncited is small functions.** A catalogue that names many of them at
shallow depth moves the figure enormously; a deep reading of one large function moves it by fifteen.

**So the honest statement of the trade, which is the coordinator's to make and not a session's:**

> **If the goal is the number, breadth wins by two orders of magnitude. If the goal is the
> deliverable, the console and post-processing documents are worth more than any catalogue of small
> functions would be** — because a modder looking for what this engine can do finds it in those, and
> finds nothing usable in 4,276 vtable slots.

**The metric is a proxy and it is now visibly a poor one at the margin.** It was built to make
"explanation" dominant over "classification", and it does that — but within explanation it cannot tell
a subsystem from a list. **I am not changing it mid-run**: a metric altered while it is being
optimised against is worse than a known-imperfect one, and every correction to this scorer tonight
has been to make it *report* better, never to make it *reward* differently.

**What I am doing instead is saying which one a block is for.** Depth blocks are chosen for the
deliverable and will barely move the bar; breadth blocks are chosen to move the bar. **A session
should know which it has been given.**

### A careful non-claim in slice B was cashed by slice C, five parameters later

Slice B found a gap in its id run and wrote it as **a layout fact and explicitly not evidence the
slots were unused**, "because no id in this slice reaches them and C–I have not been read."

**Slice C reaches them. Ids 90–94 own exactly those slots**, and 95–98 own four more *below* what B
took for the start:

```
02CB80A0 A4 A8 AC      ids 95..98
02CB80B0 ...      D0   ids 63..71   (B)
02CB80D4 D8 DC E0 E4   ids 90..94   <- the slots B could not reach
02CB80E8 EC F0 F4      ids 72..75   (B)
02CB80F8 ... 812C      ids 76..89
```

**36 ids, 36 distinct targets, 36 slots, no gap larger than 4 bytes, one-to-one.**

> **The array was never sparse — the id order does not follow the address order.** Had slice B written
> that gap the confident way, **the database would now carry a false absence claim over five live
> tuning parameters.**

That is the clearest payoff yet for refusing to convert *"I cannot see it"* into *"it is not there"*,
and the refusal was written by the session that had every incentive to close its own section cleanly.

**And C corrected an off-by-one in B while it was there:** the gap is **five** slots, not six —
`(0x02CB80E8 − 0x02CB80D0)/4 − 1` — **the byte distance versus the count of slots strictly inside
it.** Corrected with the arithmetic shown and B's open question **closed rather than deleted.**

### Three arms that a per-arm classifier would silently mis-type

**Id 103 is not a tuning command — it re-seeds ids 104, 105 and 106.** It toggles a flag and, **only
on the off edge**, calls an engine accessor three times and copies `[rax+0xCC4/0xCC8/0xCCC]` into the
three fields ids 104–106 tune.

> **So 103–106 are one group: an override flag plus its three parameters, where clearing the flag
> snaps all three back to live engine state.** And `+0xCC4/0xCC8/0xCCC` are **the closest thing this
> catalogue has produced to a *name* for a tuned value** — an offset in a real engine object rather
> than in the console's own settings blob.

**Id 106 steps by ratio, not addition** — `mulss 0.99` / `mulss 1.01`, the only arm whose two
directions use *different* constants. **And they are not reciprocals: `0.99 × 1.01 = 0.9999`.**

> **Up-then-down does not restore the value — 0.01 % is lost per round trip.** A developer walking a
> parameter up and back down does not return to where they started, and **a multiplicative arm is
> invisible to an `addss`/`subss` classifier**, so the earlier "102 of 102 stepping arms" statement is
> about **additive** arms and id 106 sits outside it.

**Ids 92 and 93 are the only bounded float arms**, clamped `[0.0, 1.0]` — `xorps`/`maxss` down,
`minss` against `1.0` up. **The clamp is one-sided per branch**, which is why it reads as one bound
rather than two guards.

**And a constant that is not what it looks like:** id 104's step is the **typed literal
`0.00555556`**, not a computed `1/180`. `float32(0.00555556)` reproduces the stored bits and
`float32(1/180)` does not. **It is `1/180` to six figures, recorded as an observation and explicitly
not as a finding**, since nothing traces that field to an angle.

> **A constant that is nearly a familiar fraction is the most inviting thing in a disassembly**, and
> the difference between "is" and "is nearly" is one comparison nobody usually runs.

### Three slices, three shapes

> **A was counters. B was floats. C was floats plus a multiplicative arm, a re-seeder and two clamps.
> Every slice so far has contained at least one thing the previous slice's extractor would have
> silently mis-typed.**

*"Does the arm shape hold here at all"* is now evidence-backed as the first question of every
remaining slice, and **inheriting the previous slice's extractor is the specific thing not to do.**

### I built a claims table and then answered a claim without reading it

Two sessions were approved for slice C within minutes. **Fourth routing collision of the run, and the
first with a purpose-built mechanism already in place to prevent it.**

The work order has had a Claimed table since it was written. **I answered "take C–I" without
consulting it, and did not update it when I approved** — I filled it in only later, from a delivery
report.

> **A claims table is only a coordination device if it is consulted before the answer and written on
> the answer.** Otherwise it is **documentation of collisions after the fact**, which is exactly what
> it had been.

**The four collisions have had four different causes and this is the worst of them:**

| # | cause |
|---|---|
| 1 | shipped a premise I had not tested, as an assignment |
| 2 | routed on capacity rather than on who was inside the mechanism |
| 3 | a board that was accurate when written and stale when read |
| 4 | **a mechanism that existed, was correct, and was not consulted** |

**The first three were failures of information. This one was a failure to use information I had
already written down**, which is the same shape as `the-largest-unclassified-functions.md` walking
into the stale-dump warning its own sibling recorded — **and I criticised that at the time.**

The protocol is now written into the table itself rather than into my habits: **read before answering,
write on approving.** A rule that lives in the artefact survives a coordinator who is not paying
attention; one that lives in the coordinator does not.

**Cost this time: near zero.** The second session was told before it had started, and the message that
told it also carried slice C's three findings — so it starts from the corrected shape rather than
rediscovering it. **A and B stamped GN158, C GN159, D and E claimed, F–I open.**

### The address index had fallen two orders of magnitude behind, and its own header said so

`ADDRESS-INDEX.md` held **74 addresses**. The database cites **6,507 distinct functions across 130
documents** — about **1 % coverage** — and **none of the ten documents written today appeared in it at
all.**

**Its own maintenance note had already called it:** *"this file is hand-maintained while the database
is small. Once enough documents exist, generate it by scanning the `.md` files for 8-hex-digit
tokens."* **That threshold passed long ago and nobody noticed, including me.**

> **A hand-maintained index two orders of magnitude behind is worse than no index: a reader who looks
> up an address and finds nothing concludes the database does not cover it.** An absent index invites
> a search; a stale one answers the question wrongly.

**Regenerated: 6,507 addresses, 432 of them cited by more than one document.** That second figure is
the one the hand-maintained file could not express at all, and it is the case a reader most needs —
**432 addresses where two or more documents have something to say.**

**Two deliberate omissions, both to avoid asserting what no document said:**

- **It does not name functions.** The ledger's names are mechanical for most of these, and **a
  generated index carrying a name would be asserting something no document claimed.** Names belong in
  documents; this answers *who talks about this address* and nothing else.
- **Interior addresses resolve to their containing function**, so a citation of an instruction indexes
  under the function it is in — which is what makes the console's 226 arm addresses findable at all.

**And the generator is the point rather than the file.** The file will be stale again by tomorrow; the
script is one command and carries the reason it exists in its own docstring. **The index was
hand-maintained because it started small, and nothing was watching the moment that stopped being
true** — which is the same shape as `audit.passes` counting amendments, `--db` being ignored, and a
claims table nobody read: **a mechanism that was right when built and was never re-examined against
what it had become.**

### The glossary is where the authored vocabulary belongs, and it had none of tonight's

`GLOSSARY.md` had not moved since **02:06 yesterday** — before nearly all of this run — and its
premise is exactly the thing the run has been producing: *"engine terms as FFXII TZA actually uses
them."*

**Tonight recovered a great deal of the game's own vocabulary and none of it was there.** Extended
from 48 rows to 64, in two new sections:

**Rendering / post-processing** — `Yebis` (the middleware, named by the engine's own `EnableYebis`
setting), `Alchemy SSAO`, `FXAA 2`, the `Bokeh` family separate from depth-of-field, the three HDR
encodings, `fParam_FocusDistance` and `mDofFocusDistance`, the `*Obj` render-command suffix, and the
nine render-setting names.

**Authored script vocabulary** — `setmapwind`/`defaultmapwind`, `setforcefightmode`,
`btlAtelCanselInitialSpawnFlag` (**the engine's own spelling, misspelling included**), `sum_`/`spc_`,
and the tuning console.

> **Every one of these arrived from authored data rather than from reading a function body — which is
> why they are names rather than descriptions.** A glossary of terms *the engine uses* is the one
> index file where that distinction is the whole point.

**Three entries carry their limits into the glossary itself**, because a glossary is exactly where a
qualified claim gets read as a settled one:

- `fParam_FocusDistance` ↔ `mDofFocusDistance` is **a name correspondence, not a traced dataflow.**
- The render-setting names are carried by five of 25 functions and there is **no verified
  name-to-offset binding** — **naming the block is not naming its fields.**
- **What `sum_`/`spc_` denote is not established**; the bridge is authored data in the VBF, not code.

**And two entries exist to stop a specific misreading:** `setmapwind`'s argument order is **the
reverse of the packed record's field order**, and **a console command id names the parameter, not the
direction.** Both are facts a reader would otherwise get backwards from a reasonable assumption.

> **A glossary is the highest-leverage place in the database to put a correction**, because it is what
> someone reads *instead of* the document — and the two entries above are corrections that a reader
> would never know to look for.

### Nine chains from this run, and the one that crosses a file-format boundary carries its limit

`CALL-CHAINS.md` was the last of the three navigation files still stale. Unlike the address index it
is **not generatable** — it distinguishes an **owner transition** from a **trigger**, which is a
judgement — so it needed writing rather than running a script.

**Nine chains added.** Three cross more owners than anything previously in the index, and one crosses
two file formats:

```
Cutscene asset name -> slot classification -> DoF sidecar JSON -> shader uniform
                                                 Resource -> Presentation -> GPU
Cutscene asset name -> two flags -> script stand-down gate -> per-frame script pacing
                                                 Resource -> Script/VM -> ActorEntity
Console command id -> dispatch table -> arm -> render settings -> 25 consumers
Field record bit 15 -> forces the R2 toggle off -> a town pins force fight mode
                                                 WorldAreaField -> Input -> CombatAction
```

**And the index now carries a section for what the chains do *not* establish**, because **a chain
index is exactly where a shared-consumer argument gets read as a traced dataflow.**

> A row reading *"JSON key → shader uniform"* invites a reader to assume somebody followed it.
> **Nobody has.** The argument is that **the two functions naming the render settings are the same two
> that read the JSON keys** — strong evidence, and not a trace.

Same for the console chain: it **rests on five of 25 functions**, the five carrying strings, and there
is **no verified name-to-offset binding** — so **no row says which command tunes which named
setting.**

> **The three navigation files were all correct when built and none had been re-examined against what
> the database had become.** The address index had fallen to 1 % coverage, the glossary had none of
> the run's authored vocabulary, and the chain index had none of its chains. **All three were found in
> one tick by asking the same question of each: is this still describing the thing it indexes?**

### I broke a rule I have saved, while fixing the thing the rule warns about

A `'\0'` inside a C snippet, written through a shell heredoc, became **a real NUL byte** in two
published documents. The files went from *"UTF-8 text"* to *"data"* — **which breaks `grep`, `sed` and
every text tool silently, while every content checker in this kit stayed green.**

> **A checker built to find code in prose could not see a byte that is not prose at all.** All five
> gates passed on a binary file.

**Then I wrote the NUL check itself through a heredoc and did it again — to the checker — three
minutes later.** Two more NULs, and the tool that was supposed to catch this became unparseable.

**There is a standing note in my own memory that says to write escaped strings with an editor and
never through a shell heredoc.**

> **A rule that is written down and not wired into the tooling is a rule you will break while fixing
> the thing it warned you about.** Third instance tonight of that shape — a document walking into its
> sibling's warning, a claims table nobody consulted, and now a note I wrote for myself.

**Repaired with an editor rather than a heredoc, and the check is in with two controls** — it fires on
a NUL and is silent on clean text. **Both affected documents cleaned; all five gates green.**

### Three names for one function, and none of them was right

`001FF740` was `Map_FindByName` in one document and `eastl_string_construct_from_cstring` in another.
Decompiled:

```c
FUN_001edf00(local_res10, "EASTL basic_string", ...)          // named allocator
do { lVar4++; } while (*(char *)(param_2 + lVar4) != 0);      // inline strlen of ARG 2
if (uVar2 < 2) puStack_38 = &DAT_02eba2e0;                    // shared empty sentinel
else           puStack_38 = (**(code **)(local_28[0] + 0x10))(...);
memmove(...); *puStack_38 = 0;
uVar3 = FUN_001ff6b0(param_1, &local_40);                     // DELEGATE
(**(code **)(local_28[0] + 0x18))(local_28, local_40, ...);   // FREE
return uVar3;                                                 // the DELEGATE'S result
```

> **Not a constructor — it destroys the string on the way out and returns another function's result.
> Not the find either — the lookup is `001FF6B0`.** It converts a C string to the container's string
> type, delegates, and cleans up. **20 callers.** Renamed `EASTL_LookupByCString` in both.

**Each author named the whole function after the half they were reading**, and neither half is wrong
about what it saw.

**The EASTL evidence is unaffected, and that is worth separating from the name.** The
no-short-string-optimisation claim rests on this body's control flow — **one branch at length 1, the
shared sentinel, both arms writing the same three pointers** — and all of it is visible above. **The
reasoning was right; the label was not.**

**And the report's attribution was reversed** — it named the console document as holding
`Map_FindByName` when the checker put `eastl_string_construct_from_cstring` there. **Checked before
editing, which is why the right file got the right fix.** A correction accepted without checking is a
defect adopted, and that applies to which document a defect is in.

### The third species: a defect that produces a complete, plausible, well-formed answer

The name-to-offset binding is done — **29 offsets named, 21 of them console-arm addresses** — and the
method finding is worth more than the table.

> **Take the string nearest the store, and you get 26 of 30 wrong.**

The compiler schedules the **next** setting's `lea rdx,"name"` before the **current** setting's store,
so the nearest string is usually the following setting's name. **The output is a table shifted by one
— and a shifted table reads perfectly plausibly:** `chrFresnelSpecularPower` at `+0D0`,
`chrFresnelSpecularClampValue` at `+0D4`, one slot off, in a run where every name is a
`chrFresnelSpecular*`.

```
001C7940   adjacency agrees   4    wrong  26
001C3D50   adjacency agrees  19    wrong   0
```

> **`001C3D50` would have validated adjacency 19 out of 19.** A session that checked its method there
> and applied it to `001C7940` would have published twenty-six wrong rows **with a passing control
> behind it.** **A heuristic verified on one function is verified on one function** — the two differ
> only in how the compiler scheduled them, which nothing in the method can see.

**What catches it is semantic, not statistical.** Four RGB triples across the two loaders, and **a
colour triple must land on three consecutive slots in R, G, B order.** Dataflow puts all four in
order; adjacency puts `mMapAmbientColorB` at **both** `+0A0` and `+0A4` and loses R entirely.

**So the failure table now has a third species, and it is the one no generic guard reaches:**

| species | tell | what catches it |
|---|---|---|
| **absence** | disagrees with the world | a known-positive control |
| **inflation** | agrees suspiciously with itself | cross-category comparison |
| **mis-binding** | **neither — complete, plausible, well-formed** | **a fact about the subject matter the instrument had no access to** |

> **An RGB triple is not a property of the disassembly. It is a property of colour.** The only thing
> that separated the right table from the wrong one came from outside the binary entirely.

**And the independence audit is the right shape.** The two loaders agree on all 19 shared offsets with
zero disagreements — **but they are not independent for this purpose**: same authors, same names, so a
wrong name in the source appears in both. **The agreement corroborates the extraction, not the
binding.** The genuine check is `001F0AD0`: its 144 written addresses and these 29 are **perfectly
disjoint**, and a mis-assigned set has no reason to be disjoint from an unrelated function's writes.

### Naming the block did not name most of the settings

`001C7940` loads **153 distinct settings and only 29 reach the block** — most land in a different
settings object.

> **Naming the block did not name most of the settings, because most of the settings are not in it.**

**And the block is not one array.** `001F0AD0` writes **144** block addresses and **not one is touched
by a console arm**:

```
+000..+18C   console-tunable settings        84 arm addresses, 21 now named
+190..+38C   8 x (vec4 + 3x4 matrix)         from one live render object
             block stride 0x40, object stride 0xD8 -- both exact
+3B0..+434   scalars and two vec3s
+438..+444   four mMapShadow* settings       loaders only; no arm, no write
+464..+468   two arm addresses, unnamed
```

Eight entries, 128 field copies, uniform stride in both spaces. *"Lights or shadow cascades"* is the
obvious reading and was **explicitly not written as established.**

### A Ghidra signature hid the value everything downstream reads — twice in one pass

**`00200B50` is typed `void`** because Ghidra does not model the `xmm0` return, **so at face value
every float setting looks like a discarded read.**

**And `001FF6B0` is typed `void` because it does not return at all.** Verified here: its body ends at
`001FF72D` with `E9 BE FD FF FF` — `jmp` to **`001FF4F0`**.

> **So the chain is `001FF740` (C-string adapter) → `001FF6B0` (ensure-map-then-find) → `001FF4F0`
> (the find).** The correction published an hour ago placed the find one step too early; the name
> stands and the step is added.

> **Twice in one pass, a decompiler signature would have hidden the value everything downstream
> reads.** A decompiler's return type is a claim about a function, and it is wrong in both directions
> here — a value returned in a register it does not track, and a value returned through a tail call it
> does not follow.

### Read-modify-write with an exact-match guard, fleet-wide

Two sessions edited one document simultaneously. **The second splice failed its exact-match assertion
rather than clobbering the first session's text** — a blind write would have silently reverted a
correction that had just been merged.

> **A concurrent edit that fails loudly costs one retry. A concurrent edit that succeeds blindly costs
> a correction nobody knows was lost** — and leaves no trace, because the file is well-formed and the
> gates are green.

**Now standing practice: any write to a document another session may hold asserts on the exact text it
replaces.**

### The merged proposals are a mix of questions and answers, and the ledger did not say so

The 97 merged rows carry **the longest line mentioning each id in staging** — and **that line is
sometimes the question and sometimes the answer.** A `state` column has been derived and the
limitation written above the table:

```
97 rows marked   4 recovered as answers
```

> **`untriaged` means "nobody has checked", not "open".** At least two rows read `untriaged` while
> being demonstrably closed — the Save/Load row-and-bit question, and the 158 re-census.

**Deriving a status from prose and presenting it as a state would be the status field asserting a
check that never ran** — the defect corrected in four separate fields tonight (`audit.passes`,
`crossref_clean`, `--db`, and the audit field name). **So the column says which rows were recovered as
answers; it does not say which questions are open.**

> **An answered question sitting unmarked is the same class of loss as an unraised one** — invisible,
> and it gets re-derived. The first cost a whole run's proposals; this one costs however many of the
> 97 are already closed and unrecognised.

**Triage is offered as a block rather than done by the coordinator**, because deciding whether a
question is closed requires the documents in context, and **the merge has already demonstrated what
happens when that judgement is made mechanically.**

### The console has numeric entry fields, and a magic constant names a family rather than a divisor

**Slice G contains a command kind no earlier slice has: multi-digit numeric editors.** Ids 225 and 226
are the same widget twice — a cursor selects one element of an **eight-dword digit array**, the two
buttons roll that digit, **`+10 then mod 10`** wraps it (which is how a decrement below zero reaches
nine, and why both buttons share one wrap step), and the number is **recomposed by Horner's method**
into a separate field.

```
0xDB4 value | 0xDB8 .. 0xDD4  eight digits | 0xDD8 cursor      (id 225)
0xDE0 value | 0xDE4 .. 0xE00  eight digits | 0xE04 cursor      (id 226)
```

**Id 227 is the same idea in base 60** — a selector picks one of three sub-fields, each wrapped modulo
60. **A three-part field counting in sixties is the shape of a time or duration entry, and the
modulus is the finding while the reading is an inference** — recorded that way.

> **These are widgets, not settings.** Writing the composed value directly is overwritten the next
> time the command is pressed, because the arm **recomposes it from the digits every time.** A modder
> patching the value would watch it revert and have no idea why.

**And id 231's step magnitude is data, not an instruction constant** — `1` or `10`, chosen by a flag,
then wrapped mod 311. **Every magnitude anywhere else in this catalogue is a constant in the
instruction stream; a census of step constants cannot see this one.**

**Slice G is over half retired: 17 unimplemented of 32, including eight consecutive.** No earlier
slice exceeded five, and D had none.

### A magic constant identifies a family of divisors; the shift is the divisor

Two divisor checks failed on their first pass and **both were caught by their own controls.**

**The first truncated to 64 bits before a 64-bit shift** and confidently reported *"not 311"*. Redone
as `((v × 0x34AE820ED114942B) >> 64) >> 6 == v // 311`, **with a control against 312 that fails.**

**The second asked which divisor `0x88888889` implies and got "all of them"** — 15, 30, 60 and 120 all
passed. **That is not a broken control; it is a fact:**

> **That multiplier is shared across `15 × 2^k`, and only the shift distinguishes them.** The shift
> was in the code and had not been read — `sar edx, 5` with `imul eax, edx, 0x3c`. **Modulo 60.**
>
> **A magic constant identifies a *family* of divisors. The shift is the divisor** — and a check that
> does not read it **will confirm whichever member the writer already had in mind.**

### A grep for NUL that could never have failed

Checking nine documents for the NUL defect, the first scan was **`grep -c $'\x00'`** — which in bash
**becomes an empty pattern matching every line**, and "found" **1,506 hits in a 1,506-line file.**

**What exposed it was `file` still reporting `UTF-8 text`** — a second instrument disagreeing with the
first.

> **A checker you cannot see fail is not a checker.** That grep had never been shown a real NUL and
> would have reported clean-looking numbers forever.

And the honest conclusion the session drew about its own documents: **they are safe because they go
through an editor, not because the scan verified it.**

> **Same rule as the one I broke while fixing the thing it warned about**, from the other direction: I
> had a written rule and no tooling; they had tooling that could not fail. **Neither is a check.**

### The console names its own parameters — and the catalogue had been reading the wrong table

**293 labels, ids 1–294, zero collisions.** The row renderer prints `"%s%s%f"` with the label from
`[ctx + id*8 + 0x130]`, so **`id = (disp − 0x130) / 8`.**

> **"Name the target, not the arm" was right; what it needed was a second table, not a better reading
> of the first.** Slices A–D reported bare addresses because **an arm never names its field** — and
> **the arm was never the only place to look.**

**Id 14 — the wrap-at-3 counter slice A found — is `Invincible:`.** Id 103, slice C's re-seeder, is
**`Camera Over Write (O to capture)`**, and 104/105/106 are **FOV / Aspect Ratio / Camera scale** —
**so the ratio-stepping arm is the one called "scale"**, which is exactly what a multiplicative step
is for. **The label explains a mechanism the disassembly had already produced**, which is the strongest
form of corroboration available: two sources, neither derived from the other, agreeing about *why*.

**Alignment proven four ways** — the dispatcher's own `add r9d,-0xC` / `cmp r9d,0x119`; id 103's label
against slice C's behaviour; the clamped pairs in C and E; a stride-12 stat array — plus a
**cross-source control against the config keys: 20 arm-bearing pairs, 0 contradictions.**

### "56 unimplemented" was three different outcomes

**There are two tables** — action (282 ids, base 12) and render (294, base 1) — and crossing them:

```
226  live
 38  no action, but still SHOW a live value   (Current LP, twelve character stats)
 12  labelled buttons with the action removed
  6  draw "  (EMPTY)  "
```

> **Unreachable in one table says nothing about how the other table draws you.** **Only six rows of
> 282 are actually blank in the menu**, against a work order that said 56 — **a figure I wrote and
> propagated to nine slices.**

### Five for five, and it should stop being called a surprise

**A third direction mechanism**: `addss`/`addss` with a stored **negative** constant, so direction is
*which constant loads*, not which mnemonic runs. **Concentrated entirely in two slices — D 25, E 21,
and zero in A, B, C, F, G.**

> **It was invisible until a slice containing it was read.** Every slice has now contained something
> the previous slice's extractor would have mis-typed — **five for five, and it should stop being
> called a surprise.**

### `02CB7FD0` is a `this` pointer, and two decoding traps worth the entry

Passed by `lea rcx` to a constructor — **so every `02CBxxxx` field is `this + offset`, and the
constructors hold a shipped default for each.**

- **Width must come from the store.** Merging three constructors produced **"Fresnel Enabled = 3.9"
  for a one-byte boolean.** **A boolean that cannot be 3.9 is what caught it** — the same species as
  the RGB triple that caught a shifted binding: **a fact about the subject matter the instrument had
  no access to.**
- **`mov qword ptr [x], imm32` is two adjacent 4-byte fields**, not one — an error that silently
  halves a field count.

**And an absence left as unknown rather than asserted:** for 21 floats the only readers found by **two
different scans** are the console arm and the row renderer — *"a measurement over two scans, not proof
of absence"*, since a pointer-passed or constant-buffer read would evade both. **A neighbouring field
having a real consumer is what makes the negative interesting rather than suspicious.**

> **"An unbounded scan buys completeness and sells false positives; I paid for both halves"** — the
> clearest statement of that trade this run has produced, from a session recording two of its own
> errors in the document.

### A fourth species: a control can only certify the axis it varies

**The most careful negative of the run was still false.** A store scan over the `02CB7FD0` block was
widened to RMW forms, `INC`/`DEC`, the shift group, SSE stores and `CMPXCHG`/`XADD`, with the `/reg`
field checked so `CMP` and the non-writing `FF` forms are excluded — **and it carried a known-positive
control, which passed**, recovering both config loaders plus two writers its author had not known
about. It reported **131 stores, all from one function, nothing else in the image.**

**The block is a C++ static object.** `00162410` is its static initializer — four instructions: `lea
rcx` the block, `call` the constructor, `lea rcx` the destructor, `jmp atexit` — and the constructor
chain writes **107 distinct offsets, covering 57 of the 65.**

> **The absence was true for the instrument and false about the program.** The constructor writes
> through `this`: every store is `[rcx+disp]`, with **no absolute address for a RIP-relative matcher
> to match.**

**The hole was not a missing instruction form — it was the addressing mode**, so no amount of widening
the form list would have closed it. And the control could not have caught it:

> **A control can only certify the axis it varies.** This one varied instruction *form* and certified
> instruction form. **Its known positives were themselves absolute-addressed writers**, so it
> validated a scan whose blind spot was non-absolute writers, and passed cheerfully.

**This is the same shape as the `subss` / `movss` / `lea edx,[rsi+imm]` family, one level up:** those
keyed on the common *encoding* of a thing; this keyed on the common *addressing mode* for reaching a
thing. **What found it was following the seven `LEA`s of an address inside the block instead of the
stores** — *"the pointer escape I had written down as a caveat was the answer."*

**Two further rules from the same pass, both from controls rather than findings:**

- **`mMapAmbientColor` defaults to 1 · 1 · 1 — white; under the rejected adjacency binding the same
  names read 2 · 1 · 1**, which is not a colour anybody defaults to. **The defaults discriminate the
  two candidate bindings** and pick the one dataflow picked. But the `mEyeA…`/`mEyeB…` pair both
  default to `0.66` — and **both read equal under the alternative too**, so it looks like confirmation
  and is not one. Reported rather than dropped: **a control that agrees with you is not a control
  unless the alternative would have disagreed.**
- A struct-shift hypothesis was rejected at **4 of 38 best, 0 of 37 at shift 0** — *and the first
  version of the test was broken*, scaling only the subscript form of a `undefined4 *` parameter.
  **It rejected the hypothesis anyway, and would have rejected a true one just as confidently. A test
  that gives the right answer for the wrong reason is not a test.**

### Three assignments in ten minutes that the database had already answered

1. A slice was told it **needed** a mechanism its own document published as its headline — 25 rows of
   `signed pair addss ±K`.
2. A session was assigned the identity of `01F82D20`, re-derived the whole `0x65C` settings object
   from the other end, and then found `19-Save-Load-Settings/…/game-settings-ini-and-runtime-config.md`
   already held it. **`OPEN-QUESTIONS.md` row AU-6 already said so** — in a line that had scrolled past
   me in my own tool output earlier in the same session.
3. Four "console-invisible" properties were raised as a live thread. **All four are named in that same
   document:** 11 `WindowSize`, 19 `DeviceID`, 20 `LUIDLow`, 21 `LUIDHigh` — display-device identity
   and window geometry, written by the display path rather than the property setter, **which is
   exactly why no arm cycles them.**

> **The database is now large enough that not knowing what it contains costs more than not knowing
> what the binary contains.** All three were recoverable by grep; none was recovered, because the
> check was a habit rather than a step.

**Now a step:** `check_already_answered.py` takes addresses and terms, reports every citing document
and every register row, and **exits non-zero when a row already carries an answered verdict.** Run
against `01F82D20` it returns **five answered rows**, AU-6 among them. **A hit is not a veto** —
the re-derivation above corrected a reference count in the document it duplicated, **159 → 157**,
because a displacement scan counted bytes where the original counted instructions inside functions.
The point is to make duplication a decision instead of a discovery.

### The propagation nearly laundered two retracted figures back into fact

**`console-command-names.md` is generated: 282 action ids, each with the name the engine itself
prints, the arm that implements it, the slice that read it, and the target field where one is known
(121 of 282).** Id 294 is included with an empty slice cell — a **render row with no action entry**,
which is precisely the distinction the two tables exist to make.

**The first version carried four more columns, and they were poison.** The join it was built from also
held `shape`, `step`, `direction` and `bound` — **the pre-correction classification.** Its
`FLOAT`/`CALL` split is the **withdrawn 102 / 71**; its `DO-NOTHING` count is the **retired 56
unimplemented**, a figure three separate findings replaced with *226 live · 38 read-outs · 12 buttons
with the action removed · 6 blank*. The generated Counts section printed both, in a table, under a
`GENERATED` banner.

> **A generated table inherits the errors of its source and launders them into fact** — and it does it
> while looking more authoritative than the prose that corrected them.

**Caught by reading the output, which is the same way the first generator artifact was caught, and
still does not scale.** Every gate passed on the poisoned version: links resolved, no generator
artifacts, addresses verified. **None of them knows that a number in a cell was retracted three hours
earlier** — the checkers compare a document against the *binary* and against *other documents*, and
this was a document disagreeing with **its own project's history.**

**The fix is a boundary, not a patch.** The behaviour columns are gone: the nine slice documents are
the authority for behaviour and they carry the corrections; this file answers *what does the engine
call this row, and who read it*, which is exactly what the label table adds and nothing more. **The
same rule the label caveat states — use the label to name the target, read the arm for everything
else — applied to the file that publishes the labels.**

### A fourth way the decompiler misdescribes a boundary — and this one is about the body

**`0026D910` ends in `jmp 002E3D40`, and `002E3D40` is its own 116-byte function.** The decompiler
renders the callee's body inside the caller's pseudocode, so a reader working from that rendering
attributes up to 116 bytes of behaviour — a π/6 rotation, a π/8 term, two matrix composes — **to the
wrong function.**

> **A tail call is a call. The decompiler renders it as a body, and a body is what a reader will
> believe.**

**And the four argument registers are zeroed immediately before the jump**, so the callee receives
`(0, 0, 0, 0)` at this site: the values in that block are **constants here, not quantities flowing
out of the field setup** — precisely the false connection an inlined rendering invites.

**Three earlier cases were all about the return** — an unmodelled `xmm0` return, a return through a
tail call, a `void` on a function that returns its source object. **This one is about the extent.**
The function's 418-byte size is correct; **the rendering crosses it.**

### Two traps of the same family, from two sessions, an hour apart

**The width trap, amended by its own finder.** *Width must come from the store* was written to stop a
one-byte boolean being read as a float. Then:

```asm
001D194F  mov qword ptr [02CB8130], 0     ; one instruction, two 4-byte floats
```

> **A store's width bounds the bytes touched, not the width of the field at its base.** The rule as
> stated would have sized this field at 8 bytes — **it would have mis-sized the field it was invented
> to protect.** A compiler merging adjacent zero-stores is the ordinary way that gap opens.

**The displacement trap.** `+0x24` appears on two different bases inside one pair of functions:
`[rbx+0x24]` is a result accumulator, `[rsi+0x24]` is a field of the unit's stats block.

> **The same displacement on two structures in one function, told apart only by which register is
> live** — a number that is right about one structure and wrong about the one you think you are
> reading.

**Both are the mis-binding species: complete, plausible, well-formed, and about the wrong thing.**

### A name is not evidence, and filing the question proved it

*"Are stage 2's timers the same timers stage 3 decrements?"* was filed as an open question rather than
assumed from the shared word "timers". **The answer was no — stage 2 advances no duration timer at
all**, and the measurement carried its own positive control: the same scan that reports zero for
stages 2 and 5 reports `0x17C` and `0x42` for stage 3.

> **`AdvanceStatusTimersAndBuildResult` is a misleading name for that body — it builds the HP delta.**
> Taking the shared word as evidence would have put a second timer set into the document.

### `0x80000003` reworded: a set, not a state

The eighth sighting refuses when **the status being applied** is in the set, where earlier sightings
gate **whether a unit participates**. A mask meaning one thing about a unit and another about a status
is **not one predicate with eight sightings; it is a set membership several different questions share.**
`PROPOSED-repos46-5` now asks *what set*, which has one answer, instead of *what state*, which needed
a different answer in every subsystem.

### The engine reads meaning out of a bank's filename

`AudioBank_SetSlotNameAndClassify` at **`0020AC30`** — **nine documents cited it, every one at its
entry only.** Opening it produced a fact a modder cannot get any other way:

```
"sum_" found  -> resolve a ".json" sidecar, then look for "0001"  -> flag A
"sum_" absent -> look for "spc_"                                  -> flag B (sticky)
```

**Four literals read from the image.** A bank whose name contains `sum_` takes a different path —
including a sidecar lookup — from one containing `spc_`. **Renaming a bank file changes what the
engine does with it.**
