## The respawn ledger, and a second imported name that was wrong — 2026-09-08

**New:** [`when-a-group-is-wiped-and-when-it-comes-back.md`](../05-Spawn-Encounter-Lifecycle/Group-Completion-And-Respawn/when-a-group-is-wiped-and-when-it-comes-back.md).
**Backlog: 9 of 64 imported.** `check_already_answered.py` first: *"no existing coverage found — the
block is new."*

### What a player gets

**The game does not count corpses; it keeps a checklist.** Each of **64 spawn groups** holds a 64-bit
`memberMask` of the members it is waiting for and a 64-bit `deadMask` of those confirmed dead, and an
encounter completes when `(memberMask & deadMask) == memberMask`. Killing the same member twice does
nothing — the bit is already set — and a member outside the mask cannot complete a group however many
of them die.

**Respawn waits are in seconds, already frame-rate corrected**, so the same wait elapses at 30 and at
60 fps.

### ⚠ The second imported name to be wrong, and this one had teeth

The research prose calls `00235FB0` **`SpawnEntry_GetElapsedTicksSinceLastDeath`**. The body:

```c
divisor = (int)(*(float*)0x01DFE0B8 * 30.0f);     /* 30 at FrameLimit=30, 60 at FrameLimit=60 */
elapsed = (*(u32*)0x0208D45C) / divisor - record->u32_0C;
```

**It returns seconds, not ticks**, and `+0x0C` is a second-stamp. `0x01DFE0B8` is the frame-rate scale
this database documented earlier today under `FrameLimit`, so the divisor is literally the frame rate.

> **Carried across unchecked, that name puts a factor of 30 or 60 into any reimplementation of
> respawn timing — and at 30 fps the scale is `1.0f`, so the bug would be invisible in exactly the
> configuration most likely to be tested first.** Two imports, two corrected names. The "a name is a
> lead, not a source" rule is not ceremony.

**Not over-corrected:** `GetRespawnCooldownTicks` (`+0x10`) keeps its imported name, because this
document never saw it compared against `00235FB0`'s output. Its unit is **unverified** and filed as
`EE-1` rather than silently changed to match the neighbour.

### The ledger, derived from the reset loop's own bounds

`SpawnGroup_ResetLifecycleLedger` walks `02EC13D0`→`02EC19D0` with a `0x60` stride, which reads like
96-byte entries. **It is four 24-byte entries unrolled**, and the death handler proves it by indexing
the same table `lea rax,[rcx+rcx*2]` / `[rdi+rax*8]` — a ×24 stride from `0x02EC13C0`:

```
{ u64 memberMask; u64 deadMask; u8 flags; }   1,536 bytes / 24 = exactly 64 groups
```

**In BSS** — checked against `SizeOfRawData`, not assumed — so every mask starts at zero. Which yields
the sharpest open question in the set: **a zero `memberMask` satisfies the completion test
immediately**, so something must populate it before the first death, and that writer is unidentified
(`EE-2`).

### One template, nine copies, one dead branch

Nine accessors share a seven-check prologue instruction for instruction, and all nine contain the same
unreachable arm: `movzx eax, dl` followed by `test eax,eax / js`. A byte zero-extended to 32 bits
cannot be negative. **Recorded as a compiler/template artifact rather than a guard**, so a reader does
not go looking for the condition that triggers it.

### Not claimed

The two completion arms — bit 47 set versus cleared, ledger flag, presentation event `0x2005` versus
`0x2008` — are **read but not explained**; what sets the selecting bit is `EE-3`. `00307140`,
`00238B70` and `00238AE0` are called with the constant `1` on completion and **were not read**
(`EE-5`). The kind gate `[+0x698]+0x05 == 1` is **not decoded** (`EE-6`).

### Gates

`check_links`, `check_consistency`, `check_questions` green; `verify_doc_addresses` ok (36 addresses,
13 entry / 15 interior / 8 data).

## Seven verbs, and the calling convention behind all of them — 2026-09-08

**New:** [`the-script-to-native-calling-convention.md`](../01-Script-VM-Native-Bridge/Spawn-Verbs/the-script-to-native-calling-convention.md).
**Backlog: 20 of 64.** `check_already_answered.py`: *"no existing coverage found — the block is new."*

### The verbs were the smaller half

The backlog's `Script_VM_Native_Bridge` cluster turned out to be `VM_Spawn*` wrappers around the
**exact native functions documented in the previous block** — the script side of the same lifecycle.
Reading seven together exposed something none of them shows alone: **the calling convention every
native verb uses.**

```c
void VM_Verb(VmResultCtx *result /*rcx*/, SpawnCtx *target /*rdx*/,
             VmEventCtx *event /*r8*/, VmValueStack *stack /*r9*/);
```

Uniform across all seven; the unused registers are simply never touched, which is how the shape can
be *read off* rather than assumed.

### ⚠ Arguments arrive in reverse

`VM_Spawn_BindEntryAndMarkCapTracked` pops twice from one stack and passes the **first** popped value
as argument 2 and the **second** as argument 3. **The first value popped is the last the script
pushed.**

> **Both arguments are integers, so a reimplementation that reads them left to right compiles, runs,
> and silently binds the wrong entry.** This is the same failure shape as the respawn-units error
> caught in the previous block: a wrong assumption that no type system will catch.

### The result convention, with its stride derived

```asm
0026B4E0  movsx rax, byte ptr [rcx + 0x11]      ; slot index, SIGNED
0026B4E5  lea   r8, [rax + rax*4]               ; x5 ...
0026B4F0  mov   byte  ptr [rax + r8*8 + 0x15], 2    ; ... x8 = stride 40, tag 2 = int32
0026B4F6  mov   dword ptr [rax + r8*8 + 0x0C], edx
```

**40-byte result entries, tag at `+0x15`, int32 payload at `+0x0C`.** And the slot index is read
**signed** with nothing bounds-checking it (`EF-2`).

### The rule that makes return types readable at a glance

- **A verb that returns a value ends `jmp VMResult_WriteInt32`.**
- **A verb that returns nothing ends `jmp <native target>` or `ret`.**

**The tail target is the return type.** Two of seven return; five do not.

### Two verbs do more than forward, and one of them hides a failure

`VM_Spawn_ApplySelectedUnit` applies the unit, then calls `ActorWork_HasAppliedUnitDefinition` and
only raises the actor operation if a definition actually took. **It returns nothing either way, so a
script whose spawn request did not take cannot tell.**

`VM_Spawn_SetEntryMapAndResetTransientEntries` turns its integer through `002640C0`/`002650B0` before
the native call — **the verb's argument is an id, not a pointer**, which the native function's own
signature does not reveal.

### Disposition C applied

Four of the eleven cluster entries are **5-byte thunks**. Recorded as forwarders under disposition
**C** — named, boundary stated, not individually explained. That is what the disposition is for.

### Not claimed

**Only tag `2` is proven** — the 40-byte entry plainly supports more types and the rest of that family
is unread (`EF-1`), so **only int-returning verbs can be reimplemented faithfully today**. And nothing
here connects a verb to the **script opcode that calls it** (`EF-5`) — the bridge is read entirely
from the native side, which is precisely the gap that would make this actionable from a script editor.

### Gates

`check_links`, `check_consistency`, `check_questions` green; `verify_doc_addresses` ok (32 addresses,
25 entry / 7 interior).

## 2,007 addresses the database had recorded and could not find — 2026-09-08

Following the previous block's checker fix: **do other tools share the `.md`-only assumption?**
Twenty-four scripts walk the database and twenty-three filter to `.md`.

**For most of them that is correct** — `check_links` checks markdown links, `check_questions` checks
prose checkboxes, `check_provenance` checks frontmatter. A `.tsv` has none of those. **The sweep's
first useful output was ruling twenty of them out**, rather than "fixing" instruments that were not
broken.

The defect is confined to the tools that answer *"does the database already record this address?"* —
and the worst affected was `gen_address_index.py`, which builds `ADDRESS-INDEX.md`, **the canonical
"who talks about this address" artifact.**

### The measurement

| | count |
|---|---:|
| function entries cited in `.md` documents | 7,408 |
| function entries recorded in `.tsv` side files | 2,161 |
| **recorded only in a `.tsv`, in no document** | **2,000** |

1,761 of those are in `scriptvm-verb-table.tsv` and 239 in `phyre-field-schema.tsv`; **1,757 carry an
owner.** A reader looking any of them up in the address index found nothing and would reasonably
conclude the database did not cover it.

### ⚠ A third zero today that meant "wrong query"

The first patched run reported **"0 more recorded only in a side file"** — flatly contradicting the
2,000 measured independently minutes earlier. Cause: `ADDR` is
`` re.compile(r"`(?:0x)?(0[0-9A-Fa-f]{7})`") `` — **it requires markdown backticks.** A TSV column
holds bare hex, so the pattern matched nothing at all.

> **One extractor cannot serve two source formats.** The `.md` pattern's backtick anchor is *correct*
> for prose — it is what stops ordinary numbers being read as addresses — and *useless* for a table.
> Split into `ADDR` and `ADDR_BARE`, the count came back **2,007**.
>
> **It was caught only because an independent measurement already existed to contradict it.** That is
> the third instrument today whose zero meant "the query does not fit the data".

**Cross-validation, with the discrepancy explained rather than smoothed:** 2,007 against 2,000, a
0.35 % difference, from two independently written scans. `gen_address_index.py` resolves interior
addresses to their containing function and restricts to numbered category folders (3 side files);
`tsvgap.py` matched exact entries and also scanned `_types/` and `_experiments/` (5 files). Both known
differences push in opposite directions.

### The fix respects a distinction the database already holds

**A verb-table row is a transcription, not an explanation** — `check_named_not_cited.py`'s own rule.
So the side-file addresses are now:

- **listed in `ADDRESS-INDEX.md` under a separate *"Recorded only in a side file"* section**, marked
  `table only`, so lookup works;
- **reported as their own line in `COVERAGE-DIMENSIONS.md`** — *"recorded only in a `.tsv` side file,
  explained by no document"*, **1,865 of 28,661 authored (6.51 %)**;
- **not folded into the citation count**, which would have inflated coverage by six points for work
  nobody has done.

*(1,865 against 2,007 because the coverage figure counts only **authored** functions, excluding
generated code and thunks — the denominator that report uses throughout.)*

### Not claimed

**No new understanding of any of the 2,007.** They were already recorded; this makes them findable
and honestly categorised. **The citation figure moved from 20.10 % to 20.50 % only because the
address-form fix in the previous block let previously-missed `0x`-prefixed citations count** — not
because anything was learned.

## The actor record is recycled, not constructed — 2026-09-08

**New:** [`the-record-behind-every-actor.md`](../04-Actor-Entity/Actor-Storage-Record/the-record-behind-every-actor.md)
and `ActorStorageRecord` in the type store — **41 fields, validated, 0 errors.**
**Backlog: 21 of 64.** Prior art: only the backlog itself.

`ActorStorage_InitializeRecord` (1,439 B) is the largest entry in the whole import backlog, and
charter §29 names actor hierarchy as high-leverage. Track **C** was still the weakest.

### What a player gets

**When an area reloads or an enemy respawns, the engine does not build a new actor — it takes an old
record out of a pool and resets part of it.** *Part* is the finding.

```asm
00266573  and byte  ptr [rbx + 0x14], 0x7F        ; clear bit 7, keep the other seven
002666B0  and byte  ptr [rbx + 0x13], 0x3C        ; keep ONLY bits 2-5
0026665A  or  byte  ptr [rbx + 0x0E], 0xF0        ; SET the top nibble
002666F1  and dword ptr [rbx + 0x1C], 0xFFFFDEFF  ; clear bits 8 and 13
```

**Eleven bytes are read-modify-written rather than assigned.** For a freshly allocated object every
one of those masks would be equivalent to a plain store and the compiler would have emitted one.

> **The masks exist because the previous contents matter.** A recycled actor inherits bits from
> whatever occupied that slot before it, and only the bits this routine names are guaranteed fresh.

### The base register was proved stable before any offset was believed

`rbx` is loaded **once**, at `0026656A`, from `[rdx + index*8 + 8]`, and reappears only as an epilogue
restore. **A base reassigned mid-function would silently merge two structures' offsets into one
layout** — the failure this check exists to prevent, and it takes one grep.

The table is an **array of pointers with an 8-byte header**, and the record's very first written field
is `mov word ptr [rbx], r10w` — **the record stores its own slot index.**

### Two correspondences, and why they are `PROBABLE` and not `PROVEN`

The movement document reads an actor with a packed byte at **`+0x03`** (`& 0xE0 == 0x60`, a kind gate)
and a context pointer at **`+0xB8`**. This record has a packed byte at `+0x03` — masked **`& 0x1F`**,
the *complementary half of the same byte* — and a `+0xB8` context pointer, read and never written.

> **Two independent offsets agreeing, with complementary masks on one byte, is real evidence.** It is
> also exactly what two types sharing a prefix would look like. Recorded as **`PROBABLE`** in the type
> store and filed as `EH-1` with the test that would settle it: one function that takes both.

### A blind spot this function walks straight into

`lea r11, [rip - 0x146556]` loads **the image base into a register**, and globals are then addressed
as `[r11 + …]`. **That form is invisible to `rip_data_refs.tsv`**, so any "which globals does
`00266530` touch" answer from `globals_index.py` is incomplete **by construction**. Noted in the
document so the negative is never read as absence.

### Coverage

Type store: **2 types, 81 fields, 1,767 of 1,912 declared bytes (92.4 %), 47 named (58.0 %)** — and
**six undeclared spans totalling 140 bytes are reported as gaps**, not hidden. `0x11C` is recorded as
a **lower bound**, not a size: no allocation site was read.

### Not claimed

**Not one flag bit's meaning.** The masks are exact and the semantics are entirely unread (`EH-4`) —
which is itself the strongest evidence the bits are individually meaningful. **Nobody calls
`00266530` in this document** (`EH-6`): "records are recycled" is a structural fact here, and *when a
player would see it* needs the callers. Eight callees, six of them unread.

### Gates

`check_links`, `check_consistency`, `check_questions`, `types_index --validate` (0 errors) green;
`verify_doc_addresses` ok (21 addresses).

## The actor pool, and a headline of mine that was wrong — 2026-09-08

**`EH-1`, `EH-2` and `EH-6` all answered**, and one of them by overturning what I wrote in the
previous block.

### ⚠ The correction first

Last block's headline was **"the actor record is recycled, not constructed"**, inferred from eleven
read-modify-write masks: *for a freshly allocated object those masks would be plain stores, so the
previous contents must matter.*

**The sole caller `memset`s the entire pool to zero immediately before calling the initialiser on
every record** (`00861EC0`, confirmed as `memset`). **There is no previous occupant.** The inference
was sound in form and false in fact, because I had reasoned about the callers without reading them.

**What the masks actually protect is `+0x03`** — written by the *carve loop* before the initialiser
runs, and **read three times and never written** by the initialiser. The document keeps the original
text, struck through and marked, per *corrections are permanent record*.

> **The lesson is not "read the callers".** It is that **an inference from instruction form alone
> reached a confident conclusion about a lifecycle**, and the one call site that would have refuted
> it was four instruments and one grep away. `EH-6` was already filed as the open question; it should
> have been answered before the headline was written, not after.

### `EH-6` — exactly one caller

All four instruments, both controls passing: `E8` **1** · `E9` **0** · code memory-operand **0** ·
data qword **0**. `ActorStorage_AllocateAndInitializeRecords` (`002679F0`) ←
`ActorSystem_InitializeManagerRuntime` (`0026CE60`) ← `0025BFB0` / `0032F1B0`.

### What the allocator actually does

One block, sized from a descriptor table, zeroed, carved:

```
payload = Σ roundup16(kindTable[k].size) × count[k]
total   = 2 × align16(count×8 + 0x17) + payload
```

then each record's pointer goes into a table at `pool + 8 + slot×8` — **exactly the array shape the
initialiser reads** — and four per-kind counters at `ctx+0x1D0` are prefix-summed into `ctx+0x1D8`.

### `EH-2` — the size, and how far out my lower bound was

The table at `0x01E0C328` is eight `{u8 kind, u8 sub, u16 size}` entries: **808, 936, 816, 840, 720,
1760, 1760, 1640**. Records are **720–1,760 bytes by kind**, not one size.

**`0x11C` = 284 was correctly labelled a lower bound — and it was an underestimate by three to six
times.** The label is what kept it honest; the type store now carries the per-kind sizes with the
table as evidence.

### `EH-1` — from `PROBABLE` to `PROVEN`

```asm
00267AFA  movzx ecx, byte [rdx+3] / and cl,0xE0 / or cl,r9b  / mov [rdx+3],cl
00267B07  and cl,0x1F / movzx eax,byte [r8] / shl al,5 / or cl,al / mov [rdx+3],cl
```

```
record[+0x03] = (kindCode << 5) | (sequenceWithinKind & 0x1F)
```

**The byte `Movement_SetSteeringMode` gates on is written by this loop, with this encoding.** Its test
`(& 0xE0) == 0x60` selects **kind 3** — the 1760/1760/1640 entries. Not two offsets agreeing: one
writer, one reader, one encoding.

> **Only kind-3 actors can be steered.** Kinds 0, 1 and 2 return immediately from
> `Movement_SetSteeringMode`, which is now a statement about the game rather than about a mask.

### Not claimed

**What kinds 0, 1 and 2 are.** Four kinds exist and only kind 3 is tied to a behaviour. **What any
flag bit means** is still entirely unread (`EH-4`), and the six undeclared spans (`EH-3`) are
unchanged — the record being 1,760 bytes rather than 284 means the *undeclared* fraction is far larger
than §4 implied, and the type store's gap report says so.

### Gates

`types_index --validate` 0 errors; `check_links`, `check_consistency`, `check_questions` — below.

## The action boundary from the code side, and a metric of mine that was inflated — 2026-09-08

**Backlog 24 of 64.** Three `CombatAction`/`CombatFormula` entries, **appended to the document that
already owns the subject** rather than made into a competing one.

### ⚠ My own contract metric was double-counting

`COVERAGE-DIMENSIONS.md` reported **2 behavioural contracts**. There is **one**. The detector counted
any document whose frontmatter carried a `contract:` key — and `_experiments/EXP-001` carries
`contract: <path>` as a **reference to the contract it tests**.

**A 100 % overstatement of the program's weakest dimension**, in a report whose entire purpose is not
to overstate. Fixed: a contract must declare **both** `contract:` and `scope:`. Now **1 of 215
(0.47 %)**.

*(Mid-block I also mis-read a grep and briefly believed a second false positive existed in
`17-Presentation-Rendering`. That file's `contract:` is in its body, not its frontmatter, and the tool
never counted it — the tool parses frontmatter only. Corrected before it reached a file.)*

### `check_already_answered` stopped a duplicate for the third time today

The `0x21E` action boundary looked like a discovery. It is **`AT-8`**, already developed far further
than I had it — from the **data** side: `action_data.bin`, count `0x21F` = 543, 60-byte records, the
file length confirming the executable's bound.

**So this block's contribution is the code side**, delineated against what `AT-8` already says.

### Three independent consumers, and the engine's own names for the halves

**`BattleUnit_AdvanceActionState` (`00307BE0`, 137 B)** splits on it:

```c
r = (u->u16_714 > 0x21E) ? BattleUnit_AdvanceExtendedActionState(u)   /* 00305080,  249 B */
                         : BattleUnit_AdvanceStandardActionState(u);  /* 00304850, 2034 B */
```

> **2,034 bytes of machinery below the boundary against 249 above.** The ledger already names the two
> halves *Standard* and *Extended*; the size ratio is the part worth staring at.

**`BattleAction_CheckTargetEligibility` (`003083B0`)** rejects any id above 542 **before looking at
anything else**. `AT-8` called that space *"target-carrying"* from the data file; **this is the same
statement from the code**, derived independently.

### One byte, two consumers, opposite senses

`BattleAction_CheckTargetEligibility` and `SpawnGroup_RecordMemberDeathAndHandleCompletion` open on
the **same gate** — `BattleUnit + 0x698`, then byte `+0x05` against `1`:

- **kind 1 → not targetable**
- **kind 1 → required for the death to count toward a spawn group**

Complementary rather than contradictory; a dying-or-dead state reads naturally. **That reading is
filed as `EI-1`, not asserted.** What is established is the pairing.

### Also read

`BattleRuntime_ResetPersistentStatePrefix` (`00386C10`, 95 B): **two parallel tables of 64-byte
entries** at `0x0208D480` and `0x0208DE80`, chosen by the same `+0x05` byte tested against `0`, with
**only the first 32 bytes of an entry cleared.** What survives the reset is not established — the
same caution the actor initialiser earned.

### Not claimed

What lies above id 542 (`EI-2`) · the meaning of kind 1 (`EI-1`) · what `FUN_004697C0` does on a
successful advance · **the 596-byte body of `CheckTargetEligibility` past its two opening gates**,
which is why the backlog records that entry as **partial**.

### Housekeeping

**`PROGRAM-STATE.md` was several blocks stale** despite being the file this skill says to read first

## The first contract that could be parity-tested without the game — 2026-09-08

**New:** [`CONTRACT-field-music-selection.md`](../18-Audio/CONTRACT-field-music-selection.md).
**Contracts: 2 of 215 (0.93 %)**, both at `CONTRACT READY` — and this figure is now trustworthy, the
double-count having been fixed in the previous block.

Contracts were the weakest measurable dimension after runtime validation. This one was chosen for a
property none of the other candidates has: **field music selection is a pure function.** No
allocation, no RNG, no threading, no state written, no ordering dependence — `(fieldId, progress,
table) → trackId`.

### Every structural claim in the source document was re-derived, and all survived

The owning document's page stride, 11/5 bit split, `4 + 3*count` run stride, ladder walk and the
`track 0 → -1` fold were checked instruction by instruction against the binary. **All confirmed.**

**One near-miss worth recording.** At `003EAA84` the progress value is `movzx`-extended — *zero*
extension — while the document says it is *sign*-extended. That looked like a correction to file.
It is not: `003EAB10` holds a **second** instruction, `movsx r11d, r11w`, applied just before the
ladder. Both are true, at different points, and the effective comparison is signed 16-bit.
**Checked before claiming; no false correction was published.**

### What the contract adds over the prose

- **`-1` means four different things** — out-of-range field, missing page, no covering run, or a
  resolved track of `0` — and **the caller cannot distinguish them.** A real constraint on any
  reimplementation that wants to explain why an area went silent.
- **Page entries are absolute 32-bit addresses**, sign-extended and dereferenced immediately, not
  offsets — so the table can only live in the low 2 GB.
- **The table pointer at `0x02B5E0D0` is not null-checked**, though everything after it is.
- **The coverage test is `start + len >= fieldId`**, so a run with `len = 0` still covers exactly one
  field.
- The progress fetch happens **before** the bounds check, so an invalid field id still costs the call.

### The parity plan, and the line it refuses to blur

**Testable today, with no game running:** `CALCULATION` (synthetic tables exercise every branch,
including `len = 0`, `count = 0`, `track = 0` and `progress > 0x7FFF`), `STRUCTURAL`, and
`EDGE-CASE` across the four routes to `-1`.

**Requires the game:** `INTEGRATION` — the real table's contents (`DG-1`).

> **Passing calculation parity on synthetic tables proves the algorithm, not the outcome.** Whether
> the reconstruction picks the same track as the shipped game depends on data this contract cannot
> reach. **A parity claim from synthetic tables alone must say "algorithm, not data"** — written into
> §16 so the distinction survives the person who wrote it.

### Not claimed

What populates the table (`DG-1`) · what a track id indexes (`DG-2`) · whether any shipped run uses
more than one ladder entry (`DG-3`) · who calls it (`DG-4`). **`readiness: CONTRACT READY`, not
`RECONSTRUCTION READY`** — §13 is empty, as it is for every entity in this database.

### Gates

`check_links`, `check_consistency`, `check_questions` green; `verify_doc_addresses` ok (5 addresses).

## 17. Implemented and differential-tested — 2026-09-08

**Reconstruction:** [`../../../Reconstruction/Game/Audio/field_music.c`](../../../Reconstruction/Game/Audio/field_music.c)
**Test:** [`../../../Reconstruction/Tests/Differential/diff_field_music.py`](../../../Reconstruction/Tests/Differential/diff_field_music.py)

**Result: 1,200 cases over 20 synthetic tables, 0 mismatches** — 575 resolving a real track, 625
resolving `-1`.

**The reference side is the shipped machine code**, not a second reading of the disassembly: the 229
bytes at `003EAA70` are mapped at their real virtual address and executed under Unicorn, with
`FieldData_GetVariable0` stubbed at its own address as `mov eax, imm32 ; ret`. Both sides receive the
same table image at the same base, which §3 makes mandatory — the page entries are absolute addresses.

### Two things the test had to be fixed to be worth anything

**The first run crashed the driver with an access violation**, and the cause is a property of the
format worth recording here: **there is no chain terminator.** The walk ends only when a run's `start`
exceeds the query, so a page whose chain stops short runs on into whatever follows it in memory. The
shipped data must therefore always end a page with a run whose `start` is above every field id that
can reach it. **A generator that does not do the same produces crashes rather than test failures** —
which is how this was found.

**The first green result was weak and was not reported as a pass.** 313 of 396 cases resolved `-1`,
so "0 mismatches" was mostly two implementations agreeing on the same *failure*. Biasing field ids
toward spans a run actually covers moved the split to 575/625, and only then was the result
meaningful.

### ⚠ This entity skipped two rungs of the ladder, deliberately

`readiness` moves from `CONTRACT READY` to **`DIFFERENTIAL TESTED`**, passing over `RUNTIME
VALIDATED` and `RECONSTRUCTION READY`. That is not an oversight and it should not become a precedent
by accident:

> **For a pure function with an emulatable reference, running the original's own bytes substitutes
> for runtime validation *of the algorithm*.** There is no state, no ordering and no RNG for a live
> process to reveal that emulation does not already show.
>
> **It substitutes for nothing about the data.** The real table is still unread (`DG-1`), and
> `INTEGRATION` parity remains untestable. **An entity with state, timing or RNG cannot take this
> shortcut** — for those, the ladder's ordering is load-bearing.

### Parity status, by dimension

| dimension | status |
|---|---|
| `CALCULATION` | **PARITY over synthetic tables** — 1,200 cases, 0 mismatches |
| `STRUCTURAL` | parity — the layout in §3 drives both sides |
| `EDGE-CASE` | parity — all four routes to `-1`, plus `len = 0`, `count = 0`, `track = 0`, `progress > 0x7FFF` |
| `INTEGRATION` | **NOT TESTED** — needs the shipped table (`DG-1`) |
| `RNG`, `TIMING`, `SERIALIZATION`, `STATE-TRANSITION` | not applicable |

**Known intentional divergence, excluded from comparison:** a NULL table pointer faults in the
original and returns `FIELD_MUSIC_NONE` in the reconstruction. The test names it in its output rather
than skipping it silently.

## 2026-09-08 — Second reconstruction: does the differential harness generalise?

**`GameSettingConfig_ApplyQualityPreset` (`001DE4F0`, 71 B) reimplemented and differential-tested.**
`Reconstruction/Game/Config/quality_preset.{h,c}` vs the shipped bytes under Unicorn.

```
cases                 : 600
  changed the settings: 532
  left them unchanged : 68
mismatches            : 0
```

### Why a second one at all, and why this one

The first reconstruction proved the harness works. It did **not** prove the harness *generalises* —
`FieldMusic_Select` is the easiest possible shape: pure, returns a scalar, no state. This one was
chosen to break both of those assumptions deliberately:

| | `field_music` | `quality_preset` |
|---|---|---|
| what is compared | a **return value** | **resulting memory** — 31 int32s after the call |
| the input tables | **synthetic** — the real one is built at runtime | **the game's own `.rdata`** at `0x00900CC0` / `0x00900CE0` |

**The second column is the stronger evidence**, and it is worth being precise about why. Parity over
synthetic tables shows the *algorithm* matches. Parity over shipped tables shows the algorithm matches
**on the data the game actually ships** — a reconstruction can agree on invented input and still be
wrong about the real thing, and only the second test can see that.

### The case class that a careless suite would have omitted

The original **does not validate `quality`**. So `-1`, `4` and `7` index the 31 × 4 matrix outside the
intended column, reading a neighbouring row or off the end of the table. Those are in the suite, and
**both sides agree there too.**

> **This is the distinction between reproducing a function's *intended* behaviour and reproducing the
> function.** A reconstruction that clamped or validated `quality` would pass every in-range case and
> silently diverge wherever the game itself is sloppy. The charter asks for the second thing.

### What did NOT move, and why that is the point

`CONTRACT-game-setting-config.md` covers **five** operations — construct, load, parse, apply,
serialize. **One** is now differential-tested. Its `readiness` stays **`CONTRACT READY`**.

> Promoting a subsystem on the strength of its smallest operation is precisely the overstatement the
> readiness ladder exists to prevent. `001DE4F0` is 71 bytes; `001DE5D0` (parse) is 1,919. The ladder
> is per-entity, and the entity here is the subsystem.

`INTEGRATION` parity remains untested for both reconstructions, and for the same underlying reason in
each case: nothing yet establishes **when** the game invokes these — `AX-6a` (when the graphics-apply
callback fires) for this one, `DG-1` (the shipped music table) for the other.

### Deliberate interface divergence, recorded not hidden

The original reads its tables from fixed addresses; the reconstruction **takes them as parameters**.
Hardcoding the shipped bytes would be transcription rather than reimplementation, and could never be
run against a modified table — which is exactly what Level 1 modding needs from Level 2 work.

## 2026-09-08 — `AX-6a` answered: the graphics-apply chain is a button press

**The two functions with zero callers are the procs of two row objects in the in-game Config screen.**
`AX-6`, `AX-6a` and `AX-2` are all answered by the same read; three new questions (`DI-1`, `DI-2`,
`DI-3`) are filed in their place. New document:
[the Config screen](../16-UI/Config-Screen/the-config-screen-and-what-a-setting-change-runs.md).

### The instrument, again, not the inspection

The prior block left `AX-6a` with an explicit prediction: *"answering it needs the registrar's dispatch
semantics — not more call-graph walking."* **The prediction was right about the method and wrong about
the shape.** There is no registrar. `0023BD40` is the screen's own proc; it builds 24 rows and hands each
child its proc through `00244F50(size, proc, initMsg)`, which stores it at object `+0x00` — the widget
header already documented in `16-UI/Widget-Object-Model/`.

Two instruments were load-bearing, and each was the only one that could have worked:

| | |
|---|---|
| **`E9` jmp rel32** | `001CD040` reaches `001D1660` by a **tail jump**. `001D1660` has **zero `E8` call sites in the entire image.** An `E8`-only reading calls a 13,753-byte retail dispatcher unreachable. |
| **code memory operand** | `0023B330`, `0023B6F0`, `0023BD40` and `0023BCC0` are each materialised by exactly **one `lea`**, and by nothing else. |

Negative results were only meaningful because each instrument had its own positive control:
`E8` → `001DE4F0` (1 site); `E9` → `001D1660` (1 site); code operand → `0023B6F0` (1 ref);
raw qword → `005C5230`, the default widget proc, **2,527 occurrences in `.rdata`**. Under that last
instrument all four chain functions score **0** — they are in no vtable and no data table.

### The check that makes the row table trustworthy

Three tables, read separately, agree:

```
descriptor table 00914710   24 records x 20 B   kind 0 -> build no child      rows {0,2,3,11,14,17}
jump table       0017DD5C   23 arms, row - 1    default arm                   rows   {2,3,11,14,17}
jump table       0017E1AC   23 arms, row - 1    default arm, returns -1       rows   {2,3,11,14,17}
```

> **Nothing forced that agreement.** The descriptor table is data the screen walks at construction; the
> two jump tables are compiler output for two unrelated `switch` statements. They were read by different
> means and they name the same five dead rows. Row 0 is absent from the jump tables only because the
> index is `row - 1`.

A second, independent check fell out of a different block entirely: row 10 reads `cfg + 0x48` =
`setting[18]`, and `0017D8F0` — read weeks earlier, for the `FrameLimit` chain — returns
`cfg->setting[18]`.

### What the answer costs

`AX-6` was standing as *"PARTLY ANSWERED — the timing is not statically provable."* **It was provable.**
And the answer is the unwelcome one: **nothing applies a quality preset at startup.** Construction copies
preset column 0 into all 31 settings while `Quality`'s own column-0 value is `1`, and **that mismatch
stands in the shipped game** until the player opens Config and moves the Image Quality row. The earlier
document had written *"if the graphics-apply callback fires before the first frame, the mismatch is
transient and invisible — this document does not claim it does."* It does not fire.

### Two documents corrected

- **`CONTRACT-game-setting-config.md`** said *"`0017E070` reads 16 settings in one pass."* The **count is
  right and the mechanism is not**: it is a 23-arm jump table returning **one** value, and 16 is the number
  of distinct settings across all arms. A right number can hide a wrong mechanism.
- **`the-282-command-parameter-console.md`** names `001D1660` `DevConsole_DispatchCommand` and says the
  console *"has exactly one entry point."* Every fact stands and the entry point is now named: **the retail
  Config screen**, driving 16 of the 282 ids. The name overstates. **A debug arm inside a shipped
  dispatcher does not make the dispatcher a debug tool.**

### Deliberately not claimed

The two text-id columns (`0x050C`–`0x0539`, `0x0D07`–`0x0D1B`) were **not** resolved to strings; every row
name in the new document comes from the `GameSetting.ini` key that row reads, not from the label the
player sees. Rows 4 and 5 read an audio object rather than the config and are left unnamed. The six
kind-0 rows build nothing and are **not** called headings. And none of it has been seen in a live process.

## 2026-09-08 — Charter §7: the knowledge is machine-queryable, and says what it cannot answer

**`knowledge_db.py` builds a derived SQLite index in ~1 second** over 222 documents, 12,537 address
citations, 38,161 functions, 90,525 call edges, 164,489 global read/write rows, 81 type fields and
824 questions. Full description: [`KNOWLEDGE-SCHEMA.md`](KNOWLEDGE-SCHEMA.md). Two §38 first-actions
close with it — *identify weak schema capabilities* and *improve/migrate the schema*.

### Derived, not migrated — and that was the design decision

Charter §7 says not to preserve a weak schema to avoid migration work. The goal revision says, in as
many words, **do not start over and do not discard existing schemas or tooling**. Those pull in
opposite directions only if "schema" means "where the knowledge lives". It does not have to:

> **The documents stay authoritative and the index is regenerated from them.** A derived index
> cannot silently disagree with its sources — rebuild it and any disagreement is gone. The
> hand-maintained `ADDRESS-INDEX.md` once held 74 addresses against 6,504 cited, two orders of
> magnitude behind, and nobody noticed. A one-second rebuild leaves drift nowhere to live.

The artifact is gitignored. Nothing gates on it. **Making it a gate would mean trusting it more than
the documents it is copied from.**

### `caller_is_eh` is a column now

`edges.tsv` offers unwind-funclet and catch-handler callers to any `awk`, and that evidence class
cost a prior branch 182 classifications. The census is **3,834 of 90,525 edges, 4.24 %**.
**Materialising the flag turns "remember to filter" into "write a `WHERE` clause you can see."**
`query callers` excludes them; `query callers-including-banned` prints both, so the difference is
visible instead of assumed.

### The deliverable is the *unsupported* list

**15 of 21 tracked queries are supported. Six are not**, and each names the source that would have to
exist first: field-level writers (needs a per-type field xref pass — `global_refs` is address-keyed
and cannot see `[reg+disp]`), script-opcode callees, resources by subsystem, functions with known
behaviour but unresolved parameters, **contradictions** and state-machine dependents.

> **A schema that answers 15 of 21 and says which 6 it cannot is worth more than one that answers 21
> by inventing data.** `DJ-2` files the contradiction gap, which is the largest: this project
> overturns its own claims often enough that the correction history is real evidence, and it is
> currently only greppable.

### What the first run measured

**The charter's own vocabulary is stated in 6 of 218 non-template documents — 2.75 %.** Six declare a
maturity level, six a readiness rung. Every §7 query of the form *"everything at L2"* is therefore
answerable and nearly empty. **That is a labelling backlog, not a knowledge gap** (`DJ-1`), and the
right response is explicitly *not* to bulk-label: a rung asserted without re-reading the document is
the silent promotion the confidence vocabulary exists to prevent.

**And it is not the number `COVERAGE-DIMENSIONS.md` reports.** That file counts rung words appearing
anywhere in prose (`CLASSIFIED` in 33 documents, `IMPLEMENTED` in 23). Both are correct; a rung named
in a sentence is a *mention*, a rung in frontmatter is a *claim about that document*, and only the
second can answer a query. Neither number should be quoted without its instrument.

### Three defects, all found by making the index answer questions already answered another way

| symptom | cause | fix |
|---|---|---|
| 813 questions read; `check_questions.py` reads **824** | a second regex over `OPEN-QUESTIONS.md`, blind to two-column and continuation rows | **import the gate and call its parser.** One file, one parser. |
| **3** contracts; `program_coverage.py` says 2 | `_templates/CONTRACT.md` carries `contract:` and `scope:` because it *is* the shape of a contract | `is_template` column, filtered by every built-in query |
| **28** readers of `02F9736C`; `globals_index.py` says 27 | one row per *site*, not per *function* — `002A9980` reads it twice | group by function, return a site count, name the unit |

> **The third pair were both right.** They answered different questions and their row counts silently
> meant different things — the trap this project keeps re-encountering. **The fix is never to pick a
> winner; it is to make the unit visible in the output.**

Two cross-checks passed unchanged, and they are why the rest is trusted: the EH-edge census
reproduced **3,834 / 90,525** exactly, and `callers 0017DB90` reproduced the two `awk`-derived
callers from the previous block.

## 2026-09-08 — The index picked the block: the most-called undocumented function in the game

**`0063BC00` — 373 call sites in 369 distinct functions, and no document had ever named it.** It was
not found by intuition. The knowledge index built earlier the same day was asked one question:

```sql
-- the highest-connectivity callee that no document cites
SELECT e.callee, COUNT(DISTINCT e.caller) FROM edges e JOIN functions f ON f.entry = e.callee
 WHERE e.caller_is_eh = 0 AND f.is_generated = 0 AND f.thunk != 'true' AND f.body_bytes > 40
 GROUP BY e.callee HAVING (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM citations c WHERE c.resolved_entry = e.callee) = 0
 ORDER BY 2 DESC
```

> **That is the schema paying for itself in the first block after it existed.** "Which core function
> has nobody looked at" was previously unanswerable without a bespoke script; it is now one query,
> and the `caller_is_eh = 0` clause that keeps banned evidence out is visible in the text rather than
> remembered.

The answer is `Phyre::PClassDescriptor`'s **lazy resolve**: `return base_+0xC0 + (int32)offset_+0xF8`,
behind an override at `+0xD8` and three flag bits at `+0xFC` (31 *skip prepare*, 30 *prepare done*,
29 *pointer handed out*). Written up as §10 of
[the class descriptor system](../22-Middleware-PhyreEngine/Reflection-And-Class-Metadata/class-descriptor-and-metadata-system.md).

**The flags offset was anchored, not guessed.** The static initialiser at `00166080` writes
`[02E405AC] &= ~2` and `[02E404B0] = vtable`; the difference is **exactly `0xFC`**, the field
`0063BC00` reads. Walking the RTTI at `vtable − 8` names the object
`Phyre::PClassDescriptorConcrete<Phyre::PWorldMatrix>`.

### Two of that document's own open questions fall out of the RTTI table

**`Q-5` — `Concrete<T>` versus `ForType<T>`.** Intersecting the distinct `T` of each template form:
**392 types have both, 0 have a leaf form without a `ForType<T>`**, 17 have only a `ForType`. The
zero is what makes it an answer rather than an impression: `ForType<T>` is the common base, and the
leaf form says how the type may be *constructed*.

**`Q-7` — are the RTTI classes and the reflected classes the same set? No, and neither contains the
other.** 409 types are reflected of 2,248 RTTI classes, and **only 114 of those 409 (27.9 %) carry
RTTI of their own.** The other 295 are plain structs — `CD3D11_BLEND_DESC`,
`Phyre::PAnimation::PAnimationChannel`. **Reflection here exists to serialise, not to dispatch**, and
that is a different idea from polymorphism.

### `00633240` has zero call sites and 703 tail jumps

`00633240` and `006332A0` are **byte-identical twins**, 93 bytes each, both installing the
`PClassDataMember` vtable. Their reachability is not identical at all:

| | `E8` | `E9` | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `00633240` | **0** | **703** | 703 |
| `006332A0` | 138 | 194 | 332 |

> **An `E8`-only reading finds `00633240` unreachable and the pair under-counted by two thirds.**
> Third time in this database that the `E9` instrument gave the only correct answer. Neither address
> — nor `0063BC00` — occurs as a raw qword anywhere in the image, against a control that does:
> `005C5230`, **2,527** occurrences. So none of the three is in a vtable.

### A number that matches, and was not promoted

`0063BC00` has **369** distinct callers. The RTTI names **331 + 38 = 369** instantiable descriptor
classes. The equality is exact.

> **It is filed as `DK-1`, unproven.** The confirming test failed: only **15 of the 369** callers
> carry an RTTI identity, all slot 10 of `WithoutDefaultConstructor<T>` — 15 of 38, not 38 of 38.
> **A coincidence in two counts is a lead, not a mechanism**, and writing it down as one would have
> been the cheapest wrong claim available today.

### A correction, and a near-miss that reading first prevented

**`2,134 RTTI classes` in §2 is superseded by 2,248** — and the difference is not growth. Comparing
the current `classes.tsv` against the `.pre-as9a` backup that produced the old figure: **only 573
names are common to both**, because the earlier demangler emitted fragments like
`$00$0BA::?$SeadObject` for roughly three quarters of the corpus. The old table was not smaller so
much as unusable as identities. The current one is corroborated by an independent hand-walk of the
RTTI from a vtable.

**The near-miss:** the document lists `00633240` beside a family count of `138`, and `006332A0` has
exactly **138** `E8` call sites. That looked like a number attached to the wrong address. **Reading
the table first showed the `138` is a count of functions carrying the
`PClassDataMember.DeletingDestructor` ledger tag — not callers of anything.** No error, and the
correction was never written.

## 2026-09-08 — The widget message protocol: 32 ids over 251 handlers

**Every menu, window, list, gauge and options row in FFXII is the same object answering numbered
messages, and nobody had enumerated the ids.** New tool `widget_messages.py`, new document
[the widget message protocol](../16-UI/Widget-Object-Model/the-widget-message-protocol.md), new side
file `widget-message-handlers.tsv`.

| | |
|---|---:|
| constructor call sites | **280** |
| handlers recovered from those sites | 276 (98.6 %) |
| distinct handlers, confirmed | 239 |
| distinct handlers, candidate only | 13 |
| **population** | **251** |
| decoded EXACTLY | **211** (84.1 %) |
| upper bound only — excluded from every count | 11 |
| unparsed — *not* "answers nothing" | 29 |
| **distinct message ids** | **32** |

### The distribution is the finding

**Ids 1 (97.6 % of handlers), 18 (65.4 %) and 2 (58.3 %) are answered by more than half the widgets
in the game.** Six more sit between 16 % and 30 %. Everything else is answered by fewer than one
widget in ten.

> That is the shape of a **lifecycle-plus-events** protocol, not a flat command set. A
> reimplementation needs the first nine ids to get anything on screen; the tail is per-widget.
> **Five of the 32 have a meaning** — 3, 4, 5 from the draw pass; 10, 12, 13 from the Config screen —
> and **all five were recovered elsewhere. This block named none of them**, and says so: *"18 is
> answered by two thirds of widgets so it is probably update"* is the guess the confidence
> vocabulary exists to prevent. `DL-1`.

### Three defects the controls caught, and the third is the instructive one

The decoder was checked against three handlers read **by hand two blocks ago for an unrelated
reason** — the Config screen's rows. That is the strongest kind of control available here: the
answers existed before the tool did.

**1. A linear scan cannot see a handler chosen on a backward branch.** `lea rdx, 0023B330` sits at
`0023C0CD` and jumps *back* to the constructor call at `0023BFFF`, so an address-order scan
attributes `0023B6F0` to that call and never sees `0023B330` at all. The fix reports every
code-address `lea` into a handler register inside a constructor-calling function as a **candidate**,
and `0023B330` is one. **Without it the tool scores two of three controls and looks fine.**

**2. Decoding either compiler shape alone reports a subset.** `0055CD40` tests `cmp eax, 0x11D / je`
for one outlier id and *then* falls into a 23-arm dense switch. The first version listed it as
answering exactly one message, id 285, when it answers 285 plus twelve of 1–23. Both decoders now run
and are unioned.

**3. A relaxed pattern produced a confident wrong answer, not a weaker one.** An early dense decoder
accepted a `cmp` followed by *any* `ja` within 120 instructions. It reported `0023B6F0` — five ids,
known by hand — as answering **ids 2 and 3**, because a distant unrelated `ja` bound to a `cmp` from
the middle of the chain.

> **This is the failure mode worth writing down.** Loosening a pattern to raise coverage does not
> yield a vaguer answer; it yields a precise wrong one, and nothing downstream can tell the
> difference. The fix was to require the whole shape — offset adjustment, bound check, `ja`, **and a
> resolvable jump table** — and to report a dense switch whose arms cannot be read as an **upper
> bound** excluded from every census, rather than as a list of ids.

An earlier run of that same loose decoder published a census with ids up to 53 answered by 9–14
handlers each. **Those were default arms of unresolved switch tables counted as live messages.** The
census in the document is the one produced after the shape was tightened.

### Denominators, deliberately kept apart

Confirmed handlers and candidates are separate columns. Exact, upper-bound and unparsed are separate
buckets, and **only the exact ones have a denominator**. 251 is a **floor**: a handler installed by
writing `[obj] = fn` directly, with no constructor call, would not appear in any of the three
buckets, and whether such handlers exist is unmeasured — `DL-2`.

## 2026-09-08 — The widget lifecycle, named: construct, reconcile, pre-destroy, destroy

**Four of the widget message ids are now named, and they are the four most universal.** Nine of 32
total. `DL-1` moves from OPEN to PARTLY ANSWERED; `DL-3` filed. Written up as §8–§10 of
[the widget message protocol](../16-UI/Widget-Object-Model/the-widget-message-protocol.md).

| id | share of handlers | sent by | meaning |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| **1** | **97.6 %** | `002465F0` at `00246748` | **construct** |
| **2** | 58.3 % | `00248030` | **generation reconcile** |
| **15** | 27.5 % | `00244F00` at `00244F34` | **about to be destroyed** — self only |
| **18** | **65.4 %** | `00245020`, then `002473B0` recursively | **being destroyed** — self and whole subtree |

**None was inferred from frequency.** The previous block refused to guess these precisely because
*"18 is answered by two thirds of widgets so it is probably update"* was available and worthless.
Each id here was read from the function that **sends** it.

### The two shares that differ, and why

15 reaches only the widget being destroyed; 18 is broadcast down the whole subtree by `002473B0`,
walking `+0x18` (first child) and `+0x20` (next sibling). **So two thirds of all widgets in the game
have something to undo when an ancestor goes away, and only a quarter need warning about their own
destruction.** The census shape was explained by the mechanism, not the other way round.

### A zero that could not be true

The sender scan, in its first form, matched only messages **built on the stack**. It reported
**zero senders for id 18** — a message 65.4 % of handlers answer. **"Nobody sends it" was never a
possible answer**, so the zero meant the instrument was wrong. The missing shape is the static
`.rdata` record — `00915058 = {15,0,0}`, `00915070 = {18,0,0}` — the same shape the draw pass
already used at `009151C0`. Adding it took the census from 118 sites / 37 ids to **163 sites /
49 ids**.

> **Fourth zero in this database that meant "wrong query", not "nothing there."**

### The framework / application boundary

Splitting senders by whether they live inside the widget core (`00244000`–`00249000`):

```
framework only  : 3, 5, 8, 9, 17, 18, 19, 24, 25
both            : 1, 2, 4, 12, 14, 15, 20, 23
application only: 0, 10, 13, 16, 26, 29-53, 61, 92, 95, 114, 119, 192, 285-289
```

**No id above 25 has a sender inside the widget core.** The low ids are the framework's own protocol;
everything above is defined by the game code using it. Id 16 is the most widely sent application
message — 20 sites in 20 distinct functions, all outside the core.

### The cleanest evidence available

`0057E8D0` and `0057EB30`, 117 bytes each, answer **only ids 1 and 18** and differ only in which
global they touch (`02CA99D0` / `02CA99D8`): publish `self` into a singleton on 1, null it on 18,
tail-jump to the default handler for everything else. **A singleton widget, and nothing else.** Two
independent handlers of identical shape is as close to a controlled experiment as static analysis
gets.

### Two cross-checks that landed on prior art

- `00247930(self, n)` writes `word [self+0x44] = n`. The widget-constructor document records `+0x44`'s
  low word being initialised to `0x64` = 100 — **this is the setter, and the handler above passes
  exactly 100.**
- Message 2's traversal syncs `+0x40` **bit 17** against the global `0208ED5C`; `002465F0` **seeds
  that same bit from that same global** at construction, which the same document records as *"bit
  `0x20000` from a global"*. `0x20000` is bit 17. **Two documents written for different reasons
  anchor the same bit to the same global.**

### Not claimed

Any **ordering guarantee**. `00244F00` sends 15 then calls teardown, which broadcasts 18 — on the path
it takes. It has a second path (`00244DD0`, 301 B, when `flags & 0x21 == 0x21`) that was not read.
`DL-3`.

## 2026-09-08 — The input name registry: 240 names recovered, and the #1 unexplained global explained

**`Button_Square`, `Button_X`, `Button_0` and `Button_LeftMB` are the same channel.** The game's
binding name space holds **143 names over 113 channels — 30 of them synonyms**, plus a separate
97-name keyboard registry. All 240 recovered from the image, **0 unrecovered**. New tool
`named_registry.py`, new document
[the input name registry](../15-Input/Input-Name-Registry/the-input-name-registry-and-channel-aliases.md).

### The block was picked by the index, again

`knowledge_db.py` was asked for the highest-connectivity undocumented callee, and `00879570` came
back: **132 bytes, 143 callers, tagged `FFXII.Input`, no document.** Its twin `00876C80` had 97.

### What they are

Byte-identical registry inserts for a string-keyed list with duplicate rejection — `0x11` for a null
key, `0x12` for a duplicate, push-front otherwise. The `strcmp` is **inlined** as
`movzx edx,[rax] / movzx ecx,[rax+r8]` with `r8 = key − n->name`, so **no string-function xref finds
it**. Every caller is a CRT static initialiser: `lea rcx, <node>` / `call` / register a destructor.

> **The list is not in the image; the registrations are.** Both heads are written once at startup —
> which is exactly why they sat at the top of the unexplained-globals table. **`02EB9D80` was rank
> #1** (1 writer, 148 readers) and **`02EB83B8` rank #3** (1 writer, 102 readers). Both are now
> explained: they are the two list heads.

RTTI at `vtable − 8` names the node types: `Phyre::PInputs::PInputChannelSemantic` (143) and
`Phyre::PInputs::PInputKeySemantic` (97). **The key registry is a strict subset of the channel
registry** — measured: names only in the key registry, **0**; names only in the channel registry,
**46**.

### The alias table

| value | names |
|---:|---|
| 11 | `Button_0` = `Button_LeftMB` = `Button_Square` = `Button_X` |
| 12 | `Button_1` = `Button_A` = `Button_Cross` = `Button_MiddleMB` |
| … | 16 groups in all; channels 11–26 are the sixteen pad buttons |

**Mouse buttons are not separate channels** — `LeftMB`/`MiddleMB`/`RightMB` are 11, 12, 13, the same
as Square/Cross/Circle.

### It answers half of an open question in another document

The keymap document asks what the *"1–3 and 11–27 bands"* are, and notes that
`PInputMouseButtonSemantic` and `PInputJoypadButtonSemantic` *"give conflicting values under one
record framing."*

> **They do not conflict — they are aliases in one channel space.** A framing that expects two
> disjoint tables must read a deliberate synonym as a contradiction. The 11–26 half is answered; the
> 1–3 band and 27 stay open as `DM-2`, now with a sharper statement: **no registered channel name
> carries a value in `1 … 10` or `27`.**

### A count corrected, and how the error was made

That document records the `PInputKeySemantic` member records as **95 × 32 B at `01F45700`, values
`123 … 29`**. The table is **97 records at `01F456C8`, values `123 … 28` plus `Empty = 0`**.

```
documented : 01F45700 .. 01F462C0   ->  95 records, 123 .. 29
actual     : 01F456C8 .. 01F462C8   ->  97 records, 123 .. 28  and  Empty = 0
missing    : Empty (0) low end, Key_A (28) high end
```

> **The span was anchored on the `value` field at node + 0x18 rather than the node base**, so it
> stopped one record short at each end. **Counting a table by subtracting two endpoint addresses
> fails silently by one at each end; enumerating its members counts them.** `Key_A`'s *name* was in
> that document's own string-run entry — only its record went uncounted.
>
> The field order was also wrong — `{typeRef, namePtr, next, value}`, not
> `{value, typeRef, namePtr, 0}` — and **nothing else in that document depends on it.** Its
> `keymapCode = semantic − 1` mapping, verified there 28 of 28, is untouched by either correction,
> and this block did **not** re-verify it.

### Deliberately not claimed

That the same `− 1` offset applies to the `Button_*` channels (`DM-3`) — the keymap document proved
it for keys only. That the alias groups stay merged downstream (`DM-1`). That 143 and 97 are complete
registries rather than complete sets of **static registrations found in the image**. And nothing
about analogue axes: every name recovered is a button or a key.

## 2026-09-08 — Third reconstruction: the first over a pointer structure

**`NameRegistry_Register` reimplemented and differential-tested against the shipped 132 bytes at
`00879570`.** `Reconstruction/Game/Input/name_registry.{h,c}`, harness
`Tests/Differential/diff_name_registry.py`.

```
cases                  : 154   (143 real nodes, 11 injected)
return codes           : OK x144, NULL_KEY x1, DUPLICATE x9
return-code mismatches : 0
resulting list         : reference 144 nodes, reconstruction 144 nodes, SAME ORDER
```

Goal 2 moves **2 → 3** implementations and **2 → 3** harnesses. Parity-certified stays **0**.

### Why this one, after two array-shaped tests

| test | what is compared |
|---|---|
| `field_music` | a **return value** |
| `quality_preset` | a **flat array**, over the game's own tables |
| `name_registry` | a **linked list** — after 154 insertions, every return code *and* the chain walked from the head |

Both sides are handed **the same image regions at the same virtual addresses** — the real 143-node
array out of `.data`, the real name strings out of `.rdata` — because the nodes reference each other
and their names by absolute address. At different bases they would not be receiving the same input.

### Real data alone would have been a weak test, and the suite says so

**Every registered name in the shipped image is distinct.** A suite built only from real nodes
**never once takes the duplicate path**, and would have reported parity on error handling it never
executed. The injected cases:

| injected | result | what it shows |
|---|---|---|
| re-register 8 nodes already inserted | `DUPLICATE` ×8 | the scan finds a node already in the list |
| a node whose name pointer is zero | `NULL_KEY` | the `0x11` path |
| a node whose name is a **copy** of `Button_R2` at a different address | `DUPLICATE` | **the comparison is a string comparison, not pointer identity** |
| a node with a name nothing else uses | `OK` | the insert still works after the failures |

> The reconstruction uses `strcmp` where the original inlines
> `movzx edx,[rax] / movzx ecx,[rax+r8]` with `r8 = key − name`. Reproducing the pointer-difference
> trick would be transcription; it would also make the reconstruction wrong the moment the
> comparison stopped being a `strcmp`. **The copied-name case proves the equivalence instead of
> assuming it** — and it is the only case in the suite that can.

The harness **fails** if either error path went unexecuted, rather than printing a green result over
an untested branch.

### A reporting bug in the harness, caught by its own census

The first run printed `re-register -> OK` for all eight re-registrations, directly beneath a census
reading `DUPLICATE x9`. **The census was right and the line under it was wrong**: the display used
`cases.index(node)`, which finds the *first* occurrence — the original registration — not the
re-registration. Fixed to take the last occurrence.

> Worth recording because the numbers disagreed with the prose **in the same block of output**, and
> the prose was the part a reader would have quoted.

### Readiness, and what did not move

`15-Input/Input-Name-Registry` moves to **`DIFFERENTIAL TESTED`**. It is a **one-operation subsystem**,
so unlike `CONTRACT-game-setting-config` — where one tested operation of five left the readiness
deliberately unmoved — there is no larger surface being over-promised here.

**`INTEGRATION` is still not covered.** The real registration order is the **CRT initialiser order**,
which this test does not know and does not claim; both sides are simply given the same shuffled
order. Nothing here shows the shipped list comes out in any particular arrangement.

## 2026-09-08 — Track C: the type store goes from 2 types to 181, and the game-type gap stays visible

**`PROGRAM-STATE` names track C (type reconstruction) as one of two critical paths, and the type
store held two types.** 682 member records over 179 classes had been recovered into
`22-Middleware-PhyreEngine/.../phyre-field-schema.tsv` and never wired into `_types/`. New tool
`types_import_phyre.py`, new [`_types/README.md`](../_types/README.md).

```
types  :   2 ->  181     (2 hand-read + 179 imported)
fields :  81 ->  694     (81 hand-read + 613 imported)
validate: 0 errors, 8 gaps - all 8 in the two hand-read types
```

### The derivation I set out to use is unsound, and the tool proves it every run

The obvious way to get sizes from a table of `(offset, type name)` is
`size[i] = offset[i+1] − offset[i]`. The first version of the importer did exactly that and produced
a table of "stable" engine-type sizes.

**Then the cross-check killed it.** Take only members whose C type is a genuine primitive, so the
true size is known independently, and compare it against the delta:

```
tested                        : 245
delta == the primitive's size : 202  (82.4 %)
delta >  the primitive's size :  43  (17.6 %)
```

> **A sixth of the time the next recovered member is not the next member.** The reflection table is a
> *sample* of each class's members, so a delta measures "distance to the next member anybody
> recovered" — not a size. The first version reported
> `sce::Vectormath::…::VVector3` as a stable 16 bytes; it shows deltas of **16, 32 and 36**, and
> `VPString` shows **8, 24 and 88**. Modal-voting would have produced confident wrong sizes for
> exactly the engine types that have no other evidence.
>
> **Sizes now come from the C primitive table or stay `UNRESOLVED`.** 344 of 613 members (56.1 %)
> have one. Byte coverage: **1,201 of 30,578 (3.9 %)** — a floor, since every engine-typed member
> counts as zero, and the honest reason these are `SIGNATURE RESOLVED` rather than `TYPE RESOLVED`.

### A silent merge that passed validation

The grouping key is the leaf class name. **A template container has one leaf name and many
instantiations**, so `PArray` merged **60** distinct full class names into one row and `PSharray`
merged **9**.

> Their members sit at the same offsets in every instantiation, so the merge produced **no overlap
> and the validator reported nothing**. A silent merge that passes validation is exactly the kind
> that survives. Both are now imported at `CLASSIFIED` with an evidence column that opens
> `MERGED LEAF NAME: N distinct full class names share it ... this row is NOT one struct.`
> **177 of 179 are unambiguous** — the point is that the number is stated, not that it is small.

### Two tools had to change, and the second change was the important one

**`types_index.py`** could not parse `size = UNRESOLVED` — it crashed. A store that cannot record an
unknown size forces a guess, which is backwards. It now treats a non-numeric size as "no declared
size" and skips the checks that need one. It also takes **readiness into account**: a type at
`SIGNATURE RESOLVED` or below is sample-derived and its gaps are expected, so they are not warned
about. **The two hand-read types still show all 8 of their gaps**, including a 1,476-byte tail on
`ActorStorageRecord` — which is the whole point, since 179 imported types would otherwise have
buried them.

**`program_coverage.py` labelled its metric "game types in the `_types/` store".** After the import
that row would have read **181**, reporting a ninety-fold jump in precisely the number the charter's
L2 gap is about. It now counts engine and game types apart:

```
GAME types in the _types/ store          :   2
engine / middleware types in the store   : 179
fields recorded / of those named         : 694 / 660
   of those, fields on a GAME type       :  81
```

> **The import moved the engine number and left the game number exactly where it was.** That is the
> correct outcome and it is why the metric had to be split before the import could be reported at
> all: a coverage number that silently changes meaning is worse than one that stays small.

## 2026-09-08 — The actor record's tail: what a static scan can see, measured

Last block ended on the program's clearest number: **GAME types in the type store = 2.** This block
went at the larger of the two — `ActorStorageRecord`, up to 1,760 bytes with **1,476 of them
undeclared** — and the result is mostly a measurement of how far a static instrument reaches.
New tool `actor_field_scan.py`, new side file
[`actor-record-offsets-observed.tsv`](../04-Actor-Entity/Actor-Storage-Record/actor-record-offsets-observed.tsv).

### The anchor

`+0x03` is a proven discriminator — `(kind << 5) | (sequence & 0x1F)` — so a kind decode is
unmistakable: `movzx eax, byte [reg+3]` followed by `shr eax, 5` or `and eax, 0x1F`. **55 functions
contain it**, and in each the register held an actor pointer at that instant. Enumerating
`[thatreg + disp]` in those functions yields **70 distinct offsets**.

| | |
|---|---|
| recall against the 41 offsets the constructor proves | **41 of 41 (100 %)** |
| precision inside `0x000`–`0x118` | **41 of 62 (66.1 %)** — a **floor**, since the constructor's set is not a complete layout either |
| offsets found beyond `0x118`, in the 1,476-byte tail | **8** |

### The first instrument was abandoned because its own control condemned it

A linear forward **taint** was written first — mark the register at the decode, follow it, drop it on
a write or a clobbering call. It recovered **4 of 41 known offsets, 9.8 %.**

> **Not weak — useless**, and the control said so before one new offset was published. An actor
> pointer is copied and reloaded constantly; a taint that dies at the first reload cannot see the
> accesses that matter. Narrowing the call-clobber to the x64 volatile set changed nothing. It was
> replaced with something deliberately cruder — every access on the same register anywhere in the
> same function — whose cost is stated as precision rather than hidden.

### The type store falsified half the promotions, immediately

Six offsets were seen through **two or more independent functions** and promoted. `types_index.py`
returned **3 errors**:

```
ERROR  ActorStorageRecord 0x044 overlaps the previous field   (0x040, 8 B)
ERROR  ActorStorageRecord 0x05C overlaps the previous field   (0x058, 8 B)
ERROR  ActorStorageRecord 0x107 overlaps the previous field   (0x106, 2 B)
```

> **They are not new fields — they are proof the constructor-derived sizes are too coarse.** A single
> `mov qword ptr [rec+0x40], 0` proves those eight bytes are *zeroed*; it does not prove they are
> *one field*. Actor code reading a dword at `+0x044` proves a boundary inside it.
>
> The three declared fields were **narrowed** to the extent the zeroing store actually justifies,
> rather than the observations being forced in beside them. Two of the three now leave a visible gap
> behind them, which is the correct outcome. Store back to **0 errors**, 700 fields.

**Adding six rows produced three corrections to rows that were already there.** That is the type
store earning its validator.

### The honest conclusion, which is the point of the block

**Eight observed offsets across 1,476 bytes is close to nothing, and that is the finding.** The
kind-decode anchor reaches the header and stops: the systems that own the tail already hold a typed
actor pointer and never re-derive the kind. Recovering it needs a different instrument — following
the pointer through its owning systems, or **runtime observation of a live record**. `DN-1`.

Three offsets were promoted (`+0x068`, `+0x0C0` — an 8-byte pointer read by 3 functions — and
`+0x0E8`), all at `PROBABLE`, none in the tail. **`ActorStorageRecord`'s declared coverage moved from
`0x11C` to `0x11C`.** The tail is exactly as undeclared as it was; what changed is that the database
now knows *why*, and by how much a static anchor falls short.

## 2026-09-08 — The widget contract, and the reconstruction that corrected it twice

**Third behavioural contract, for the subsystem three separate blocks went into.**
[`CONTRACT-widget-object.md`](../16-UI/Widget-Object-Model/CONTRACT-widget-object.md), `subsystem`
scope, ten operations, `CONTRACT READY`. Then §12's reproduction formula was implemented and tested
in the same block, which is the only way to find out whether a contract is actually implementable.

```
cases                     : 320   (20 real object sizes x 16 environment combinations)
header bytes compared     : 192 per case
  non-zero in the densest : 20    (so 172 of 192 must stay ZERO)
mismatches                : 0
```

Goal 2 moves **3 → 4** implementations and harnesses. Parity-certified stays **0**.

### Sparseness is a test dimension the other three harnesses cannot reach

`field_music` compares a return value, `quality_preset` a 31-int array, `name_registry` a linked
list. **None of them can catch a spurious write.** Here only 20 of 192 header bytes are non-zero, so
a reconstruction that wrote one stray byte anywhere in `0x00..0xC0` fails — and passes every other
harness in the tree.

### Writing the reconstruction corrected the contract twice, immediately

- **`+0x40` bit 14 is not merely cleared.** `002466D1` clears `0x4000`, then `002466F2` ORs back
  `(pooled & 1) << 14` from the **fifth argument**. Bit 14 means *"this object came out of the fixed
  112-slot pool"*. The contract had recorded only the clear.
- **The construct message carries both payload qwords**, not just one: `00246726` reads `[rsi+8]`
  and `0024672F` reads `[rsi+0x10]`. The contract said `msg->b` was the caller's argument.

> **Both were written into the contract from a careful read, and both were wrong until something
> had to execute them.** That is the argument for testing a contract in the block that writes it.

### A stub that broke the ABI, and the zero it produced

The first run returned **192 zero bytes on the reference side** — which reads like *"the constructor
writes nothing"*.

> The `memset` stub used `rep stosb` without saving `rdi`. **`rdi` is callee-saved in MS x64, and
> the constructor does `mov rdi, rcx` *before* calling memset and then uses `rdi` for every header
> store.** So every write landed at `obj + size`. **A stub must honour the calling convention of the
> function it replaces**, and a stub that does not can produce a clean, plausible, entirely wrong
> answer. Fifth zero in this database that meant "wrong instrument".

A second failure was more honest about itself: `Invalid memory fetch at 005C5230` — the **default
handler**, which the constructor substitutes for a NULL proc. The null-proc path is real and taken,
and forgetting to stub it is what proved it.

### Readiness deliberately unmoved

`CONTRACT READY` stays. §2 lists **ten** operations and **one** is tested; §13 is still empty.
Promoting the subsystem on the strength of its header writer is exactly the overstatement the ladder
exists to prevent — the same call made for `CONTRACT-game-setting-config` and for the same reason.

**Not tested:** everything past `+0xC0` (objects run to `0xBC08` and their procs write the rest), the
destroy broadcast (needs a real tree), and the construct message itself.

handler == table[+0x00] at 01EED720+0x20*id: 1,224 agree, 0 disagree

## 2026-09-08 — 1,158 unread verb handlers become one shape and a remainder

Last block produced a frontier: **1,158 of 1,224 script verbs have a native handler no document
cites.** Reading them one at a time is not a plan. `script_verb_shapes.py` classifies the whole
population instead. New document:
[the shape of the verb population](../01-Script-VM-Native-Bridge/Verb-Dispatch/the-shape-of-the-verb-population.md).

```
1,224 verbs -> 1,166 distinct handlers

  CONST         1   0.1 %      no call, no jump, no memory
  TAILJUMP    141  12.1 %      one unconditional jmp
  CALL1       402  34.5 %      exactly one direct call
  LINEAR      449  38.5 %      several calls, still no branching
  BRANCHING   173  14.8 %      has control flow of its own
  unclassified  0
```

**993 of 1,166 handlers (85.2 %) contain no conditional branch at all** — their whole behaviour is
the call chain, readable in one pass. Disposition **B** for 85 % of the script bridge, by a rule
anyone can re-run. The 173 that branch are disposition **D**, and the census's real value is that it
**names them** rather than leaving 1,158 in a blob.

### The first taxonomy was wrong and its own numbers said so

A first cut used call and jump counts and dropped **53 % into `OTHER`** — including `setvelr` and
`sin`, plainly straight-line wrappers with two calls each.

> **A taxonomy that cannot classify half its population is measuring the taxonomy, not the
> population.** Recutting on *"does it branch at all"* took `OTHER` from **621 to 0**.

### Where the wrappers go

Of the **583** verbs whose handler is a single call or a bare tail-jump, **240 (41.2 %) funnel into
one function**, `00267E10`, and 38 more into `00267DB0`. The top ten targets absorb **333 of 583
(57.1 %)**.

`00267E10` and `00267DB0` are the typed argument-pop helpers — **prior art**, documented in two
existing script-bridge pages. What is new is the distribution.

> *"240 of 583 single-call verb handlers are nothing but an integer argument pop"* is a statement
> about the whole population that no per-function document could make. **The helpers were already
> known; nobody had counted how much of the bridge is just them.**

The dispatch record is 32 bytes and holds **three** code pointers — begin `+0x00`, poll `+0x08`,
result `+0x10`. **The import that adopted this table yesterday took only the first**, leaving 261
mappings unread in a file the database had just accepted:

```
poll   +0x08 : 122 non-null of 1,224;  121 in .text on a function entry
result +0x10 : 139 non-null of 1,224;  138 in .text on a function entry
```

Both exceptions are on call id `05D7`, the last record in the extent, and hold `FFFFFFFF`. **Written
as `SENTINEL` rather than dropped.** The table now carries all three columns; the 261 poll and result

> **Adopting a file is not the same as reading it.** The verification last block was real and its

## 2026-09-08 — The contradiction ledger, and what it says about our own instruments

**`DJ-2`, filed as "the single biggest schema gap", is closed.** Charter §7 requires the knowledge to
answer *"all contradictions involving a subsystem"*, and until now the corrections lived only as
prose and strikethrough. New tool `contradiction_index.py`, new
[`CONTRADICTION-LEDGER.md`](CONTRADICTION-LEDGER.md), new `_index/CONTRADICTIONS.tsv`.

```
117 of 219 documents contain a correction marker
251 strikethrough spans
 33 DATED correction headers of the five tracked kinds  ->  33 ledger records
```

Supported §7 queries **17 → 19 of 24**; unsupported **5 → 4**.

### 33, not 165

An early grep counted 165 by including `ANSWERED 20…`. **Answering a question is not overturning a
claim.** The ledger tracks `CORRECTED`, `RETRACTED`, `SUPERSEDED`, `WITHDRAWN`, `OVERTURNED` and
nothing else, and the number moved by a factor of five when the pattern was tightened.

### What is mechanical and what is not

Document, line, kind, date and any addresses on the line are extracted with **no judgement**, and
refilled on every re-run. **`claim`, `correction` and `instrument` are hand-written**, never
overwritten by the tool, and read `UNSUMMARISED` until someone writes them.

> **A summary produced by a regex would be a fabrication with a citation attached.** All 33 were
> summarised by reading the site.

The audit log is **excluded** — it is the narrative, the documents hold the claims — so corrections
that live only there are a known, deliberate gap.

### The database's own history validates its own rules

Counting the **instrument** rather than the subject:

```
recount                   3     no-reader-found          3
assumed-single-instance   3     E8-only-reachability     3
wrong-name-table          2     premise-wrong            2     misread-field  2
...17 more, one each
```

> **`E8-only-reachability` is tied for the most frequent cause of a wrong answer** — three
> corrections in three different categories, all from asking *"who calls this"* with one instrument:
> a function with no caller but a base-relocation-certified pointer; a gil counter that missed three
> callers reaching it through a five-byte thunk; a census where **a thunk is a sink in the call
> graph**.
>
> The mission prompt's four-instrument rule was written from experience. **It is now measured**, and
> the measurement says it is load-bearing rather than cautious.
>
> Two more of the top four are the same mistake in different dress: `assumed-single-instance` — one
> map where a class argument selects five bases, one thread where nine procedures exist — and
> `no-reader-found`, three rows of *"nothing reads this"*, all wrong. **"I could not find one" is not
> "there is not one", and between them those two account for 6 of 33 corrections.**

### Deliberately not claimed

That 33 is the number of times this database has been wrong. It is the number of **dated correction
headers in documents**. Undated corrections, audit-log-only corrections, and claims quietly rewritten
are all invisible to the extractor — and a category with more corrections is not less reliable;
`99-Unresolved-Residual` leads partly because it is where the hardest questions are sent.
